There has never been one who did not follow these principles.
Chapter Thirteen: Reversing the Norm
Chapter Thirteen: Reversing the Norm
Your servant has heard that the downfall of the Three Dynasties
was not due to the law itself;
rather, the controllers of the law were not the right people.
Therefore, understanding the law
is [to understand] the traces left by the former kings;
if it is not the right person,
the Dao will not be practiced in vain.
Therefore, Yǐn Wén Zǐ said:
"Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music,
titles, laws, punishments, and rewards,
these eight,
are the techniques used by the Five Emperors and Three Kings to govern the world."
Therefore, benevolence
is what is used to broadly bestow upon things,
and also what produces bias and selfishness.
This is the reverse of benevolence.
Commentary says:
According to ritual,
family benevolence should not extend to the state,
and high officials should not collect public benefits.
Confucius said:
"The Son of Heaven loves the world,
and the feudal lords love their territories;
Not being able to exceed in loving someone,
is detesting private favors."
Therefore, understanding the biased benevolence,
the ruler detests it.
Righteousness is
that by which moral integrity is established and conduct is carried out,
it is also that by which flowery falseness is achieved.
It is the opposite of righteousness.
Discussion says:
To lose oneself in the pursuit of serving the country,
to face a great juncture and not be swayed,
this is true righteousness.
Like Yú Qīng, the chancellor of Zhao,
abandoning the position of chancellor and forsaking the ruler,
in order to assist in the crisis of Wei and Qi;
or Wú Jì, Lord Xinling,
stealing tallies and forging orders,
in order to respond to the urgent situation of Lord Pingyuan.
The righteousness of betraying the public for the sake of one's party is achieved,
while the integrity of guarding one's duty and serving one's superior is abandoned.
Therefore, Lord Máo criticized Wú Jì, saying:
"To Zhao, there has been accomplishment,
but to Wei, it is not considered satisfactory."
All such cases as these
are flowery falsehoods.
Ritual is
that by which respect and carefulness are carried out,
it is also that by which laziness and negligence are produced.
It is contrary to propriety.
The discussion says:
During the Hàn 漢 dynasty, they wanted to establish rites,
Emperor Wén 文 said:
"Elaborate rites and adorned appearances
are of no benefit to propriety;
personal transformation is what is acceptable."
Therefore, he abolished them.
Guō Jiā 郭嘉 said to Cáo Gōng 曹公:
"Yuán Shào 袁紹 is elaborate in rites and abundant in ceremonies;
you, sir, embrace naturalness and ease.
This is how you will achieve victory."
Strict adherence to hardship is difficult to maintain,
therefore, it breeds laziness and negligence. Music is
what harmonizes emotions and aspirations,
and it is also what breeds licentiousness and abandon.
It is contrary to music.
The *Yuè* 《樂》 ("Music") book says:
"The music of Zhèng 鄭 and Wèi 衛
is the music of chaotic times;
the music of Sāng Jiān 桑間 and Pú Shàng 濮上
is the music of a destroyed nation."
Therefore, Yán Ān 嚴安 said:
"Beautiful and extraordinary rarities
accordingly please the ears and eyes.
Therefore, indulgence in nourishment leads to excess;
indulgence in music leads to licentiousness;
loss of propriety leads to ornamentation;
loss of teaching leads to hypocrisy.
Hypocrisy, ornamentation, licentiousness, and excess
are not the way to guide people." Reputation is
what rectifies hierarchy,
and it is also what breeds arrogance and usurpation.
It is contrary to reputation.
this is the behavior of a criminal.
Therefore, the superior man prohibits it.
Zheng Lun 第十六 (Correct Discourses, Section Sixteen)
Zheng Lun 第十六 (Correct Discourses, Section Sixteen)
Confucius said:
"The Six Arts are unified in principle.
*Lǐ* (rites/etiquette) regulates people,
*Yuè* (music) expresses harmony,
*Shū* (writings/documents) guides affairs,
*Shī* (poetry) conveys intent,
*Yì* (changes) explains transformation,
*Chūnqiū* (spring and autumn annals) explains righteousness."
Sīmǎ Tán 司馬談 said:
"*Yì* (changes) records Heaven, Earth, *yīnyáng* 陰陽 (yin and yang), the four seasons, and the five elements.
therefore it excels at transformation;
*Lǐ* (禮) [Rites] manages human relations,
therefore it excels at conduct;
*Shū* (書) [Documents] records the affairs of the former kings,
therefore it excels at governance;
*Shī* (詩) [Poetry] records mountains, rivers, valleys, birds, beasts, grass, trees, females and males,
therefore it excels at portraying customs;
*Yuè* (樂) [Music] is that by which one is established,
therefore it excels at harmony;
*Chūnqiū* (春秋) [Spring and Autumn Annals] distinguishes right and wrong,
therefore it excels at governing people."
Therefore, it is said:
enter their country,
His teachings can be known.
In his conduct,
he is gentle and sincere,
this is the teaching of the *Book of Poetry* ["Shī"];
knowledgeable and far-sighted,
this is the teaching of the *Book of Documents* ["Shū"];
broad, magnanimous and kind,
this is the teaching of *Music* ["Yuè"];
pure, tranquil, refined and subtle,
this is the teaching of the *Book of Changes* ["Yì"];
respectful, frugal, dignified and reverent,
this is the teaching of *Rituals* ["Lǐ"];
arranging words and comparing events,
this is the teaching of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* ["Chūnqiū"].
Therefore, the fault of the *Book of Poetry* is foolishness,
the fault of the *Book of Documents* is deception,
the fault of *Music* is extravagance,
the fault of the *Book of Changes* is treachery,
the fault of *Rituals* is excessive formality,
the fault of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is disorder.
In his conduct,
he is gentle and sincere without being foolish,
then he has deeply understood the *Book of Poetry*.
Zǐ Xià said:
"When sounds become patterned, they are called music.
The music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
and its government is harmonious;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
When the government is aberrant;
the music of a fallen state is mournful and longing,
the people are in distress.
Therefore, to rectify gains and losses,
to move Heaven and Earth,
to influence ghosts and spirits,
nothing is closer than the *Book of Poetry*."
The Grand Historian said:
"The *Greater Odes* speak of kings, dukes, and great men,
and their virtue extends to the common people;
the *Lesser Odes* criticize their own gains and losses,
and their influence reaches those above.
Although what is said is different,
their harmony of virtue is one and the same."
During the Jìn dynasty, when the royal government declined,
Lǔ Bāo of Nányáng wrote "On the Spirit of Money,"
and Cài Hóng of Wú Commandery composed "Isolated Resentment."
Former histories consider the music of a chaotic era to be resentful and angry,
their government is aberrant.
This is what is meant by that.
To be familiar with affairs, understand the distant, and not deceive,
then one is deeply versed in the *Book of Documents*.
The *Book of Documents* records the ways of emperors and kings,
the documents of model rules, instructions, proclamations, and oaths,
and the three thousand disciples
all received its meanings.
To be broad and learned, easygoing and virtuous, without being extravagant,
then one is deeply versed in the *Book of Music*.
The *Yuè*
(Book of Music) says:
"Generally, music
arises from the human heart.
they are expressed in sound.
Sound that becomes patterned is called music.
Therefore, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
and its government is harmonious;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
and its government is perverse;
the music of a dying state is mournful and longing,
and its people are distressed.
The principles of music
are interconnected with governance.
*Gōng* is the ruler,
*shāng* is the minister,
*jué* is the people,
*zhǐ* is affairs,
*yǔ* is things.
If these five are not in disorder,
then there will be no discordant sounds.
If *gōng* is in disorder, then it is dissolute,
and its ruler is arrogant;
if *shāng* is in disorder, then it is beaten,
and its ministers are corrupt;
if *jué* is in disorder, then there is sorrow,
and its people are resentful;
if *zhǐ* is in disorder, then there is grief,
Diligence in their affairs;
if yǔ (羽) is disordered, there is danger;
their resources are depleted.
If all five are disordered,
mutually encroaching upon each other in turn,
this is called negligence.
If it is like this,
the day of the state's destruction is not far off.
Now, the enlightened kings of high antiquity who promoted music,
did not do so to amuse the mind and indulge the will,
but to invigorate the blood vessels,
circulate the spirit,
and harmonize and rectify the mind.
Therefore, the gōng (宮) sound moves the spleen and harmonizes and rectifies trust;
the shāng (商) sound moves the lungs and harmonizes and rectifies righteousness;
the jué (角) sound moves the liver and harmonizes and rectifies benevolence;
the zhǐ (徵) sound moves the heart and harmonizes and rectifies ritual;
the yǔ (羽) sound moves the kidneys and harmonizes and rectifies wisdom.
Therefore, hearing the gōng (宮) sound,
causes people to be gentle, relaxed, and magnanimous;
hearing the shāng (商) sound,
causes people to be upright and fond of righteousness;
hearing the jué (角) sound,
causes people to be compassionate and loving;
hearing the zhǐ (徵) sound,
causes people to delight in goodness and be fond of giving;
hearing the yǔ (羽) sound,
causes people to be orderly and fond of ritual.
Now, propriety enters from the outside,
while music emerges from within.
Therefore, the sage kings caused people's ears to hear the sounds of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng" hymns,
their eyes to see the ceremonial rites of dignified demeanor,
their feet to perform the appearance of respectful reverence,
and their mouths to speak the Way of benevolence and righteousness.
Thus, the *jūnzǐ* can speak all day, and wickedness has no way to enter."
Bān Gù 班固 said:
"Music
is what sages delight in,
and it can improve people's hearts;
its influence on people is profound.
Therefore, the former kings instilled their teachings through it.
People possess the nature of blood, *qì* (vital energy), heart, and intelligence,
but do not have constant states of sorrow, joy, liking, or anger.
They respond to stimuli and then move,
and then their minds and dispositions take shape.
Therefore, when the subtle and melancholy sounds are produced,
the people think of sorrow;
when the clear, harmonious, and leisurely sounds are produced,
the people are peaceful and happy;
when the coarse, fierce, and vigorous sounds are produced,
the people are resolute;
when the incorruptible, upright, correct, and sincere sounds are produced,
the people are solemn and respectful;
when the generous, harmonious, and compliant sounds are produced,
the people are kind and loving;
when the debauched, deviant, and dissolute sounds are produced,
And the people were dissolute and disorderly.
The former kings were ashamed of this disorder,
therefore they established the sounds of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng" hymns.
Rooted in emotions and nature,
based on measurements and numbers,
regulated by ritual and righteousness,
harmonizing the concord of vital energy,
guiding the practice of the Five Constants,
making it so that yang does not scatter,
yin does not accumulate,
forceful qi does not become angry,
gentle qi does not become fearful,
the four emotions flow freely within,
and manifest externally.
Sufficient to move the good heart of people,
and not allow evil qi to make contact.
"This is the method by which the former kings established music."
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"When a state is destroyed and people are killed,
it is not that there is no music,
but its music is not joyous.
A drowning person
does not not laugh;
a criminal
does not not sing;
a madman
does not not dance.
The music of a chaotic age
resembles this."
Fàn Yè said:
"Now, bells and drums
are not the essence of music,
but the instruments cannot be dispensed with.
The three sacrificial animals
are not the essence of filial piety,
but nurturing cannot be abandoned.
To preserve the instruments but lose the essence
is a failing of music.
To harmonize the qi with harmonious sounds
is the flourishing of music.
To emphasize nurturing to the detriment of conduct
is a burden on filial piety.
To practice filial piety in order to provide nurture
is the greatness of filial piety."
It is argued:
The east, associated with the note *jiǎo*, governs benevolence;
the south, associated with the note *zhēng*, governs propriety;
the center, associated with the note *gōng*, governs trustworthiness;
the west, associated with the note *shāng*, governs righteousness;
the north, associated with the note *yǔ*, governs wisdom.
This is the constant principle.
Now, the Grand Historian *Tài Shǐgōng* believes that:
the *zhǐ* mode moves the heart and harmonizes and rectifies wisdom;
the *yǔ* mode moves the kidneys and harmonizes and rectifies propriety.
Thus, to have the *zhǐ* mode govern wisdom,
and the *yǔ* mode govern propriety,
is remarkably different from the old rules.
Therefore, it is not something that a junior scholar can fully comprehend.
To be pure, clean, refined, and subtle without being harmful
is to be profound in the *Yì* (Book of Changes).
The subtlety of the *Yì*
is that love and hate attack each other,
distance and closeness are taken into account,
thus it cannot accommodate everyone,
and comes close to harming them.
To be respectful, frugal, solemn, and reverent without being tiresome
is to be profound in *Lǐ* (rites/propriety).
The Grand Historian *Tài Shǐgōng* said:
"I went to the *Dàxíng* Ritual Official
and observed the additions and subtractions of the Three Dynasties,
and then I knew that rituals were made based on human feelings,
and ceremonies were created based on human nature.
The way of humanity
encompasses myriad rules and regulations,
all-pervading.
It entices progress through rén yì (benevolence and righteousness),
and restrains with punishments.
Therefore, those with profound virtue attain high positions,
and those with great emolument enjoy favor and glory.
This is how the entire realm is unified and the myriad people are regulated.
The human body finds comfort in riding,
so golden carriages and adorned yokes are made to enhance its splendor.
The eye appreciates five colors,
so elaborate embroidery and patterns are created to express its ability.
The ear delights in bells and chimes,
so harmonious octaves are tuned to soothe its mind.
The mouth savors five flavors,
so abundant delicacies and choice salted meats are prepared to satisfy its palate.
The heart cherishes treasures and goodness,
so jade and precious stones are carved and polished to convey its sentiments.
Therefore, the grand carriage has only rush mats,
the leather cap and linen skirt are simple,
the red strings [of the instrument] are played plainly,
the great broth is unseasoned and the drink is water,
to guard against extravagance
and remedy its excesses.
Thus, the order of ruler and ministers, court officials, the honored and the humble, the noble and the base,
down to the common people, carriages, clothing, palaces, dwellings, food, drink, weddings, funerals, and sacrifices,
all matters have their proper appropriateness,
and all things have their appropriate regulations.
When the Zhōu 周 dynasty declined,
ritual and music were abandoned,
the high and low transgressed against each other.
The family of Guǎn Zhòng 管仲,
came to possess three returning concubines.
Those who adhered to the law and upheld righteousness
were insulted by the world;
those who were extravagant, excessive, and presumptuous
were considered glorious and honorable.
Even the most outstanding disciple of Zǐxià's 子夏 school
said,
"When I go out and see powdered faces and magnificent finery, I am delighted;
when I come in and hear the Master's Way, I am joyful;
these two contend in my heart,
and I cannot decide."
How much more so those of average ability and below,
gradually steeped in improper teachings,
and influenced by prevailing customs?
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 had to rectify names in Wèi 衛;
the place where he resided was not in harmony.
How lamentable it is!"
Bān Gù 班固 said:
"Humans contain the qi of heaven and earth, yin and yang,
and possess emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.
Heaven bestows these natures without moderation,
and sages can regulate them,
but cannot eliminate them.
Therefore, they imitated heaven and earth to create ritual and music,
Therefore, it is through them that we communicate with the spirits, establish human relationships, rectify emotions, and regulate all affairs.
Human nature has the affections of male and female and
the distinction of jealousy,
therefore the rites of marriage were established.
There is the order of interaction between seniors and juniors,
therefore the rites of village drinking were established.
There are the emotions of sorrow for the dead and longing for the distant,
therefore the rites of mourning and sacrifice were established.
There is the heart of respecting and revering superiors,
therefore the rites of court audience and visitation were established.
In sorrow, there are regulated expressions of weeping and leaping;
in joy, there are appropriate manners of singing and dancing.
The upright man is sufficient to express his sincerity,
and the wicked man is restrained from his errors.
Therefore, if the rites of marriage are abandoned,
then the Way of husband and wife will be difficult,
and the sins of licentiousness will increase.
If the rites of village drinking are abandoned,
then the order of seniors and juniors will be chaotic,
and the litigations of contention and strife will be troublesome.
If the rites of mourning and sacrifice are abandoned,
then the kindness between flesh and blood will be thin,
and those who betray their lord and forget their origins will be numerous.
If the rites of court audience and visitation are abandoned,
then the positions of ruler and subject will be lost,
and the gradual rise of encroachment will begin.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"To pacify those above and govern the people,
Nothing is better than ritual;
in changing customs and altering habits,
nothing is better than music.
To govern the world through yielding and deference,
this is what ritual and music are about.”
To connect words and compare events without confusion
is to be deeply versed in the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
Hú Suí said:
"In the past, why did Kǒngzǐ compose the *Chūnqiū*?"
The Grand Historian said:
"I heard Dǒng Shēng say:
'Because the ways of the Zhōu dynasty declined,
Kǒngzǐ became the Minister of Justice of Lǔ;
the feudal lords harmed him,
the high officials obstructed him.
Kǒngzǐ knew that his words would not be heeded
and his Way would not be practiced,
so he made judgments on the two hundred and forty-two years,
to serve as a model for the world,
to censure the Son of Heaven,
to demote the feudal lords,
to punish the high officials,
in order to achieve the affairs of the king.'"
Confucius said:
"I desire to record it in empty words;
it is not as good as seeing it in the deep, incisive, and clear account of events."
The *Chūnqiū*
above clarifies the Way of the Three Kings,
Judging affairs,
distinguishing suspicions,
clarifying right and wrong,
resolving hesitations,
praising good and condemning evil,
honoring the worthy and despising the unworthy,
preserving endangered states,
continuing extinguished dynasties,
mending flaws and reviving abandoned practices—
these are the greatest aspects of the Way of the King.
Reversing chaos and disorder,
and returning it to the correct path,
nothing is closer to this than the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
Within the *Chūnqiū*,
there were thirty-six instances of regicide,
fifty-two instances of state destruction,
and the number of lords who fled and were unable to protect their altars of soil and grain
is countless.
Examining the reasons for this,
all were due to losing their fundamental principles."
Hú Zhú said:
"At the time of Kǒngzǐ,
there was no enlightened ruler above,
and he was unable to be employed below,
therefore he wrote the *Chūnqiū*,
leaving behind empty words to judge ritual propriety and justice,
serving as the law of a single king.
Now, sir, you have encountered an enlightened emperor above,
"To merely stay within one's duties,
as the Master discussed,
what are you trying to clarify by that?"
Grand Scribe Sima Qian said:
"Fúxī was supremely pure and kind,
and created the Eight Trigrams of the *Book of Changes*.
The flourishing reigns of Yáo and Shùn
are recorded in the *Book of Documents*,
where rites and music originated.
The grandeur of Tāng and Wǔ
was sung by poets.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* selected the good and condemned the evil,
promoted the virtues of the Three Dynasties,
and praised the House of Zhōu,
not merely engaging in criticism and satire.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
down to the enlightened Son of Heaven,
receiving the Mandate in solemn purity,
his beneficence flows to the four corners of the earth,
yet the court officials,
strenuously extolling his sagely virtues,
are still unable to fully express his meaning.
Moreover, for worthy and capable men to go unused
is a disgrace to the state;
for the ruler to be wise and sage,
yet his virtue not to be widely known,
is the fault of the officials.
Furthermore, I am in charge of this office;
To reject the enlightened and wise [rulers]
is the greatest of sins.
What I call "narrating"
is not what is called "creating."
To compare me to the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
is wrong."
Since Zhòng Ní 仲尼 (Confucius) died, subtle words have ceased.
When the seventy disciples passed away, grand principles went astray.
During the Warring States period, the strategists roamed,
and the true and false were disputed.
The words of the various masters
were scattered in confusion.
The Ru家 (Rújiā, Confucian School),
probably originated from the Sītú 司徒 (Minister of Education),
assisting the ruler in harmonizing Yin and Yang
and illuminating moral teachings.
They roam through the texts of the Six Classics,
and pay attention to the boundaries of benevolence and righteousness.
They followed Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜,
took Wén 文 and Wǔ 武
as their models, and revered Zhòng Ní 仲尼 as their master.
This is their highest ideal.
However, those who are confused lose the subtle essence,
and those who are biased adjust their views with the times,
deviating from the root of the Dao,
and seeking to please the crowd and win favor in a superficial manner.
This is the trouble with biased Confucians.
Sīmǎ Tán 司馬談 said:
"The Ru scholars,
are broad in learning but have few essential points,
are laborious but achieve little success.
Therefore, their affairs are difficult to fully follow.
However, their exposition of the rites between ruler and subject, father and son,
and their distinction between husband and wife, elder and younger,
cannot be changed.
The Ru scholars
take the Six Arts as their model.
The classics and commentaries number in the tens.
Generations cannot fully learn them,
and constant years cannot exhaust their rites.
Therefore, it is said:
'Broad in learning but few essential points,
laborious but achieving little success.'
As for expounding the rites between ruler and subject, father and son,
and ordering the distinction between husband and wife, elder and younger,
even the hundred schools of thought cannot change them."
Fàn Yè 范曄 said:
"To wander in schools and academies,
to wear Ru clothing,
what is discussed is benevolence and righteousness,
what is transmitted is the law of the sages.
Therefore, people recognize the principles governing ruler and subject, father and son,
and families know the path to abandon evil and return to righteousness.
Since the time of Emperor Huán 桓 and Emperor Líng 靈,
the court's authority declined daily,
and the state's vulnerabilities were repeatedly exposed.
Those of average or lower intelligence,
without exception, perceive its (the dynasty's) collapse and disintegration;
thus strong and forceful ministers
cease their schemes of usurpation;
and outstanding and heroic men
submit to the principles of lowly scholars.
This is because the people chant the words of the former kings,
and those below fear the momentum of obedience and rebellion.
Consider people like Zhāng Wēn and Huángfǔ Sōng,
whose achievements settled half the empire,
and whose reputations resonated beyond the four seas.
Looking around momentarily,
a great enterprise shifts (away from them),
yet they still bow respectfully beneath a muddled ruler,
and stumble along, following the commands of flawed rites,
disbanding their armies, following the agreements they made, and without regret.
Is this not the effect of scholarship?
Therefore, our late teacher greatly praised the merits of scholarship.
How profound!"
The Daoist school
likely originated with the historians,
who recorded the successes and failures of past dynasties,
grasping the essentials and holding to the fundamentals,
using purity and emptiness to preserve themselves,
and humbleness and weakness to maintain themselves.
This is the art of those who rule and face south (the emperor).
It aligns with Yáo's ability to yield (the throne)
and the *Yì*’s (Book of Changes) constant humility;
This is its strength.
But when those who indulge in it do so,
they want to completely abandon ritual and music,
and also discard benevolence and righteousness,
relying solely on purity and emptiness.
How can this be used for governing?
This is the flaw of the Daoist school.
Sīmǎ Tán 司馬談 said:
"The Daoist school makes people's spirit focused and unified,
its actions accord with the formless,
and it provides sufficiently for all things.
Its method
relies on the great harmony of yin and yang,
adopts the good points of the Confucian and Mohist schools,
extracts the essentials of the School of Names and the Legalist school,
changes with the times,
adapts to things,
establishes trust and carries out affairs,
being suitable for everything.
Its principles are concise and easy to grasp,
with few tasks and great results.
The Daoist school advocates non-action, yet also says there is nothing it does not do.
In reality, it is easy to implement,
but its language is difficult to understand.
Its method takes emptiness and non-action as its foundation,
and uses following the natural course as its practice,
without fixed power,
without a constant form.
Therefore, one can thoroughly understand the emotions of all things,
not acting before things happen,
nor acting after things happen.
Therefore, one can become the master of all things.
Having laws and yet having no fixed laws,
one establishes one's business according to the times.
Having measures and yet having no fixed measures,
one unites with the formless.
Therefore it is said:
"The sage is not skillful,
but adheres to the changes of the times."
Emptiness is
the constant of the Dao.
Taking advantage of circumstances is
the net of the ruler.
When all the ministers arrive together,
make them each clarify themselves."
The Yin-Yang school
probably originated from the officials of Xī Hé,
reverently complying with Hào Tiān,
calendaring the images of the sun, moon, and stars,
and reverently instructing people about the seasons;
this is their strength.
When those who are fixated on it practice it,
they are bound by prohibitions and taboos,
and stuck on minor calculations,
abandoning human affairs and relying on ghosts and spirits.
This is the failing of the Yin-Yang school.
Sīmǎ Tán 司馬談 said:
"The arts of Yīnyáng 陰陽 are greatly detailed,
and involve many taboos,
causing people to be constrained and fearful.
However, their account of the great order of the four seasons
is not to be disregarded.
Yīnyáng 陰陽, the four seasons, the eight positions, the twelve degrees, and the twenty-four periods
each have their instructions and commands.
Those who follow them prosper,
those who defy them perish—
this is not necessarily so.
Therefore, it is said:
'It causes people to be constrained and full of taboos.'
Spring grows, summer flourishes, autumn harvests, winter stores;
this is the great principle of Heaven,

Preface to the Confucian School's *Jīngjì Chángduǎn Jīng*

Preface to the Confucian School's *Jīngjì Chángduǎn Jīng* Written by Zhào Ruí, a humble subject residing in the wilderness of Ānchāng Rock on Chángpíng Mountain in Qī County, Zī Prefecture, of the Táng Dynasty.
Master Zhào said:
The craftsman who makes carriages
worries that people will not value them;
the one who makes arrows
fears that people will not be wounded.
Does he truly have love or hate?
It is in fact the skill of his craft that drives him to this.
Thus, one knows that the scholars of the present age and those who rush about,
having studied books with a wide scope,
Then one considers the changes among the feudal lords;
when arts flourish with the unusual and the orthodox,
one thinks of the gatherings amidst turmoil.
These are also considerations of the past,
and necessary principles.
Therefore, the former teacher Kǒngzǐ deeply investigated their root, and worried about their outcome,
and thus composed the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
which magnifies the way of the king;
and created the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety),
which praises virtue and conduct.
Preventing sprouts and blocking the gradual,
in advance, there is something to suppress.
This is the fundamental intention of the sages in making works.
However, if laws are made based on principle,
their defects will inevitably lead to chaos.
If it comes to chaos,
how shall one save it?
Therefore, in governing the world and managing people,
one rarely hears of following the old ways.
The Three Dynasties had different rites,
and the Five Hegemons had different laws.
It is not that they were contrary,
but rather to remedy the defects.
Therefore,
though the appearance of the state is uniform,
the way of loyalty and culture must be different;
though sages and wise men share the same spirit,
the names of emperors and kings may be different.
Is it not that they establish teachings according to the times, following this,
and accomplish affairs based on things, guiding that?
Following this,
purity and corruption follow what is encountered;
guiding that,
kingship and hegemony exist in what is met.
Therefore, the principles of the ancients
were that their governance had three aspects:
the governance of a king transforms [the people],
the governance of a hegemon intimidates [the people],
and the governance of a powerful state coerces [the people].
Each has its own application,
and cannot be changed.
Guǎnzi said:
“A sage can assist the times,
but cannot defy the times.
The wise are good at planning,
but are not as good as being timely.”
Zōu Zǐ said:
“Political teachings and cultural substance
he discusses the overall situation,
not adhering to minor details.
Although he claims benevolence and invokes righteousness,
he doesn't reach the level of the Three Kings,
but in supporting what has fallen and stabilizing what is tilting,
his goal is the same.
Fearing that Confucian scholars are mired in what they have heard,
and do not understand the differing strategies of the Kingly Way and the Way of the Hegemon,
therefore, I have described them using the arts of "Length and Shortness"
for those who manage and adapt to circumstances.
Creating a title,
totaling sixty-three chapters,
compiled into ten volumes,
named *Cháng Duǎn Jīng* (長短經, The Classic of Length and Shortness).
The main purpose lies in securing the foundation, reforming current malpractices, and understanding rise and fall, order and chaos.
All are fully recorded in the chapters,
to serve as a long-term plan for future generations,
and to create the ultimate way of governance,
not to correct the world and boast of customs,
seeking fame and reputation.
I have merely revealed what I have seen and heard,
hoping to inspire future wise men.
All those who hold positions,
may they be fortunate enough to consider this in detail.
The Most Important Principles, First
The Most Important Principles, First
Your subject has heard Lǎozǐ say:
"Govern the state with correctness,
Use surprise tactics in warfare,
And gain the empire through non-interference."
Xún Qīng said:
"The ruler is one who excels at employing officials;
the common man is one who excels at his own abilities."
Fù Zǐ said:
"Let the scholar-officials divide their duties and listen [to instructions],
let the lords of the feudal states divide their territories and defend them,
let the Three Dukes oversee the directions and deliberate,
then the Son of Heaven can sit with folded hands and govern correctly."
How can I demonstrate that this is so?
During the time of Yáo,
Shùn was the Minister of Education,
Qì was the Minister of War,
Yǔ was the Minister of Works,
Hòu Jì was in charge of agriculture,
Kuí was the music master,
Chuí was the master craftsman,
Bó Yí was the minister of rites,
Gāo Yáo was the judge,
Yì was in charge of driving away birds and beasts.
Yáo could not do even one of these things;
how could he be a ruler,
and these nine men be his ministers?
What is the reason for this?
Yáo knew about the matters of the Nine Assignments (jiǔ fù zhī shì),
so he instructed his nine sons to each be responsible for their respective tasks,
and they all successfully completed their duties, thus achieving the Nine Accomplishments (jiǔ gōng).
Yáo then capitalized on these successes to rule the world.
Emperor Gāodì of the Hàn dynasty said:
"In devising strategies within the tent,
and securing victory from a thousand *lǐ* away,
I am not as good as Zǐfáng;
in stabilizing the nation,
comforting the people,
providing supplies and provisions,
and ensuring the supply lines are never cut off,
I am not as good as Xiāo Hé;
in commanding an army of a million,
ensuring victory in every battle,
and capturing every city attacked,
I am not as good as Hán Xìn.
These three men
are all outstanding individuals.
I am able to employ them,
and this is why I possess the world."
*Rén Wù Zhì* (Appraisal of Human Abilities) says:
"The responsibility of a single office
is to use one flavor to harmonize with five flavors;
the governance of a state
is to use a flavorless base to blend the five flavors.
Therefore, a minister considers his ability to handle duties as capability,
A ruler's ability lies in using people effectively;
a subject's ability lies in speaking effectively;
a ruler's ability lies in listening effectively;
a subject's ability lies in acting effectively;
a ruler's ability lies in rewarding and punishing effectively.
Because they are different,
"A skilled craftsman builds palaces;
to make a circle, he must use a compass;
to make a square, he must use a set square;
to make something level and straight, he must use a plumb line.
Once the work is completed,

Sūn Qīng said:

if he wants to be good at driving and reaching distant places,

their work is not laborious,

This is being able to use what one does not possess as if one possessed it.
If a ruler does not understand the Way of the Ruler, it is not so.
If he does it himself, then he cannot employ the worthy;
if he cannot employ the worthy, then the worthy will dislike him.
This is why accomplishments and fame are harmed,
and why the state is endangered.
It is said:

the ruler is able to govern the many abilities."

The ruler guards his Dao,

The former kings knew it to be so;
therefore, they used what was not theirs as if they already possessed it—

Employ the greedy, employ the foolish.
The wise are pleased to establish their merit,
The brave are fond of acting on their ambitions,
The greedy decisively seize their profit,
The foolish do not cherish their lives.
Utilize them based on their inherent nature,
This is the subtle authority of the army."
*Huáinánzǐ* (淮南子) says:
"Among all things under Heaven,
Nothing is more deadly than the poisonous *xīdú* (谿毒)
and *fùzǐ* (附子, aconite),
Yet a good doctor bags it and stores it away,
Because it has its uses.
When the deer ascends the mountain,
Even Dàzhāng (大章, a strong man) cannot climb;
And as for those below them,
even shepherd boys could pursue them.
Talents have their varying lengths.
The Hú people are adept at riding horses,
the Yuè people are adept at boats.
With different forms and diverse categories,
if you give them tasks for which they are not suited, they will fail."
Emperor Wèi Wǔ's edict stated:
"Those who are good at advancing and taking may
not necessarily be capable in conduct.
Those who are capable in conduct
may not necessarily be good at advancing and taking.
Was Chén Píng truly of steadfast conduct?
Was Sū Qín truly trustworthy?
Yet Chén Píng stabilized the Hàn dynasty's enterprise,
and Sū Qín aided the weak Yān state.
It was because they were entrusted with their strengths."
Judging from this,
if Hán Xìn were made to work on women’s needlework,
Dǒng Zhòngshū were to serve in the military,
Yú Gōng were to gallop in diplomatic persuasions,
and Lù Jiǎ were to hear lawsuits,
they would certainly not have the achievements of the past,
and the prominent reputations of today.
Therefore, the way of entrusting people with their strengths
must be carefully examined.
The discussion states:
Wèi Huánfàn said:
Emperors and kings employ people by
assessing their character and entrusting them with tasks according to their talents.
In times of strife,
strategies and plans come first.
After the realm is settled,
loyalty and righteousness are paramount.
Therefore, Jìn Wén (晉文) acted upon Jiù Fàn's (咎犯) plan
but rewarded Yōng Jì's (雍季) words.
Gāozǔ (高祖) employed Chén Píng's (陳平) wisdom
but entrusted the future to Zhōu Bó (周勃)."
An ancient saying goes:
"In times of peace and stability,
those with high virtue hold high positions;
in times of emergency,
those with great merit receive generous rewards."
Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) said:
"Lǎozǐ (老子) excels at cultivating his nature,
but cannot be relied upon in times of danger;
Shāng Yāng (商鞅) excels at administering the law,
but cannot be relied upon to promote education;
Sū Qín (蘇秦) and Zhāng Yí (張儀) excel at eloquent speech,
but cannot be relied upon to forge alliances;
Bái Qǐ (白起) excels at attacking and conquering,
but cannot be relied upon to win over the masses;
Wǔ Zixū (伍子胥) excels at plotting against enemies,
but cannot be relied upon to protect himself;
Wěi Shēng (尾生) excels at keeping promises,
but cannot be relied upon to adapt to changing circumstances;
Wáng Jiā excels at meeting enlightened rulers,
but cannot serve unenlightened lords;
Xǔ Zǐjiàng excels at clearly judging good and bad,
but cannot nurture talent."
These are the methods of those who are good at employing others.
Category of People, Third
Category of People, Third
Now, the important tools of the world,
and the great rule of the king,
all require exerting intelligence in evaluating talent,
to obtain ease in employment.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"People have five types:
There are the common people,
there are the scholars,
there are the gentlemen,
there are the sages,
there are the worthies.
If one examines these five types,
then the way of governance is complete."
What is meant by the common people is that
in their hearts they do not harbor plans for cautious endings,
from their mouths they do not utter words of instruction and correction
(laws;
correction); they do not choose the worthy to entrust themselves to,
and do not strive to establish themselves;
To see the small darkness as great and not know what to devote oneself to,
to follow things like a stream and not know what to hold onto—
this is a common person.
Those who are called "shì rén" 士人,
have a fixed purpose in their hearts,
and a principle they adhere to in their plans.
Even if they cannot fully grasp the root of the Dao and its arts,
they must have something they follow.
"Follow" (率) is like "recount" (述);
even if they cannot encompass the beauty of all virtues,
they must have a place where they dwell.
Therefore, wisdom does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be discerning in what it knows;
speech does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be discerning in what it says
"What it says" is the essence of speech;
action does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be discerning in what it is based on.
Once wisdom knows something,
once speech grasps something
(grasps its essence),
once action is based on something,
then it is as unchangeable as one's nature, life, form, and body.
Wealth and nobility cannot add to it,
poverty and lowliness cannot diminish it—
this is a "shì rén" 士人.
Those who are called "jūnzǐ" 君子,
speak with loyalty and trustworthiness, and their hearts are without malice
Jì,
to be resentful and harmful.
Having benevolence and righteousness within oneself, but not boasting in appearance.
Having clear and comprehensive thoughts, but not being dogmatic in speech.
Firmly practicing and believing in the Way,
constantly striving and never ceasing,
appearing gentle and as if one could be surpassed, yet ultimately remaining unattainable.
This is a *jūnzǐ*.
Yóurán,
the appearance of not advancing.
Yuè,
to surpass.
Sūn Qīng said:
"The *jūnzǐ* can act in a way that is worthy of respect,
but cannot make people necessarily respect him;
can act in a way that is worthy of trust,
but cannot make people necessarily trust him;
can act in a way that is worthy of being employed,
but cannot make people necessarily employ him.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* is ashamed of not cultivating himself,
not ashamed of being slandered;
ashamed of not being trustworthy,
not ashamed of not being trusted;
ashamed of being incapable,
not ashamed of not being employed.
Not enticed by praise,
not resentful of slander,
following the Way and acting accordingly,
To be upright and correct in one's conduct is called a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman)."
wèi zhī jūnzǐ yě."
What is meant by "worthy" is:
Their virtue does not exceed the limits.
The limits
are the laws.
Their actions accord with the compass and square;
their words are sufficient to be laws for the world without harming themselves.
Their words fill the world, with no faults in speech.
Their Way is sufficient to transform the common people without harming the root
(the root is also oneself).
If they are wealthy, then the world has no hoarded wealth.
*Wǎn* means
accumulating.
If they give, then the world does not suffer from poverty.
This is a worthy person.
What is meant by "sage" is:
Their virtue is in accord with Heaven and Earth;
their transformations and communications are without fixed direction.
They exhaust the beginning and end of all things,
harmonize the naturalness of the myriad things,
spread out their great Way
and thereby accomplish the true nature of things.
Their brightness rivals the sun and moon;
their transformative influence acts like spirits.
The common people do not know their virtue;
those who see them do not recognize their neighbors.
This is a sage.
鄰 (lín), is used metaphorically for boundaries.
*Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"To deliberately emphasize action,
to distance oneself from the world and differ from customs,
to engage in lofty discussions that invite resentment and slander,
is merely to be excessive.
This is what hermits of the mountains and valleys,
people detached from the world,
those who wither away and throw themselves into the abyss, delight in.
To speak of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
to be respectful, frugal, and yielding,
is merely to cultivate oneself.
This is what scholars of peaceful times,
those who teach and instruct,
wandering residents and those of broad learning, delight in.
To speak of great accomplishments,
to establish a great reputation,
to observe the rites between ruler and subject,
to rectify the hierarchy between superiors and inferiors,
is merely to govern.
This is what courtiers,
those who honor the ruler and strengthen the state,
those who seek to achieve accomplishments and annex territories, delight in.
To go to marshes and wetlands,
to dwell in secluded and open spaces,
to fish and live in leisure,
is merely to do nothing.
This is what hermits of the rivers and seas,
This is what reclusive people do,
and what those at leisure enjoy.
Blowing and breathing,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
bear-like climbing and bird-like stretching,
are all for the sake of longevity.
This is what practitioners of *dǎoyǐn* do,
what those who nurture their bodies do,
and what *Péng Zǔ*, a man of great longevity, enjoyed.
As for those who attain eminence without deliberately seeking it,
who cultivate themselves without (preaching) benevolence and righteousness,
who govern without seeking fame and achievement,
who find leisure without (retreating to) rivers and seas,
who achieve longevity without *dǎoyǐn*,
who have nothing they forget,
and nothing they lack.
Being placid and boundless,
all virtues follow them.
This is the Way of Heaven and Earth,
and the virtue of the Sage."
The *Qián Jīng* says:
"Virtue sufficient to embrace the distant,
trustworthiness sufficient to unify differences,
insight sufficient to discern antiquity,
talent sufficient to surpass the world:
these are the heroes of men.
Laws sufficient to establish teachings,
conduct sufficient to cultivate righteousness,
Kindness sufficient to win over the masses,
insight sufficient to illuminate subordinates,
this is a *jùn* among men;
conduct sufficient to be a model,
wisdom sufficient to resolve doubts,
integrity sufficient to deter the greedy and base,
trustworthiness sufficient to embrace foreign customs,
this is a *háo* among men;
upholding principles without wavering,
abiding by righteousness without resentment,
facing suspicion without seeking unprincipled escape,
encountering profit without seeking unprincipled gain,
this is a *jié* among men."
The *Rén Wù Zhì* says:
"Virtue and conduct are lofty and refined,
demeanor and bearing are exemplary,
this is called *qīng jié*;
Yán Líng and Yàn Yīng are examples of this.
Thought that penetrates to transformation,
strategies and plans are ingenious,
this is called a strategist (*shù jiā*);
Fàn Lǐ and Zhāng Liáng are examples of this.
Their virtue is sufficient to improve customs,
their methods are sufficient to rectify the world,
their strategies are sufficient to ensure victory in the ancestral temple,
this is called a national pillar (*guó tǐ*);
Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng are examples of this.
Their virtue is sufficient to lead a state,
Their methods were sufficient to rectify the village and the city,
their techniques were sufficient to weigh the appropriateness of affairs.
This is called "practical ability."
Zǐchǎn and Xīmén Bào are examples of this.
Those of pure and upright conduct,
were not able to be broadly forgiving,
they liked to censure and criticize,
distinguishing right from wrong.
This is called "judging merit and demerit."
The disciples of Zǐxià are examples of this.
Those of the Legalist school,
were not able to innovate ideas and plan far ahead,
but were able to undertake the responsibilities of an official position,
implementing intentions and displaying cleverness.
This is called "skill."
Zhāng Chǎng and Zhào Guǎnghàn are examples of this.
Those of the school of strategists,
were not able to create regulations and establish principles,
but were able to adapt to changes and use expedient power.
They had an excess of expedient wisdom,
but a lack of impartiality and uprightness.
This is called "strategic intent."
Chén Píng and Hán Ānguó are examples of this.
Being able to compose texts and write books,
this is called "literature."
Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù are examples of this.
Being able to transmit the work of the sages,
but not being able to manage affairs and implement government,
This is called Confucian learning;
Máo Gōng and Guàn Gōng are examples of this.
Eloquence that doesn't enter the Way
but provides ready responses,
this is called verbal dexterity;
Yuè Yì and Cáo Qiūshēng are examples of this.
Courage and strength surpassing the masses,
talent and strategy exceeding others,
this is called heroism;
Bái Qǐ and Hán Xìn are examples of this."
The *Jiā Yǔ* states:
"In the past, enlightened rulers always completely knew the names of all worthy men in the empire.
Once they knew their names,
they also knew their actual abilities.
Then, they used the ranks of the empire to honor them,
and the empire was governed well."
This is what it means.
Assessing Talent, Fourth
Assessing Talent, Fourth
The talents of men are varied, differing in size and capacity,
like a *shēng* (a small measuring container) that cannot hold a *hú* (a larger measuring container);
when full, it is discarded.
If someone is employed for a task they are not suited for,
how can one avoid danger?
Fù Zǐ said:
"There are nine types of talent:
First is Déxíng (德行, virtue),
to establish the root of the Dao.
Second is Lǐcái (理才, administrative talent),
to investigate the workings of affairs.
Third is Zhèngcái (政才, political talent),
to manage the system of governance.
Fourth is Xuécái (學才, scholarly talent),
to synthesize classical literature.
Fifth is Wǔcái (武才, martial talent),
to command the military.
Sixth is Nóngcái (農才, agricultural talent),
to teach farming.
Seventh is Gōngcái (工才, craftsmanship talent),
to create tools and implements.
Eighth is Shāngcái (商才, mercantile talent),
to promote national wealth.
Ninth is Biàncái (辯才, eloquence),
to excel in remonstrance and debate."
These are the ways to assess talent.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn (伊尹) said:
"Intelligence that is connected to the Great Dao,
responds to change without exhaustion,
and discerns the nature of all things;
whose words are sufficient to harmonize Yin and Yang,
regulate the four seasons,
and moderate wind and rain.
Such a person should be selected as one of the Three Dukes."
Therefore, the affairs of the Three Dukes constantly reside in the Dao.
Emperor Wén of Hàn asked Chén Píng,
"What matters do you oversee?"
He replied,
"Your Majesty, unaware of my dullness,
has allowed me to hold the position of disgraced prime minister.
The prime minister,
above assists the Son of Heaven,
harmonizes and manages the Yin and Yang,
below fulfills the suitability of the myriad things,
externally pacifies the four barbarian tribes,
internally cherishes and attaches the common people,
so that ministers and high officials
each obtain their due positions."
The Emperor said,
"Excellent!"
The Hàn Wèi Xiàng Book says:
"Your servant has heard that the *Yì* (Book of Changes) says: 'Heaven and Earth move in accordance with the natural order,
therefore the sun and moon do not miss their course,
and the four seasons do not err;
the sage moves in accordance with the natural order,
then punishments are clear and the people are obedient.'
The transformations of Heaven and Earth
necessarily arise from Yin and Yang.
The division of Yin and Yang
uses the sun and moon as its guideline.
Each has its constant duty,
and they must not interfere with each other.
An enlightened king is careful in honoring Heaven,
Be cautious in nurturing people.
Therefore, establish the office of Xī Hé (羲和),
to follow the four seasons,
respectfully instruct in human affairs.
If the ruler's movements and stillness are in accordance with the Dao (道),
and he reverently follows the Yin and Yang (陰陽),
then the sun and moon will be bright,
the wind and rain will be timely,
and the cold and heat will be harmonious.
When these three are in order,
then disasters will not arise,
people will not die young or fall ill,
and clothing and food will be plentiful.
This is the general principle of harmonizing Yin and Yang."
The details are in the *Hóng Fàn* (洪範) chapter.
One who does not miss the four seasons,
is versed in the advantages of the land,
can open up what is blocked,
and can make profitable what is unprofitable;
such a person should be promoted to one of the Nine Ministers (九卿).
Therefore, the Nine Ministers' affairs always rest on virtue.
One who is versed in human affairs,
whose actions are as straight as a plumb line,
is versed in passes and bridges,
and is substantial in managing the treasury;
such a person should be promoted to a Grand Master (大夫).
Therefore, a Grand Master's affairs always rest on benevolence.
Yáng Yóng (楊顒), the chief clerk of Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮), the Chancellor of Shu (蜀), said:
"To sit and discuss the Dao
is the role of the Sāngōng (三公);
to rise and put it into practice
is the role of the Qīng Dàfū (卿大夫)."
Those who are loyal and upright, strongly admonish,
and are without deceit or falsehood;
who discard selfishness and establish public interest,
and whose words have measure and order,
such people should be selected and appointed as Lièshì (列士).
Therefore, the work of the Lièshì (列士) always lies in righteousness.
Therefore, when morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are established, the world is rectified.
(The "Rénwù Zhì" (人物志) says:
"The virtue of pure integrity
is the responsibility of the Shīshì (師氏);
the talent of a legalist
is the responsibility of the Sīkòu (司寇);
the talent of strategists
is the responsibility of the Sāngū (三孤);
the talent for evaluating good and bad
is the assistant of the Shīshì (師氏);
the talent for skills and abilities
is the responsibility of the Sīkōng (司空);
the talent for Confucian learning
is the responsibility of the Bǎoshì (保氏);
the talent for literary composition
is the responsibility of the Guóshǐ (國史);
the talent for bravery and heroism
is the responsibility of generals and commanders.")
Tài Gōng said:
a foul mouth and a wicked tongue,
speaking evil all day long,
never ceasing even when sleeping,
are hated by the multitude,
and despised by others.
Such a person can be employed to watch over streets and lanes,
investigating wickedness and spying out misfortune.
Quick-witted and fond of doing good,
going to bed late and rising early,
and never regretting even strenuous work,
such a person is fit to be the leader of a wife and children.
Speaking first to investigate matters,
encouraging others and giving them food,
being truthful and rarely speaking,
and distributing wealth and goods equitably,
such a person is fit to be the leader of ten people.
Anxious and severe,
appearing solemn and respectful,
not accepting remonstrance,
frequently carrying out executions,
ensuring blood is drawn with every punishment,
not sparing even relatives,
such a person is fit to be the leader of a hundred people.
Fond of litigation and argumentative,
prone to envy, thievery, and aggression,
punishing people with words,
To command a group,
that is a general for a thousand men.
With a respectful appearance,
speaking from time to time,
knowing when men are hungry or full,
familiar with men's strengths and weaknesses,
that is a general for ten thousand men.
Cautious and fearful,
being more careful day by day,
drawing near to the virtuous and seeking their counsel,
causing men to know propriety,
speaking without arrogance,
with utmost loyalty and sincerity,
that is a general for a hundred thousand men.
The *Jīng* (Classic) says:
"Although a general values thoroughness and gravitas,
they must not have indecisive doubts;
although they excel at broad consultation,
they should not desire multifarious confusions."
This discusses the subtleties of generalship.
Gentle, kind, and truly superior,
with undivided attention,
recognizing the worthy and promoting them,
executing the law without bias,
that is a general for a million men.
Deeds so plentiful and renowned,
that neighboring states all hear of them,
going out and returning to luxurious dwellings,
Bǎixìng suǒ qīn,
is truly sincere and generous,
is discerning in governing the world,
is able to bring things to completion,
and also able to remedy failures,
knows astronomy above,
and knows geography below,
and treats everyone within the four seas
as if they were his own children,
such is the leader of heroes,
he is truly the lord of all under Heaven."
The *Rén Wù Zhì* (A Study of Human Abilities) says:
"Intelligence that stands out is called *yīng* (英, hero);
courage that surpasses others is called *xióng* (雄, leader).
These are the broad distinctions in names.
Intelligence,
is a part of *yīng*,
but without the courage of *xióng*, words will not be acted upon;
courage,
is a part of *xióng*,
but without the wisdom of *yīng*, affairs cannot be established.
If intelligence can plan the beginning,
but understanding cannot see the opportunity,
one can engage in seated discussions but cannot handle affairs;
if intelligence can plan the beginning,
understanding can see the opportunity,
but courage cannot act,
one can follow the norm but cannot consider change;
If one has strength surpassing others,
but courage is not put into action,
such a person can be a strongman,
but cannot be a vanguard.
If one has strength surpassing others,
and courage is put into action,
but wisdom is not enough to foresee events,
such a person can be a vanguard,
but is not sufficient to be a general.
One must be clever enough to devise plans,
perceptive enough to recognize opportunities,
and courageous enough to make decisions,
only then can one be considered a *yīng* (hero),
Zhāng Liáng 張良 is an example of this.
If one has physical strength surpassing others,
courage is put into action,
and wisdom is sufficient to foresee events,
only then can one be considered a *xióng* (chieftain),
Hán Xìn 韓信 is an example of this.
If one person possesses
both *yīng* (heroic) and *xióng* (chieftain) qualities,
then that person can last for generations;
Gāozǔ 高祖 and Xiàng Yǔ 項羽 are examples of this."
The *Jīng* (Classics) says:
"One whose wisdom is like a flowing spring,
and whose conduct can serve as a model,
is a teacher of men;
one whose wisdom can be a whetstone,
Those whose conduct can serve as a warning are
rén yǒu (human friends);
those who uphold the law and guard their positions, daring not to do wrong, are
rén lì (human officials);
those who seek immediate gratification,
and agree to every command without hesitation, are
rén lì (human servants).
Therefore, the superior ruler takes teachers as assistants,
the average ruler takes friends as assistants,
the inferior ruler takes officials as assistants,
and the ruler heading for ruin takes servants as assistants."
If you wish to see whether he will perish,
you must observe his subordinates.
Therefore, those of similar understanding see each other,
those of similar hearing hear each other,
those of similar aspiration follow each other,
and none but the worthy can employ the worthy.
Therefore, those whom advisors and attendants desire to be entrusted and employed
are the crux of survival or ruin,
and the key to success or failure.
Sūn Wǔ said:
"Which ruler possesses the dào (the Way)?
In the past, when the Hàn Wáng (King of Han) was besieged at Róngyáng,
he said to Chén Píng:
"The world is in chaos,
when will it be settled?"
Chén Píng said:
"Xiàng Wáng's character
He respectfully and lovingly treated people;
Scholars who valued integrity, frugality, and propriety mostly flocked to him.
As for those who sought rewards for their achievements and noble titles,
Respected men of the state,
They also did not attach themselves to him for this reason.
Now, Your Majesty is disrespectful and lacks propriety towards people;
Scholars who are stubborn, greedy, and shameless,
Mostly flock to Hàn.
It is truly appropriate to each discard their respective weaknesses,
and gather their respective strengths,
and then the world could be commanded and pacified with ease."
Wèi Tàizǔ said to Guō Jiā:
"Yuán Běnchū has vast territory and a strong army,
I want to attack him,
but my strength is not enough to defeat him,
what should I do?"
Jiā replied,
"The dissimilarity between Liú and Xiàng,
is known to you.
Hànzǔ only won through wisdom;
Xiàng Yǔ, although strong,
was ultimately captured by him.
I secretly assess that,
Shào has ten defeats,
you have ten victories;
although his army is strong,
it will be of no avail.
Shào is overly formal and ceremonious,
Gōng embodied a natural way,
this is a victory of Dao,
first.
Yuán Shào acted rebelliously,
Gōng acted in obedience and accordance,
leading the world with this,
this is a victory of righteousness,
second.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, governance erred on the side of leniency,
Yuán Shào used leniency to alleviate it,
therefore he was not awe-inspiring;
Gōng corrected it with severity,
and those above and below knew the rules,
this is a victory of governance,
third.
Yuán Shào was outwardly lenient but inwardly suspicious,
employing people only to doubt them soon after,
those he appointed were only relatives and offspring;
Gōng was outwardly simple but inwardly insightful,
employing people without doubt,
only based on their suitability to the task,
not asking about distance or proximity,
this is a victory of magnanimity,
fourth.
Yuán Shào had many plans but few decisions,
failing in subsequent matters;
Gōng executed plans as soon as they were obtained,
responding to changes without limit,
This is a victory in planning,
the fifth.
Yuán Shào, relying on the accumulated wealth of generations,
spoke highly of yielding and deference,
in order to gain fame and reputation.
Scholars who liked to embellish outward appearances mostly flocked to him.
Cáo Gōng treated people with sincerity,
conducting affairs with honesty and trust,
not striving for empty praise.
He led his subordinates with frugality.
He was unsparing to those with merit.
Scholars with loyalty, integrity, foresight, and substance
were all willing to serve him.
This is a victory in virtue,
the sixth.
When Yuán Shào saw people hungry and cold,
his feelings of concern
were expressed on his face.
As for what he did not see,
he worried he might not be able to attend to it,
which is what is called the benevolence of a woman.
Cáo Gōng, regarding small matters at hand,
sometimes neglected them.
As for great affairs,
dealing with the entire country,
the favors he bestowed
all exceeded their expectations.
Even what he did not see,
What is taken into consideration is always successful;
nothing is left undone.
This is his victory in benevolence;
the seventh.
Shào would let senior ministers contend for power,
and slanderous words would lead to confusion.
But you, Duke, govern your subordinates with principle,
and insidious influences cannot take hold.
This is your victory in clarity;
the eighth.
Shào cannot distinguish right from wrong;
but what you deem right, you promote with propriety;
and what you deem wrong, you rectify with law.
This is your victory in refinement;
the ninth.
Shào is fond of false displays and
does not understand the essentials of war;
you, Duke, defeat the many with the few,
and your use of troops is like that of a god.
Your soldiers rely on you,
and your enemies fear you.
This is your victory in military prowess;
the tenth."
Cáo Gōng said:
"I know it.
Shào is a person whose
ambitions are great but whose wisdom is small;
whose appearance is stern but whose courage is weak;
One is feared and restrained but lacks authority;
the army is large but its divisions and responsibilities are unclear;
the generals are arrogant and the administration's decrees are inconsistent.
Though the territory is vast,
and the grain supply is abundant,
this is precisely what will provide for us."
Yáng Fù said,
"Yuán Gōng is tolerant but indecisive,
fond of planning but rarely making decisions.
Without decisiveness, there is no authority;
with few decisions, matters are delayed.
Although he is strong now,
he will eventually be captured.
Cáo Gōng has great talent and far-reaching strategies,
makes decisions without hesitation,
his laws are unified and truly refined;
he will surely accomplish great things."
Which general is capable?
Yuán Shào led a large army to attack Xǔ.
Kǒng Róng said to Xún Yù,
"Yuán Shào's territory is vast and his army is strong.
Tián Fēng and Xǔ Yōu
are men of wisdom and strategy, planning for him;
Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì
are loyal ministers, entrusted with his affairs;
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu
are brave beyond the three armies, commanding his troops.
It will be difficult to defeat him, won't it?"
Yù
Although Shào's army is large,
its laws and regulations are not well organized.
Tián Fēng is rigid and offends his superiors;
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and does not govern properly;
Shěn Pèi is autocratic and lacks strategy;
Féng Jì is decisive but self-willed.
These two will remain to manage affairs afterward.
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and violates the law;
he certainly cannot be tolerated;
if he is not tolerated, he will surely cause trouble.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu
are merely brave men,
who can be captured in a single battle."
Later, Xǔ Yōu was greedy and did not abide by the law;
Shěn Pèi seized his wife and children.
Yōu, in anger, fled to Cáo Gōng.
Also, Yán Liáng was beheaded in battle,
and Tián Fēng died for his advice.
All were as Yù predicted.
This is how I knew we would win."
Knowing People, Fifth
Knowing People, Fifth
Your servant has heard that the principle of being a general is
to strive to understand the hearts of heroes.
However, people are not easily understood,
Knowing people is not easy.
Emperor Guāngwǔ of the Hàn dynasty, a ruler known for his keen hearing,
was mistaken about Páng Méng;
Cáo Mèngdé, a wise judge of character,
was deceived by Zhāng Miǎo.
Why is this?
It is because things that resemble each other
are what confuse the world.
Therefore, it is said:
a monkey resembles intelligence but is not intelligent.
"狙" (jū) is pronounced like "shū" in reverse, meaning to be slow or negligent.
A fool resembles a virtuous person but is not a virtuous person.
A stubborn person resembles a brave person but is not a brave person.
A ruler who brings about the downfall of a state seems wise.
A minister who brings about the downfall of a state seems loyal.
Young weeds resemble young grain.
A black cow's yellow color resembles a tiger.
White bones are mistaken for ivory.
Inferior stones are mistaken for jade.
These all seem to be something but are not.
The *Renwù Zhì* (Appraisal of Human Abilities) says:
"Light promises resemble ardor but lack trustworthiness.
Doing many things easily resembles ability but lacks effectiveness.
Advancing swiftly resembles precision but leads to quick abandonment.
Spying resembles scrutiny but causes troublesome affairs.
Making promises of generosity resembles benevolence but lacks follow-through.
Obeying to one's face resembles loyalty but leads to defiance in private."
These are cases of seeming to be something but not being it.
There are also things that seem wrong but are actually right;
there are those with great power who seem treacherous but are actually meritorious;
there are those with great wisdom who seem foolish but are inwardly brilliant;
there are those with broad love who seem insincere but are actually deeply kind;
there are those who speak honestly but seem accusatory, yet their intentions are loyal.
If not for the utmost discernment in the world,
who can grasp their true nature?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"The human heart is more treacherous than mountains and rivers,
and harder to know than Heaven.
Heaven still has the predictable seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer, and the cycles of dawn and dusk,
but people are thick of face and deep of feeling.
Therefore, there are those who appear sincere but are harmful,
there are those who are elders who act unworthily (長, zhǎng, pronounced zhú liǎng fǎn),
there are those who seem compliant but are actually astute,
there are those who seem firm but are actually lax,
there are those who seem slow but are actually decisive (釬, hàn, pronounced hàn)."
Tàigōng 太公 said:
"There are scholars who are strict but unworthy,
there are those who are gentle and kind but become thieves,
there are those whose outward appearance is respectful
but whose hearts are deceitful and arrogant,
there are those who are clever but without feeling,
there are those who are imposing but achieve nothing,
there are those who appear decisive but cannot actually make decisions,
there are those who seem confused and muddled but are actually loyal and sincere,
There are those who appear compliant and yielding but are actually effective;
there are those who seem courageous and fierce but are inwardly timid;
there are those who are muddle-headed but instead easily manipulate others.
Allow none to be excluded,
allow none to be unfulfilled.
What the world despises,
the sage values.
Ordinary people do not understand,
only those with great discernment can see its true extent."
This refers to the outward appearance of a person not corresponding to their inner feelings.
Huán Fàn 桓範 said:
"The difference between the wise and the foolish
is like that between the sunflower and the amaranth.
How can one not know what is so?
It is like darnel resembling grain;
it is similar but not the same,
it is seemingly virtuous but not truly virtuous."
Yángzǐ 揚子 in the *Fǎ Yán* 《法言》 said:
"Someone asked about what is difficult to know,
saying:
'Tài Shān 泰山 compared to ants and leeches,
the Jiāng Hé 江河 compared to puddles of rainwater,
these are not difficult.
A great sage compared to a great villain,
that is difficult!
Alas!
Only one who can distinguish what is similar
will find nothing difficult!'"

Tài Gōng said:

Fù Zǐ said:
"Knowing people is difficult,

If what they cultivate comes from the Daoists,

The nine schools have different tasks,

Observe the actions of the silent,

These four virtues may differ,
and what is observed may be subtle,
Moreover, it is not what is considered difficult.
What is considered difficult

speaking of thievery as if it were benevolence,
speaking of cowardice as if it were bravery,
speaking of deceit as if it were trustworthiness,
speaking of lewdness as if it were chastity.
They are skilled at creating semblances to confuse the truth,
using many tricks to create doubt and obscurity.
This is what common people are often confused by,
and what enlightened rulers deeply despise.
The *jūnzǐ* inwardly cleanse their hearts,
and receive people with emptiness,
maintaining a firm stance without changing direction.
This is the way of *zhēn guān* (true observation).
The Nine Schools have their principles;
this is the way of *zhēn yī* (true unity).
If one has *zhēn guān* internally and *zhēn yī* externally,
then those who cling to falsehood will have nowhere to escape.
Empty words are easily fabricated,
but if one demands the results of their actual deeds,
then the verification of right and wrong will be immediately apparent."
Therefore, Hánzǐ said:
"Everyone is asleep;
the blind do not know it.
People are all silent,
the mute does not understand.
Awaken them and make them see,
question them and make them answer,
then the mute and the blind will be at their wit's end.
Examining the teeth and gums,
observing the coat and color,
even the best horse experts like Liáng and Yuè cannot be certain about a horse;
attach the carriage and yoke the horses,
test them on the road,
then even a lowly servant can determine their worth.
Observing the green and yellow,
examining the forging and tempering,
even Ōuyě cannot be certain about a sword;
using it to cut dogs and horses on land,
using it to sever white dragons in water,
even the foolish can recognize its sharpness or dullness.
Thus, knowing that clear testing and demanding reality
is the work of a sage."
The *Rén Wù Zhì* says:
"All who have blood and breath

As for their bodies,
wood represents bones, metal represents tendons, fire represents vital energy, earth represents flesh, water represents blood,
these are the images of the Five Materials.
The substance of the Five Materials,
each has its use.:
"That which is like bones planted and standing flexibly
is called hóngyì (宏毅, resolute and firm).
Hóngyì
is the substance of rén (仁, benevolence).
Wood provides shade,
and is the substance of rén.
If the substance is not hóngyì,
one cannot achieve rén.
That which is pure and bright in spirit
is called wénlǐ (文理, refined and logical).
Wénlǐ
is the foundation of lǐ (禮, ritual propriety).
Fire illuminates and observes,
and is the foundation of lǐ.
If the foundation lacks wénlǐ,
one cannot achieve lǐ.
That which is upright and substantial in form
is called zhēngù (貞固, steadfast and firm).
Zhēngù
is the base of xìn (信, trustworthiness).
Earth invariably brings forth life,
and is the base of xìn.
If the base is not zhēngù,
one cannot achieve xìn.
Those whose sinews are strong and refined
are called courageous.
Courage
is the decisiveness of righteousness.
Metal is able to cut and sever,

If decisive but not courageous,
one cannot accomplish righteousness.
Those whose complexion is even and smooth
are called perceptive.
Perceptiveness
is the source of wisdom.
Water flows and penetrates,
thus it represents the source of wisdom.
If the source is not perceptive,
one cannot accomplish wisdom.
The five qualities have constant properties;
therefore, they are called the Five Constants (五常, Wǔcháng).
Therefore, it is said:
If straight but not firm, it is wood,
but if wood is strong and seeks excessive gain,
it loses its proper color.
If strong but not refined, it is force,
but if one lifts a cauldron and severs the kneecap,
one loses his proper strength.
To be inflexible and not upright leads to foolishness.
Being stubbornly self-opinionated
results in falling into dull-wittedness.
To be filled with *qì* (氣) but not clear leads to transgression.
Words are unclear and not smooth,
leading to unrestrainedness and lack of accomplishment.
To be unrestrained and not balanced leads to dissipation.
Loving wisdom without limit,
resulting in utter loss and ruin.
Thus, the quality of balance or imbalance lies in the *shén* (神).
*Shén* (神)
is the master of quality.
Therefore, if the *shén* (神) is balanced, then the quality is balanced;
if the *shén* (神) is imbalanced, then the quality is imbalanced.
The reality of brightness or darkness lies in the *jīng* (精).
*Jīng* (精)
is the root of reality.
Therefore, if the *jīng* (精) is wise, then the reality is bright;
if the *jīng* (精) is turbid, then the reality is dark.
The power of courage or cowardice lies in the sinews.
Sinews
are the function of power.
Therefore, if the sinews are strong, the posture is bold;
if the sinews are weak, the posture is timid.
The foundation of strength and weakness lies in the bones.
The bones
are the mechanism of this foundation.
Therefore, if the bones are thick, the foundation is strong;
if the bones are thin, the foundation is weak.
The determination of impulsiveness and tranquility lies in the *qì*.
*Qì*
is the place of this determination.
If the *qì* is abundant,
the determination will be impulsiveness;
if the *qì* is harmonious,
the determination will be tranquility.
The feelings of gloom and joy lie in the complexion.
The complexion
is the indicator of these feelings.
Therefore, a sallow complexion arises from gloomy feelings;
a cheerful complexion arises from joyful feelings.
The appearance of decline and correctness lies in deportment.
Deportment
is the outward manifestation of form.
Therefore, declining deportment arises from precarious form;
correct deportment arises from respectful form.
The movement of attitude lies in countenance;
countenance
is the symbol of movement.
Therefore, if the movement is crooked, the countenance is sorrowful;
if the attitude is upright, the countenance is dignified.
The state of slowness and urgency lies in speech;
speech
is the expression of the mind.
Therefore, if the mind is forgiving, the speech is slow;
if the mind is biased, the speech is urgent.
If one is inherently simple and plain,
inwardly wise and outwardly bright,
with strong sinews and firm stance,
a clear voice and a pleasing countenance,
and respectful demeanor and upright bearing,
then one possesses pure virtue.
People possess *qì* (氣).
*Qì* (氣)
means that sincerity resides within;
it will inevitably manifest externally.
Therefore, those whose mind *qì* (氣) is coarse and contentious have a deep and scattered voice;
those whose mind *qì* (氣) is meticulous and cautious have a harmonious and measured voice;
those whose mind *qì* (氣) is base and perverse have a rough and fierce voice;
Their voice is coarse and rough;
those whose inner disposition is generous and gentle,
their voice is warm and smooth.
The qi of trustworthiness is central and easygoing,
the qi of righteousness is timely and expansive,
the qi of harmony is simple and concise,
the qi of courage is strong and upright.
This is called "listening to the qi."
Through their voice,
one can discern their true nature.
Qi gives birth to things,
things give birth to sounds.
Sounds have hardness, softness, clarity, and turbidity,

Listen to their voice,
observe their qi,
examine their actions,

There is also observing their complexion.
Observing the complexion

jiē kě yǐ sè qǔ zhī. can all be perceived through countenance.
Truly, wisdom

True wisdom

It is also said:
Truly benevolent people

The *Rén Wù Zhì* (鑑人術/Appreciating Personalities) states:

All things of this nature,

Furthermore, there is "examining intentions."

His demeanor is broad and gentle,

Tàigōng said:
"Broad in learning and eloquent in speech,

His appearance is upright and not insulting,

Again it is said:
Giving to him does not cause joy,

Commentary says:
Tàigōng said:

If their appearance is deceitfully flattering,

A Discussion says:
Yàn Zǐ said:

This is difficult to know and discern.
Xún Yuè said:
"To examine people's true feelings,

if one observes their words and actions,
"Not necessarily pleasing oneself but conforming to the Way

This is one aspect of observing people's feelings.
Showing no change in expression due to external things affecting joy and anger,

It is also said:
"Not being delighted by material honors,
not fearing sudden attacks,

such is truly a resolute and righteous person.
It is argued:
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"In the method of selecting men,
do not select the 'jiàn' 健."
"The 'jiàn' 健
is greedy."
The drawbacks of the 'jiàn' 健 are like this.
If one's heart changes easily with things that cause joy or anger,
if one's purpose is not well-governed when troubled by affairs,
if one's heart is moved by the lure of profit,

such a person has a base heart and feigns courage.
It is also said:
"If one is easily swayed by words,
One whose will cannot be firm,
who agrees but is indecisive,

One who is tested with things and quickly makes decisions,

The Discussion says:
Tàigōng says:
"One who has a name but no substance,
whose words differ when entering and exiting,

Such is the downfall of a person of intellect and thought."
bì yú shì yǐ."
If it is difficult to tempt with things,
difficult to persuade with words,
who adheres to one thing and does not know how to change,

The Discussion says:
A person of resolve guards his principles,
a foolish and obstinate person is difficult to change.
The fact that not changing is the same,
but the foolish and the wise are different,
is because the Way acts as a governing factor.
How do we say this?
The *Xīnyǔ* says:
"One who is skilled in adapting to change
cannot be exhausted by deception;
one who is versed in the Dao
cannot be startled by the bizarre;
one who is discerning in rhetoric
cannot be confused by words;

Therefore, the *jūnzǐ*'s hearing and seeing should be broad, but their selection should be careful;
their learning should be extensive, but their conduct should be sincere.
Their eyes are not distracted by dazzling colors,
