Even if offered the wealth of Qí and Lǔ, their will does not waver;
even if offered the longevity of Sōng and Qiáo, their actions do not change.
Then they can wholly embody the Dao and determine their integrity,
dedicate themselves to their affairs and establish their merit,
and observe their Daoist career."
This is how they differ from the foolish and stubborn.
If one rejects advice and does not heed it,
is selfish and does not protect others,
forces what is wrong,
that is slandering and envying others.
A discussion:

Duke Píng of Sòng 宋平公 feasted Zhāo Zǐ 昭子.
During the banquet, there was music and drinking,
and they spoke while weeping.
Yuè Qí 乐祁, assisting,
withdrew and told people,
"Will our ruler and Shū Sūn 叔孙 both die this year?
I have heard it said:
"To feel sorrow in joy, and joy in sorrow,
is to lose one's mind.
The essence of the mind,
this is called the soul (hún魄 hún pò).
If the seven spirits (hún) depart,
how can one last long?"
This year,
Shū Sūn and the Duke of Sòng both died.
The Yǐn Duke of Zhū came to court.
He held the jade high,
and his expression was haughty.
The Duke of Lǔ received the jade low,
and his expression was submissive.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Judging by the rules of propriety,
both rulers have the aura of death about them.
To hold high and look up
is arrogance.
To lower and look down
is to act as a substitute (for one's ancestors).
Arrogance is close to disorder,
and being a substitute is close to illness.
The ruler is the master,
and they will be the first to perish, won't they?"
In this year,
the Duke died.
In the seventh year of Duke Āi,
Duke Yì of Zhū returned.
The Marquis of Wèi met with the state of Wú in Yūn.
The people of Wú screened off the lodgings of the Marquis of Wèi.
Zǐ Gòng persuaded the Grand Steward Pǐ and secured his release.
When the Marquis of Wèi returned,
he imitated the language of the barbarian tribes.
Zǐ Zhī, who was still young, said:
"The ruler will certainly not escape calamity.
Did he die among the barbarians?
They seized him, and moreover, they adopted his words,
so following him was inevitable."
Later, he ultimately died in Chǔ.
The Duke of Lǔ built a Chǔ palace.
Mù Shū said:
"The "Tài Shì" says:
'What the people desire,
Heaven will surely grant.'
The lord desires Chǔ,
therefore he builds its palace.
If he does not return to Chǔ,
he will surely die in this palace."
On the day Xīn Sì in the sixth month,
the Duke died in the Chǔ palace.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Chōu to escort Sūn Línfù to Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi feasted him,
causing bitterness for Chéng Shū'áo.
Níng Zǐ, a grand master of Wèi, said:
"Will the Chéng family perish?
In ancient times, feasts were held
to observe deportment and examine fortune and misfortune.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
'The rhinoceros horn cup is curved,
the delicious wine is thought to be mellow.
Their interactions are not arrogant,
ten thousand blessings come to seek.'
Now, this master Áo,
This is the way to invite disaster."
In the seventeenth year,
the Xì family perished.
The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi met at Shāngrèn,
and were disrespectful.
Shū Xiàng said,
"These two rulers will certainly not escape calamity.
Assemblies and court audiences
are the warp and woof of ritual.
Ritual
is the carriage of government.
Government
is the protector of the person.
Neglecting ritual and losing government
results in instability,
and therefore chaos."
In the twenty-fifth year,
Qí murdered Guāng.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Wèi murdered Piāo.
One who speaks of spiritual nature sees it existing in demeanor and bearing.

In judging a person, one first looks at their face.
The face has the Five Peaks and Four Rivers.
The Five Peaks are:
the forehead is Mount Héng,
the chin is Mount Héng,
the nose is Mount Sōng,
The left cheekbone is Tài Shān,
the right cheekbone is Huà Shān.
The Four Rivers are:
the nostrils are the Jì River,
the mouth is the Hé River,
the eyes are the Huái River,
the ears are the Jiāng River.
The Five Peaks should be lofty, steep, round, and full;
the Four Rivers should be deep and wide,
with well-formed banks.
Those whose Five Peaks are well-formed
are wealthy;
if not full, then poor.
Those whose Four Rivers are well-formed
are noble;
if not well-formed, then lowly.
The Five Officials and Six Depots:
The Five Officials are:
the mouth, one;
the nose, two;
the ears, three;
the eyes, four;
the philtrum, five.
The Six Depots are:
the two lines above are two depots,
the two auxiliary corners are four depots,
the two balances above are six depots.
If one official is good,
Noble for ten years;
one palace good,
wealthy for ten years.
If the five offices and six palaces are all good,
wealth and nobility will be endless.
The left is for literature,
the right is for military affairs.
The nine provinces and eight extremes;
the nine provinces refers to
the forehead extending from left to right,
without vertical lines,
not broken or severed,
and shaped like an upturned liver is considered good.
The eight extremes refers to
standing on the nose and looking out,
the eight directions taking shape,
and not leaning towards each other is considered favorable.
The seven gates and two symbols;
the seven gates refers to
the two *jiān* gates,
the two *què* gates,
the two *mìng* gates,
and the one courtyard center.
The two symbols refers to
the head being round to imitate Heaven,
and the feet being square to resemble Earth.
Heaven should be high,
and Earth should be thick.
If the head is small and the feet are thin,
it indicates a person of poverty and low status.
If all seven apertures are well-formed,
it indicates a person of wealth and high status.
In summary,
the forehead represents Heaven,
the chin represents Earth,
the nose represents Humanity,
the left eye represents the Sun,
the right eye represents the Moon.
Heaven should be expansive,
Earth should be square,
Humanity should be deep and broad,
the Sun and Moon should be bright.
Good Heaven indicates nobility,
good Earth indicates wealth,
good Humanity indicates longevity,
good Sun and Moon indicate flourishing.
The upper court (shàng tíng) represents Heaven,
governing the nobility or lowliness of parents.
The middle court (zhōng tíng) represents Humanity,
governing siblings, wife, children, benevolence, righteousness, years and lifespan.
The lower court (xià tíng) represents Earth,
governing fields, houses, servants, livestock, food, and drink.

Chapter Seventeen: Hegemonic Ambition
Your minister has heard that when Zhōu 周 possessed the world,
it was governed for more than three hundred years.
During the flourishing reigns of Chéng Kāng,
punishments were laid aside for over forty years and not needed.
And when they declined,
it also lasted for over three hundred years.
Tài Gōng said to King Wén:
"Though one is subordinate to one person,
he is exalted above ten thousand;
only a virtuous person can achieve this."
Therefore, King Wén personally approached and met with six people,
sought out and met with ten people,
summoned and befriended a thousand people.
Friends of his friends were called associates (péng),
associates of associates were called factions (dǎng),
and factions of factions were called groups (qún).
By befriending the virtuous people of the world in this way,
two out of every three returned to him.
Thus it was said:
"Possessing two-thirds of the world,
he served the Yīn."
This is what it meant.
Therefore, the Five Hegemons
(bà)
arose in succession.
A Hegemon constantly assisted the Son of Heaven,
promoting benefits and eliminating harm,
punishing the violent and forbidding the wicked,
rectifying the world within the seas,
in order to honor the Son of Heaven.
After the Five Hegemons had passed away,
there were no virtuous and wise men to continue their legacy.
The Son of Heaven was isolated and weak,
and his commands were not carried out.
The feudal lords acted as they pleased,
the strong bullied the weak,
and the many oppressed the few.
The King of Wú asked Wǔ Xū,
"How should we attack Chǔ?"
He replied,
"Chǔ has many officials in power who are at odds with each other,
and none of them are capable of dealing with trouble.
If you divide your army into three divisions to harass them,
when one division arrives,
they will surely all come out to meet it.
When they come out, we retreat;
when they retreat, we attack again.
Chǔ will surely be exhausted by these tactics.
Harass them frequently to tire them out,
and use various methods to mislead them.
Once they are exhausted,
then follow up with all three armies,
and you will surely achieve a great victory."
Hé Lǘ followed his advice.
This was the beginning of Chǔ's decline.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè asked the Grand Master Zhǒng,
"How should we attack Wú?"
He replied,
"There are seven stratagems for attacking Wú:
Their outlines are as follows:
Respect Heaven and serve the spirits,
in order to promote their wickedness;
Send them beautiful gifts,
in order to dazzle their will;
Send them skilled artisans,
to have them build palaces,
in order to exhaust their wealth;
Send them flattering ministers,
so that they become easier to attack;
Strengthen their remonstrating ministers,
to cause them to commit suicide;
Make strong armor and sharp weapons,
in order to take advantage of their weaknesses."
Thereupon, the King of Yuè adorned the beautiful Xī Shī,
and presented her to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú delighted in her.
Zǐ Xū remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
The King of Wú executed Zǐ Xū.
Yuè then made a glorious lintel,
inlaid with gold,
and presented it to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú accepted it,
and began building the Gū Sū Terrace,
which took five years to complete,
with the common people dying on the roads.
Yue again steamed millet seeds and presented them to the King of Wu.
The King of Wu ordered his men to plant them,
but they did not grow.
Wu experienced a great famine.
Duke Huan of Qi wanted to weaken Chu,
so he minted money
and bought live deer in Chu.
Chu heard of this,
and was delighted.
They abandoned agriculture to raise deer.
Duke Huan stored five times the usual amount of grain.
Chu had plenty of money but lacked grain.
Duke Huan then closed the borders.
Four or five out of every ten in Chu surrendered.
At the Alliance of Ke,
Duke Huan wanted to violate the agreement with Cao Zhu.
Guan Zhong therefore trusted him,
and the feudal lords consequently returned to Qi.
Therefore, it is said:
"Knowing how to give in order to take
is the treasure of governance."
Duke Huan of Zheng wanted to attack Kuai.
He first inquired about the heroes, good ministers, and eloquent speakers of Kuai,
recorded their names,
selected good fields of Kuai to bestow upon them,
created titles of offices and recorded them,
and prepared them outside the boundaries and outer gates,
consecrating them with the blood of roosters and boars.
The ruler of Kuài (鄶) thought there was internal strife,
so he killed them all.
Duke Huán (桓公) then took the opportunity to attack Kuài (鄶).
All of these are examples of feudal lords acting arbitrarily,
and the Son of Heaven's orders not being followed."
Tián Cháng (田常) usurped Qí (齊),
the Six Ministers divided Jìn (晉),
and together they became the Warring States.
This was the beginning of the people's suffering.
The Marquis of Qí (齊侯) was sitting with Yàn Zǐ (晏子) in an open-air chamber.
The Marquis sighed and said:
"How beautiful is this chamber!
Who will own it?"
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) said:
"According to your words,
it will be the Chén (陳) family?
Although the Chén (陳) family has no great virtue,
they do give to the people.
The amounts of dòu (豆), qū (區), fǔ (釜), and zhōng (鍾)
that they take from the public are small,
but what they give to the people is generous.
The Marquis levies heavily,
and the Chén (陳) family gives generously,
so the people return to them.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Although they give us no virtue,
we sing and dance.'
The Chén (陳) family's generosity
People sang and danced about it.
(They said,) "If the succession is slightly neglected,
and the Chén family is not eliminated,
then the state will truly belong to them!"
Later, he indeed usurped Qí.
Zhì Bó, along with the rulers of Hán and Wèi, attacked Zhào.
Hán and Wèi secretly plotted rebellion.
Zhì Guǒ said:
"The two kings are probably about to change their allegiance.
It would be better to kill them;
if we don't kill them,
then we should befriend them."
Zhì Bó said:
"How can we befriend them?"
Zhì Guǒ said:
"Wèi Xuānzǐ's strategist, Zhào Jiā,
and Hán Kāngzǐ's strategist, Duàn Guī,
are both capable of changing their lords' plans.
Your Lordship should agree with the two lords to destroy Zhào,
and then grant each of these two advisors a county of ten thousand households.
If you do this,
then the hearts of the two lords can be prevented from changing."
Zhì Bó did not listen.
Hán and Wèi indeed rebelled
and killed Zhì Bó.
Thereupon, strong states focused on military achievements,
and weak states focused on defense.
Alliances were formed both vertically and horizontally.
Chariots sped along, their axles bumping against each other;
armor bred lice;
the people had no one to tell their troubles to.
When Qin finally nibbled away at the empire,
and swallowed up the Warring States,
unified the government within the seas,
destroyed the cities of the feudal lords,
the laws were strict and the government severe,
and flatterers were numerous.
They sent Méng Tián to lead troops to attack the northern Hú,
and Wèi Tuō to lead soldiers to garrison Yuè,
stationing troops in useless lands,
and the people could barely survive.
When the First Emperor died,
the empire greatly rebelled.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng rose up in Chén.
Chén Shè and Wú Guǎng were garrisoning Yúyáng,
and encamped at Dàzé.
They encountered rain,
and the roads were impassable.
They realized they had missed the deadline,
and missing the deadline meant execution.
So the two men plotted and said:
"Now we have missed the deadline,
and we will be executed.
Now if we start a great undertaking, we will also die.
Since we will die anyway,
might we as well do it for the country?"
Thereupon, he first used ghosts and spirits to awe the crowd,
and then executed the officers.
He summoned his followers and said:
"You all encountered rain,
and have all missed the deadline.
Missing the deadline warrants execution.
Even if, by some chance, we are spared execution but sent to garrison,
the dead will certainly amount to sixteen or seventeen out of ten.
If a brave man does not die, then so be it,
but if he dies, then let him raise a great name.
Are lords, kings, generals, and ministers
born with special lineage?"
The followers all said:
"We respectfully accept your command."
Thereupon, they divided up and led troops to conquer territories,
and he established himself as King Chén.
Wǔ Chén and Zhāng Ěr rose up in Zhào.
Wǔ Chén roughly pacified the Zhào territory,
and took the title Lord Wǔxìn.
Kuǎi Tōng persuaded Xú Gōng, the magistrate of Fànyáng, saying:
"I, Kuǎi Tōng, am from Fànyáng.
I secretly pity that you, sir, are about to die,
therefore, I come to offer condolences.
However,
I also congratulate you on encountering Tōng and gaining life."
Xú Gōng bowed twice and said:
"How should I condole you?"
Tōng said,
"You have been magistrate for ten years,
killing people's fathers,
orphaning people's sons,
cutting off people's feet,
tattooing people's faces,
doing so to a great number of people.
Yet the compassionate fathers and filial sons dared not stab you in the stomach with their blades,
because they feared the laws of Qín.
Now the world is in great turmoil,
and the policies of Qín are not enforced,
so the compassionate fathers and filial sons will strive to stab you in the stomach with their blades,
to avenge their grievances,
and establish their fame.
This is why Tōng is here to condole you."
He said,
"How should I congratulate you on the birth of your son?"
Tōng said,
"Zhào Wǔxìn Jūn did not know of my unworthiness,
and sent people to inquire after me,
asking if I was alive or dead.
I met with Wǔxìn Jūn and told him:
'You must conquer in battle before seizing territory,
and only after attacking successfully will you take cities of the empire.
I secretly consider this dangerous.
If you use my plan,
you can seize territory without fighting,
To capture a city without attacking,
to pacify a thousand *lǐ* by sending out a proclamation,
is that possible?"
That general said,
"What do you mean?"
Thereupon, I explained,
"The magistrate of Fànyáng is the type who would prepare his soldiers
to defend the city in battle.
He is cowardly and fears death,
greedy and loves wealth and status.
Therefore, he intends to be the first to surrender his city to you,
but if surrendering to you first does not benefit him,
then the cities in the border region will all tell each other,
'The magistrate of Fànyáng surrendered first, but died.'
They will certainly strengthen their defenses and hold firm,
making each city an impregnable fortress,
impossible to attack.
My plan for you, sir,
is to greet the magistrate of Fànyáng with a yellow-draped carriage and vermillion wheels,
and have him ride swiftly through the outskirts of Yān and Zhào.
Then the border cities will all tell each other,
'The magistrate of Fànyáng surrendered first, and became rich and noble!'
They will certainly lead each other in surrendering,
like a ball rolling down a slope.'
This is what I mean by pacifying a thousand *lǐ* by sending out a proclamation."
Lord Xú bowed twice,
and prepared carriages and horses to send Tōng.
Tōng then used this argument to persuade Wǔ Chén.
Wǔ Chén, with a hundred chariots and two hundred horsemen, and the seal of a marquis,
welcomed Duke Xú.
and more than thirty cities surrendered,
as Kuǎi Tōng had planned.
Yān and Zhào heard of this,
Xiàng Liáng raised troops in Wú.
The magistrate of Wú, Xiàng Yǔ, killed the acting governor Tōng.
Thereupon, he raised troops and started the uprising in Wú.
Wú,
is now Sūzhōu.
Tián Dān raised troops in Qí.
Dān, along with some young men,
tied up a slave and intended to kill him
to show the magistrate of Dí,
and then killed the magistrate and raised troops.
Jǐng Jū raised troops in Yǐng,
Zhōu Shì raised troops in Wèi,
Hán Guǎng raised troops in Yān.
In remote mountains and accessible valleys,
heroes rose up together,
and the Qin clan was destroyed.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn's given name was Bāng,
courtesy name Jì,
His surname was Liú
, he was a native of Fēngyì in the Pèi principality,
and he was the head of a post station on the Sì River.
In the first year of the Second Emperor of Qín,
Chén Shèng and others rose in revolt,
and Shèng declared himself King of Chǔ.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú remonstrated, saying:
"General, you have devised a plan involving ten thousand deaths
to rid the world of harm.
Now, you have only just arrived at Chén,
and you are already declaring yourself king.
This is showing the world your selfish intentions.
It would be better to establish the successors of the six states,
thereby creating allies for yourself,
and then advance your army westward.
Then the countryside will be free of battles and the cities will not need to defend their walls.
Execute the tyrannical Qín,
seize Xiányáng,
and use it to command the feudal lords;
then the world can be won."
Shèng did not listen.
The people of Pèi killed their magistrate
and established Gāozǔ as the Duke of Pèi.
At this time, Xiàng Liáng was staying in Xuē,
and the Duke of Pèi went to follow him,
and together they established the Righteous Emperor.
Fàn Zēng persuaded Xiàng Liáng, saying:
"When Qín destroyed the six states,
Chǔ was the most innocent.
Since King Huái of Chǔ entered Qín and did not return,
the people of Chǔ pitied him.
Therefore, the saying goes:
"Even if Chǔ has only three households,
Chǔ will surely destroy Qín."
Now that Chén Shèng initiated the uprising,
but did not establish a descendant of Chǔ,
his power will not last long.
Now that you rise up in Jiāngdōng,
and the generals of Chǔ rise up with you,
they all vie to attach themselves to you,
because you are a general of Chǔ for generations,
and are able to re-establish a descendant of Chǔ."
Liáng then sought out Xīn, a grandson of King Huái, and established him.
They made an agreement saying:
"Whoever enters Xiányáng first will be made king."
The Qín general Zhāng Hán
greatly defeated Xiàng Liáng at Dìngtáo.
Liáng died.
Zhāng Hán thought that Chǔ was not worth worrying about,

Chǔ sent Xiàng Yǔ and others to rescue Zhào,

Pèi Gōng then attacked Wǎn,
and made it surrender.
Pèi Gōng attacked Wǎn,
but the governor of Nányáng, Lǚ Qí, defended the city and refused to surrender.
Pèi Gōng wanted to then proceed westward.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Powerful Qín is ahead,
and the army of Wǎn is behind;
this is a dangerous path."
Thereupon, he besieged Wǎn.
Wǎn was in dire straits.
Lǚ Qí wanted to commit suicide.
A retainer of his, Chén Huī, climbed over the city wall to see Pèi Gōng,

"The officials and people of Wǎn, fearing death, are firmly defending the city.
If you, Your Excellency, attack it all day,

If you withdraw your troops and leave,
Wǎn will certainly follow you.
You, Your Excellency, have already broken the agreement regarding Xiányáng.
Now you will have the trouble of a strong Wǎn.
It would be better to accept their surrender,
enfeoff its defender,
and lead its armored soldiers westward.
The cities that have not yet surrendered

Pèi Gōng said:
"Good."
He enfeoffed Lǚ Qí as the Marquis of Yīn.
He attacked Wǔ Pass
and greatly defeated the Qín army.
Zhào Gāo killed Èr Shì,
They established Zǐ Yīng 子嬰 as ruler and

Zhāng Liáng 張良 said:

Order Lì Yìjī 酈食其 to bribe the Qin general with heavy treasures."
The Qin general indeed desired to ally and head west together.
Pèi Gōng 沛公 wanted to listen to him.
Liáng 良 said:

Thereupon, they attacked the Qin army

They entered Xiányáng 咸陽 and

The Qin people offered cattle and wine.
Pèi Gōng 沛公 declined and did not accept them.
Thereupon, the people knew of his virtue.
He sent troops to defend the pass,
intending to be king of Guānzhōng 關中.
At this time,
Xiàng Yǔ 項羽 defeated the Qin army north of the Yellow River,

Pèi Gōng, through Xiàng Bó, explained himself to Yǔ.
Yǔ then killed Zǐ Yīng and established the eastern capital at Péngchéng.
He established Pèi Gōng as the King of Hàn,

The King of Hàn was unwilling to go to his fief,

Xiāo Hé said:

Moreover, the *Book of Odes* says,
'The Milky Way,'

He who can humble himself under one person,

Tāng and Wǔ are examples of this.

Thereupon, he used Hán Xìn's plan,

This is about the King of Hàn going to his domain.
Hán Xìn fled from Chǔ

Several times he spoke with Xiāo Hé,

Xìn completed the ceremony of obeisance,

"The Prime Minister has repeatedly spoken of you, General,

Xìn thanked him,

"Now, those who turn eastward to compete for power over the world,

He said:
"It is."
Xìn said:

The Hàn Wáng was silent for a long time,

Xìn bowed again and congratulated him, saying:

Xiàng Wáng can roar and shout angrily,

Xiàng Wáng treats people with respect, reverence and affection,
his words are warm and caring,
When people are ill,

But when it comes to granting titles to those who deserve it for their merits,

This is what is called the kindness of a woman.
Although Xiàng Wáng dominated China and made the feudal lords his subjects,

He violated the agreement with Emperor Yì,

When the feudal lords saw Xiàng Wáng move and exile Emperor Yì to the south of the Yangtze River,

Wherever Xiàng Wáng passed,

The world was full of resentment,

Although he was called a Hegemon,

Therefore, it is said:
His strength can easily be turned to weakness.
Now, if Your Majesty can truly reverse his ways,

Use the cities and towns of the world to reward meritorious ministers,

is because you consider Hàn to be weak.
Although the Chǔ army is strong,
the world condemns it for its unjust reputation,
because it broke its agreement and murdered Ỳì Dì.
However, the Chǔ Wáng relies on his victories and considers himself strong,
while the Hàn Wáng gathers the lords,
and returns to defend Xíngyáng.
He transports grain from Shǔ and Hàn,
digs deep moats and builds high ramparts,
dividing his soldiers to guard the passes and block the roads.
The Chǔ army returns,
isolated within the territory of Liáng,
penetrating eight or nine hundred *lǐ* deep into enemy territory.
If they want to fight, they cannot;
if they want to attack a city, their strength is insufficient;
the old and weak transport provisions from a thousand *lǐ* away.
The Chǔ troops have arrived at Xíngyáng and Chénggāo,
but the Hàn tenaciously defends without moving.
If they advance, they cannot attack;
if they retreat, they cannot be relieved.
Therefore, it is said:
Chǔ is not reliable.
If Chǔ wins,
then the feudal lords will naturally feel endangered and come to each other's rescue.
The strength of Chǔ
is only enough to attract the armies of the world.
Therefore, Chǔ is inferior to Hàn;
this situation is easy to see.
Now, Your Majesty does not side with the all-safe Hàn,
but entrusts yourself to the precarious and doomed Chǔ.
I, your servant, am perplexed by this for Your Majesty.
It is not that the troops of Huáinán are enough to destroy Chǔ.
If Your Majesty sends troops to betray Chǔ,
Xiàng Wáng will surely be delayed in Qí for several months.
Hàn's taking of the world
can be done with perfect assurance.
I, your servant, request to return to Hàn with Your Majesty, sword in hand.
The Hàn King will surely divide land and share it with Your Majesty.
Moreover, what about Huáinán?
It will surely belong to Your Majesty.
Therefore, I, your servant, offer this foolish plan,
"I hope Your Majesty will pay attention to this."
The King of Huáinán:
"I will respectfully obey your command."
Secretly he agreed to rebel against Chǔ and join Hàn,
but he did not dare reveal it.
An envoy from Chǔ was in Huáinán,
urgently pressing Yīng Bù to dispatch troops.
He was staying at the official guesthouse.
Suí Hé went straight in,
and sat in the seat above the Chǔ envoy,
saying:
"The King of Jiǔjiāng has already returned to Hàn,
how can Chǔ command him to dispatch troops?"
Bù was stunned.
The Chǔ envoy rose.
Hé then persuaded Bù, saying:
"The matter is already formed.
You should kill the Chǔ envoy alone,
and not allow him to return,
and quickly go to Hàn and combine your forces."
So he did as the Hàn envoy had instructed.
Thereupon, he killed the Chǔ envoy,
and then raised troops to attack Chǔ.
The King of Hàn went to Xíngyáng,
and sent Hán Xìn to attack Wèi King Bào,
capturing him.
The King of Hàn asked Lì Shēng, saying:
"Who is the great general of the King of Wèi?"
He said,
"Bó Zhí."
The king said,
"His mouth still has the smell of milk;
he cannot match Féng Jìng, a cavalry general under Hán Xìn."
The king said,
"He cannot match Guàn Yīng's infantry general, Xiàng Tā."
The king said,
"He cannot match Cáo Shēn.
With him present,
I have no worries."
Thereupon, the king appointed Xìn as the Left Chancellor to attack Wèi.
Xìn advanced his troops,
displaying boats as if intending to cross at Línjìn,
and Wèi gathered troops to resist him.
Xìn then ambushed troops, crossing the river from Xiàyáng using earthenware jars to transport the army,
and attacked Ānyì,
capturing the Wèi king, Bào.
Then he advanced his troops to attack Zhào.
The Hàn forces then confronted the Chǔ forces at Xíngyáng.
The Chǔ forces besieged the Hàn king.
Using Chén Píng's plan,
he secretly escaped.
The Hàn king urgently asked Chén Píng:
"Where did this plan come from?"
Chén Píng said,
"The Chǔ king, Xiàng Wáng's, loyal and steadfast ministers, like Yàfù, Zhōnglí Mò and others,
are no more than a few people.
"If Your Majesty can contribute tens of thousands of jīn
to implement counter-espionage,
sow discord between the ruler and his ministers
to create suspicion in their minds,
Xiang Yu’s Xiàng Yǔ character is such that
he is suspicious and believes slander.
Internal strife will certainly occur.
Then Hàn can take advantage of this and attack him.
Defeating Chǔ will be certain."
The King of Hàn then gave four myriad jīn to Píng,
allowing him to do as he pleased,
without questioning the expenditure.
Píng, having obtained much jīn, liberally employed counter-espionage in the Chǔ army,
declaring that generals such as Zhōnglí Mò 中離末 had performed many meritorious deeds for Xiang Yu Xiàng Yǔ,
but ultimately were not able to have land divided and enfeoffed to them:
"[They] want to unite with Hàn
to eliminate the Xiang Clan Xiàng Shì,
and divide and rule its territory."
Xiang Yu Xiàng Yǔ indeed became suspicious.
He sent an envoy to Hàn.
Hàn prepared a grand sacrificial feast,
and when he raised it to present it to the Chǔ envoy,
he feigned surprise, saying:
"I thought it was a messenger from Yàfù 亞父!
So it is an envoy from King Xiang Xiàng Wáng."
He then took it away
and presented the Chǔ envoy with inferior provisions.
The envoy returned
He reported the matter to Xiàng Wáng [項王].
Xiàng Wáng [項王] greatly suspected Yàfù [亞父].
Yàfù [亞父] wanted to urgently attack Hàn Wáng [漢王],
but Xiàng Wáng [項王] did not believe Yàfù [亞父].
Yàfù [亞父], hearing that Xiàng Wáng [項王] was suspicious,
then said:
"The affairs of the empire are mostly settled!
Your Majesty, do it yourself.
I wish to be granted leave to retire."
Xiàng Wáng [項王] agreed.
He entered the pass to gather troops
and wished to return east.
Yuán Shēng [轅生] advised Hàn Wáng [漢王]:
"Send troops to Wǎn [宛] and Yè [葉],
drawing Xiàng Wáng [項王] south across the river,
so that Hán Xìn [韓信] and the others can gather in Héběi [河北]."
Yǔ [羽]'s troops indeed led the army south across the river,
according to his plan.
Yuán Shēng [轅生] said:
"Hàn [漢] and Chǔ [楚] have been confronting each other at Xíngyáng [滎陽] and Chénggāo [成皋] for several months,
and Hàn [漢] has been in distress.
I wish that Your Majesty would march out of Wǔ Pass [武關],
and Xiàng Wáng [項王] will certainly lead his troops south.
Your Majesty should fortify your position deeply,
so that Xíngyáng [滎陽] and Chénggāo [成皋] can have a respite.
Let Hán Xìn [韓信] and others gather in the lands of Zhào [趙] north of the river,
then Your Majesty can again attack Xíngyáng [滎陽].
If this is done,
Then Chǔ's preparations would be extensive,
and its forces divided.
Hàn would be able to rest
and then fight them again.
Defeating Chǔ would be certain."
The Hàn King followed this plan
and sent out troops to the area between Wǎn and Yè.
Xiàng Wáng heard that the Hàn King was in Wǎn
and indeed led his troops south across the river,
just as Yuán Shēng had predicted.
Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr,
with tens of thousands of troops,
went east, descended Jǐngxíng, and attacked Zhào,
defeating them.
He then reported to Hàn
and requested that Zhāng Ěr be established as the King of Zhào
to pacify that state.
The Hàn King followed this advice.
Initially,
the King of Zhào and Chéng'ān Jūn Chén Yú heard that Hàn was about to attack them
and gathered troops at the mouth of Jǐngxíng.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn Lǐ Zuǒchē advised,
"I have heard that the Hàn general Hán Xìn crossed the Xīhé,
captured the King of Wèi,
captured Xià Yuè,
and recently shed blood at Èryǔ.
Now, aided by Zhāng Ěr,
they plan to attack Zhào.
With this advantage, they are leaving their country to fight far away,
their momentum is irresistible.
Your servant has heard:
To transport provisions a thousand *lǐ*,
the soldiers will have the look of hunger;
When firewood is gathered after cooking is done,
the army will not have a satisfying meal for the night.
Now, the road through Jǐngxíng
is such that chariots cannot travel abreast,
and cavalry cannot form ranks.
Traveling for several hundred *lǐ*,
their provisions will inevitably be at the rear.
I hope Your Excellency will lend me 30,000 elite troops
to take a roundabout route,
and cut off their supplies and baggage.
Your Excellency should dig deep trenches and build high ramparts,
holding the fortified camp and not engaging in battle,
so that those at the front cannot fight,
and those who retreat cannot return.
My elite troops will cut off their rear,
and they will have nothing to plunder in the countryside.
In less than ten days,
the heads of the two generals
can be delivered beneath your banner.
I hope Your Excellency will pay attention to my plan.
If not,
you will surely be captured by those two."
Chéng'ān Jūn did not listen to Guǎngwǔ Jūn.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn's strategy was not used.
Xìn heard of this and
was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, he advanced his troops to attack Zhao
and defeated them.
When Zhao was defeated,
Hán Xìn ordered the army not to kill Guǎngwǔ Jūn.
Anyone who could capture him alive
would be rewarded with a thousand gold pieces.
Consequently, someone bound Guǎngwǔ Jūn and brought him to Xìn's presence.
Xìn then untied him
and treated him as a teacher.
He asked,
"I intend to attack Yan in the north
and conquer Qi in the south.
How can I succeed?"
Guǎngwǔ Jūn declined, saying,
"I have heard that
A defeated general
should not be spoken to about courage;
a minister of a destroyed state
should not be consulted about plans for survival.
Now, I am a captive of defeat and destruction,
how can I be worthy to weigh important matters!"
Xìn said:
"I have heard that:
Bǎilǐ Xī resided in Yú and Yú perished,
resided in Qín and Qín became a hegemon.
It was not that he was stupid in Yú and wise in Qín,
it was a matter of whether his advice was heeded or not.
If Chéng'ān Jūn had listened to your plans,
someone like Xìn would also have been captured.
I entrust my heart and return to your plans,
I hope you will not decline."
Guǎngwǔ Jūn said:
"I have heard that:
even a wise man's thousand deliberations
will certainly have one mistake;
even a fool's thousand deliberations
will certainly have one correct point.
Therefore, it is said:
'The words of a madman,
a sage will choose from them.'
I only fear that my plans may not be sufficient for use,
I wish to offer my foolish loyalty.
Chéng'ān Jūn had plans for a hundred battles and a hundred victories,
but lost them in a single day,
his army was defeated below Hào,
and he died on the Zhī River.
Now you, General, have crossed the Xī River,
captured the King of Wèi,
captured Xià Shuō at Èryú,
cannot be falsified.
Therefore, they are listed thus.
Discoursing on Scholars, Seventh
Discoursing on Scholars, Seventh
Your servant has heard that Huáng Shígōng said:
"In the past, in times of great peace,
the feudal lords had two armies,
the regional governors had three armies,
and the Son of Heaven had six armies.
When the world is in chaos, rebellion arises;
When the king's beneficence is exhausted, oaths are used to punish each other;
When virtue is the same, there is no way to increase it;
Therefore, one must gather the hearts of heroes."
Therefore, it is said:
Gaining men leads to prosperity,
Losing scholars leads to collapse.
How can this be made clear?
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí (Qí Huán Gōng) wanted to see the petty official Jì.
He went three times in one day but could not get an audience.
His followers tried to stop him.
Duke Huán said,
"A scholar who is arrogant toward rank and emolument
surely disregards his lord.
A lord who is arrogant toward hegemonic kings
also disregards his scholars.
Granted that this gentleman is arrogant toward rank and emolument,
how dare I be arrogant toward hegemonic kings?"
Only after five visits was he able to see him.
The *Book* says,
"He who can find a teacher for himself becomes a king."
How can this be made clear?
King Xuān of Qí (Qí Xuān Wáng) said to Yán Chù,
"Chù, come forward."
Chù also said,
"Your Majesty, come forward."
It was debated,
"For Chù to come forward would be to admire power;
for the king to come forward would be to seek out scholars.
Rather than having Chù admire power,
it would be better to have the king seek out scholars."
King Xuān changed his expression and said,
"Is the king more esteemed?
Or is the scholar more esteemed?"
He replied,
"In the past, when Qín attacked Qí,
the decree stated:
'Anyone who dares to gather firewood within five hundred paces of the grave of Liǔ Xià Jì will
The decree stated:
'Anyone who can obtain the head of the King of Qí
one was mistaken about Zǎi Yǔ;
judging nature by appearance,
one was mistaken about Zǐ Yǔ.
However, the *Zhuan* (commentary) states:
"If one grieves without cause for worry,
worry will surely befall him;
if one rejoices without cause for celebration,
joy will surely revert to sorrow."
Thus, the heart has a precursory movement, and the spirit has precursory knowledge,
therefore, the countenance has a precursory manifestation.
Thus, Biǎn Què seeing Duke Huán
knew of his impending death;
Shēn Shū seeing Wū Chén,
knew of his secret affair with his wife.
Some leaped on horseback to dine on delicacies,
others flew to devour meat,
some became servants early and lords late,
some were initially punished and ended up as kings.
Copper cliffs could not satiate life,
jade banquets ended in starvation.
Therefore, their measuring tables, touching bones,
pointing to countenance, and extracting principles
be punished with death without pardon.'
will be enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households
and rewarded with a thousand yì of gold.'
Judging from this,
the value of the king's head
is not even comparable to the grave of a dead knight."
King Xuān ultimately used this as a pretext for military action.
King Xuān's attendants said:
"Your Majesty possesses a land of a thousand chariots
and erects bells of a thousand *shí*.
In all directions, east, south, west, and north,
none dare to disobey.
Now, the most exalted of scholars
are merely called commoners,
living on foot amidst the fields,
and are considered boorish, gatekeepers, and villagers.
The lowliness of scholars
is indeed extreme."
Chù said:
"In the time of the ancient Dà Yǔ,
there were ten thousand states ruled by feudal lords.
Shùn rose from the fields to become the Son of Heaven.
By the time of Tāng,
The feudal lords numbered three thousand.
In this present age,
those who face south and call themselves "I, the lonely one"
number only twenty-four.
Judging from this,
isn't it a matter of gains and losses?
Gradually they are being punished and extinguished,
when the time comes that their clans are wiped out,
even if they wish to be gatekeepers or neighborhood officials,
how can they attain it?
Doesn't the *Yì Zhuàn* (Commentary on the Book of Changes) say:
"Occupying a high position,
but not attaining its substance?"
Therefore, those who lack the substance but rejoice in the name are diminished;
those who lack the virtue but hope for the blessing are curtailed;
those who lack the merit but receive the emolument are disgraced;
disaster is certainly grasped.
Therefore it is said:
"Boasting of achievement does not establish one;
empty desires do not arrive."
These all boast of their names,
being outwardly splendid but lacking real virtue.
Therefore Yáo had nine assistants,
Shùn had ten friends,
Yǔ had five ministers,
Tāng had three counselors.
From ancient times until now,
there has been no one who could falsely establish a name for himself in the world.
Nothing exists [in isolation].
Therefore, the sovereign does not feel ashamed to ask frequently,
nor embarrassed to learn from inferiors,
and thus completes his Way.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Though noble,
one must take humbleness as the root;
though high,
one must take the foundation as low."
Therefore, lords and kings call themselves "gū" (孤, orphaned), "guǎ" (寡, widowed), and "bù gǔ" (不穀, unworthy).
Now, the orphaned and widowed are those in distressed and lowly positions,
and the lords and kings use these terms to refer to themselves,
is this not to show respect for the virtuous and worthy men by humbling themselves?
Fú Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
King Chéng of Zhōu appointed Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
and generation after generation they were praised for their brilliance,
thus showing clearly the value of men of worth."
A proverb says:
"Bathing need not be in the rivers or sea,
the important thing is to remove the dirt;
a horse need not be a *qí jì* (騏驥, a famous breed of horse),
the important thing is that it runs well;
a scholar need not be virtuous,
the important thing is that he understands the Way;
a woman need not be of noble lineage,
the important thing is that she is virtuous and good."
How can this be made clear?
Chún Yú Kūn said to King Xuān of Qí:
"In ancient times, people loved horses,
and Your Majesty also loves horses;
in ancient times, people loved fine flavors,
and Your Majesty also loves fine flavors;
in ancient times, people loved beauty,
and Your Majesty also loves beauty;
in ancient times, people loved talented men,
but Your Majesty alone does not love them!"
The king said:
"The state simply has no talented men.
If there were any, I, the lonely one, would also be pleased with them."
Kūn said:
"In ancient times there were Huá Liú and Qí Jì,
but today there are none.
Your Majesty chooses from the crowd,
and Your Majesty loves horses.
In ancient times there were the fetuses of leopards and elephants,
but today there are none.
Your Majesty chooses from the crowd,
and Your Majesty enjoys flavors.
In ancient times there were Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī,
but today there are none.
Your Majesty chooses from the crowd,
and Your Majesty loves beauty.
If Your Majesty must wait for men like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
before loving them,
zé Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng zhī shì,
would also not be fond of kingship."
Lǔ Zhònglián said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"Have you a fondness for scholars or not?"
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Wén has not obtained scholars, that is why."
He replied:
"Your Lordship's stable has hundreds of carriages of horses,
all are dressed in embroidered clothes and eat beans and grain,
how could there be excellent steeds like Qíjì and Lù'ěr?
The inner palace has ten consorts,
all wear white silk,
and eat fine grains and meat,
how could there be Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī?
When choosing beauty and horses, you select from the current age,
why must you wait for scholars of antiquity?
Therefore, it is said:
'You have no fondness for scholars.'" Zhāng Chǎng said in his "Letter to Zhū Yì":
"The hungry find sweet even the dregs and husks,
the full are satiated with fine grains and meat.
Why is this?
The circumstances of having and not having are different.
Formerly, Chén Píng, though wise,
had to wait for Wèi Qiàn before advancing;
Hán Xìn, though extraordinary,
relied on Xiāo Hé to be believed.
Therefore, scholars each achieve their suitability in their own time.
If one waits for the heroes of antiquity,
and only recommends those like Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng,
then this person will not advance because of your Lordship."
The 《Huáinán》 says:
"If one waits for fine-waisted horses and flying rabbits before driving,
then no one in the world would ride in a carriage;
if one waits for Xī Shī and the beauties of the Luò River before having consorts,
then one will never have a family in one's lifetime.
Thus, not waiting for the exceptional talents of antiquity but being content with what one has
means using them to the fullest extent of their abilities."
The *Yǔ* (sayings) states:
"A ship of jade and a raft of precious stones
are useless for crossing a river;
a bow of gold and a string of jade
are incapable of launching arrows.
Therefore, those who are excessively pure and without political skill
are not instruments for restoring order;
those who are refined scholars but lack governing abilities
are not supporting and helpful gentlemen."
How can this be demonstrated?
Wèi Wúzhī introduced Chén Píng to the Hàn King,
and the Hàn King employed him.
Jiàng and Guàn and others slandered Píng, saying,
"Píng committed incest with his sister-in-law and accepted bribes."
The Hàn King rebuked Wèi Wúzhī.
Wúzhī said,
"What I spoke of was
ability;
what Your Majesty heard was
Behavior.
Now, even if someone acts like Wěi Shēng 尾生 or Xiào Yǐ 孝已,
but it doesn't help in matters of victory or defeat,
would Your Majesty deign to employ them?
Now that the Chǔ 楚 and Hàn 漢 are facing off against each other,
I am bringing forward men with extraordinary plans.
If you consider their plans,
they are truly enough to benefit the state!
How can one doubt them for something like stealing from his sister-in-law or accepting gold?"
The King of Hàn 漢 said,
"Good."
Huáng Shí Gōng 黃石公 said:
"Men of purity and integrity
cannot be obtained through titles and emoluments;
men who uphold their principles
cannot be coerced through threats and punishments.
To attract men of purity and integrity,
observe the proper etiquette;
to attract men who uphold their principles,
cultivate the Way."
How can this be demonstrated?
Guō Wěi 郭隗 said to King Zhāo of Yān 燕昭王:
"The emperor dwells with teachers,
the king dwells with friends,
the hegemon dwells with ministers,
and the ruler of a doomed state dwells with servants and laborers.
If you humble yourself and serve them,
One who faces north to receive instruction
will have a hundred times himself come to him.
One who hastens forward and then rests,
who asks questions first and then remains silent,
will have ten times himself come to him.
If a person hastens as I hasten,
then one like myself will come to him.
If one leans on a stool and relies on a staff,
glancing around and pointing to give orders,
then servants will come to him.
If one acts wantonly, striking out in anger,
roaring with anger and yelling commands,
then only convict laborers will come to him."
These are the ways in ancient times to gain the service of men who valued the Dao.
Huáng Shí Gōng said:
"Ritual propriety
is where scholars return;
rewards
are where scholars will die.
Summon those to whom they return,
show them where they will die,
and those you seek will come."
How can this be made clear?
Wèi Wén Hóu's heir apparent, Tài Zǐ Jī, was discourteous to Tián Zǐfāng,
and Zǐfāng did not reciprocate with propriety.
The heir apparent was displeased
and said to Zǐfāng:
"Are the poor and lowly proud of others?
"Do the rich and noble act arrogantly towards others?"
Zǐ Fāng said:
"It is the poor and lowly who are arrogant.
How dare the rich and noble act arrogantly?
A ruler who is arrogant will lose his kingdom,
a high official who is arrogant will lose his family.
If the poor and lowly are not satisfied,
they can put on their shoes and leave.
Where can they go and *not* find poverty and lowliness?"
Sòng Yàn was the prime minister of Qí.
After being expelled and dismissed, he returned home.
He said to the officials:
"Is there anyone who can go with me to the feudal lords?"
They all held their staffs and stepped out of the ranks,
remaining silent and not answering.
Yàn said:
"Alas!
Why is it that scholar-officials are easy to find but difficult to use?"
Chén Ráo said:
"It is easy to raise up scholar-officials, but difficult to use them.
You, sir, are unable to use them;
if you are unable to use them,
then they will have feelings of discontent.
This is losing it yourself and blaming others."
Yàn said:
"What is the explanation for that?"
He replied:
"Three *shēng* of millet
If the supply to the shì (士, scholars/officers) is insufficient,
while Your Lordship has surplus grain to feed geese and ducks,
this is the first fault of Your Lordship.
The fruits in the orchards, pears, chestnuts,
are used by the women in the rear palace
to strike and throw at each other,
yet the shì (士, scholars/officers) have never tasted them even once,
this is the second fault of Your Lordship.
Fine silks and thin gauzes,
beautifully displayed in the halls,
are worn out by the wind,
yet the shì (士, scholars/officers) cannot even use them as trimming,
this is the third fault of Your Lordship.
Now, wealth
is what Your Lordship considers light;
death
is what the shì (士, scholars/officers) consider heavy.
If Your Lordship cannot practice what you consider light,
yet wants to make the shì (士, scholars/officers) dedicate what they consider heavy,
it is like keeping a lead knife
and using a Gān Jiàng (干將, a famous sword),
isn't that difficult?"
Sòng Yàn (宋燕) said:
"This is Yàn's (燕) fault."
The *Yǔ* (語, sayings) says:
"People with the same brightness see each other,
those with the same hearing hear each other.
If virtue aligns, they are intimate even without meeting;
"If sounds are the same, then even in different locations they resonate."
Hánzǐ 韓子 said:
"If inclinations to accept and reject are the same, then they agree with each other;
if inclinations to accept and reject are different, then they disagree with each other."
How can this be made clear?
Chǔ Wēi Wáng 楚威王 asked Sòng Yù 宋玉,
"Does the Master perhaps have any shortcomings in his conduct?
Why is it that the scholars, people, and commoners do not praise you very much?"
Sòng Yù 宋玉 said,
"Now, among birds there is the phoenix, and among fish there is the whale.
The phoenix soars upward for ninety thousand *lǐ* [0.5 km],
gliding about above the deep obscurity.
Now, the sparrow of the fence,
how could it be able to fathom the height of heaven and earth?
The whale sets out in the morning from the ruins of Kūnlún 崑崙,
and sleeps in the evening at Mèngjīn 孟津.
Now, the newt in a foot of swamp,

Chapter Eight: Governance
The ancient establishment of emperors and kings

It was because, in the world,

and the deceitful cheat the foolish,

Because the wisdom of one person

therefore they established the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers to assist him.

Now, the governance of education and instruction

How do I say this?
Guǎnzi said:
"To place the state on a ground that will not collapse

King Wǔ of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ, saying:

What should be done to achieve this?"
The response was:
"Attack and defense follow the same path,

are essential preparations.
Therefore, it is said:
Harmony can be used for defense, but strictness cannot;
strictness is not as reliable as harmony.
Harmony can be used for attack, but strictness cannot;
strictness is not as effective as harmony.
Therefore, when the feudal lords issue policies and enact laws,
if their policies are fair to the people,
this is called civil administration.
Treating scholars respectfully and employing officials,
if their rituals are respectful to the people,
this is called civil propriety.
Hearing lawsuits and judging punishments,
if their governance is benevolent to the people,
this is called civil execution.
Therefore, if these three civil qualities are established in governance,
and principles are followed,
yet one defends and fails to preserve,
or attacks and fails to conquer,
from ancient times to the present,
such a thing has never been heard of."
