one must consult public opinion,
Consider its timeliness and suitability;
employ it only when absolutely necessary;
unless there is a major reason,
do not follow it.”
Those who understand the times
can be established as leaders.
Fàn Lǐ 范蠡 said:
"When the time has not arrived,
It cannot be forced to grow;
if a matter is not thoroughly investigated,
it cannot be forced to completion."
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"A sage can assist the times,
but cannot go against the times."
The *Yǔ* [Discourses] says:
"A sage cultivates preparedness to await the opportune time."
One who is discerning about the times,
perceptive about employment,
and capable of providing for the officials,
can be supported as a ruler.
A Discussion says:
Xún Qīng said:
"If one steals the methods of a true king
and has the people of a true king implement them,
then he too will become a true king;
if one steals the methods of a hegemon
and has the people of a hegemon implement them,
then he too will become a hegemon;
if one steals the methods of a state doomed to ruin
and has the people of a state doomed to ruin implement them,
then he too will be doomed to ruin.
If one works with a virtuous man who accumulates ritual propriety,
then he will become a true king;
if one works with officers who are upright, sincere, and trustworthy,
then he will become a hegemon;
if one works with people who are scheming and subversive,
then it will perish.
These three
are what an enlightened ruler carefully selects;
this is being able to discern talent in employing them."
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 said:
"Those in high positions who are not benevolent
should not be entrusted with the state's power;
those who do not yield to the worthy
should not be given positions of honor;
those who avoid punishing relatives
should not be made commanders;
those who do not value fundamental matters
should not be entrusted with governing cities."
He also said:
"If the worthy are rewarded based on their abilities,
then the ruler will be esteemed;
if warriors are rewarded based on their merits,
then soldiers will readily die for the cause.
If these two are established in the state,
then the world will be governed well."
Fù Zǐ 傅子 said:
"The assessment of commanderies and counties has six aspects:
first, assessment based on education and instruction,
then officials will value virtue;
second, assessment based on honesty and fundamentals,
then officials will value conduct;
third, assessment based on talent and responsibility,
then officials will be careful in their selections;
Fourth, use service duties to assess fairness;
then officials will be cautious in their duties.
Fifth, use agricultural quotas to assess equality;
then officials will be cautious in their responsibilities.
Sixth, use judicial cases to assess litigation;
then officials will be cautious in their judgments.
This is how to equip officials."
Therefore, it is said:

"Clarify the registers, examine the decades and fives (groupings of households), limit the fields of laborers, establish criminal laws, establish rulers, emphasize agriculture and sericulture, eliminate frivolous occupations, encourage learning and emulation, examine talents and skills, select the valiant and robust, cultivate military preparations, strictly enforce prohibitions and commands, be faithful in rewards and punishments, correct idleness, and observe harsh and oppressive conduct."
These fifteen things,
even if a sage were to rise again,
he would surely speak of these things.
If you wish to discuss the changes in length and shortness (advantage and disadvantage),
therefore establish the way of governance as a constant.
*Jūn Dé* Ninth
*Jūn Dé* Ninth
The Three Sovereigns were without words,
their transformations flowed to the four seas,
therefore the world had nowhere to attribute merit.
Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng,
are called the Three Sovereigns.
The Emperor embodies Heaven and models Earth,
with words and commands,
and the world is peaceful.
Ruler and ministers yield merit,
transformations are practiced in the four seas,
The common people did not know the reason why.
Therefore, even if the envoys were not rewarded for their meritorious service with ritual,
it was beautiful and harmless.
Huángdì 黃帝,
followed the order of Heaven and Earth,
seasonally sowed the various grains,
diligently applied his mind, strength, ears, and eyes,
economized on the use of water, fire, and seasonal resources,
and possessed the auspicious signs of the virtue of Earth.
Therefore, he was called Huángdì 黃帝.
Zhuānxū 顓頊
nurtured resources to suit the land,
regulated time to mirror Heaven,
relied on spirits to establish righteousness,
governed the Qi to educate and transform,
purely and sincerely performed sacrifices.
All things that moved and were still,
both great and small deities,
wherever the sun and moon shone,
were all made sharp and refined.
Gāoxīn 高辛,
took the wealth of the land and used it sparingly,
cherished and taught the myriad people and benefited them with instruction,
calculated the days and months to welcome and send them off,
understood the spirits and respectfully served them.
His appearance was lush and flourishing,
his virtue was exceedingly high.
Dì Yáo 帝堯,
His benevolence was like Heaven,
his wisdom was like the spirits,
approaching him was like the sun,
looking up to him was like the clouds,
he was rich but not arrogant,
noble but not complacent.
Yú Shùn 虞舜,
in goodness, nothing was so subtle as to not be evident,
in evil, nothing was so hidden as to not be revealed.
He relied on nature for rewards and punishments,
and entrusted governance to the will of the people.
Therefore, he could achieve control through inaction (wúwéi 無為),
guiding the Way towards utmost harmony.
The common people used it daily without realizing it,
their virtue being in accordance seemed natural to them.
This is the virtue of the Five Emperors.
A true king controls people with the Way,
causing them to submit their hearts and minds.
It is discussed that:
Hán Xìn 韓信 said:
"Xiàng Wáng's 項王 conquests were all destructive,
the people did not feel close to him,
merely coerced by his power,
forced into submission.
Although nominally a hegemon,
in reality, he lost the hearts of the people.
Therefore it is said:
his strength was easily turned to weakness."
Zhūgě Liàng said:
"The people of Jīngzhōu,
those who submitted to Cāo
were coerced by the force of his army,
they were not truly convinced.
Now, if the general truly orders a brave general to cooperate and work together with Jīngzhōu,
the army of Cāo will surely be defeated."
From these words,
if people's hearts are not convinced,
its power is easily broken.
Therefore, the way of a true king
is to make people submit in heart and mind.
To set up rules and prepare for decline,
to have meticulous governance and military preparedness,
but without the need for battle and bloodshed,
the world will be at peace,
the ruler will have no doubts about his ministers,
and the ministers will have no doubts about their ruler.
The state will be stable and the ruler secure.
Ministers can retire with righteousness,
also beautiful and harmless.
In the past, the wise kings of the Three Dynasties,
initiated great eras,
with different systems of culture and substance,
but with consistent good reputations.
Therefore, it is said:
The people of the Xià valued loyalty.
The flaw of loyalty is rusticity.
To rescue simplicity, nothing is better than reverence;
the Yīn 殷 people reformed and cultivated it.
The flaw of reverence is obsession with ghosts;
to rescue from ghosts, nothing is better than culture;
the Zhōu 周 people corrected and changed it.
The flaw of culture is superficiality;
then one returns to loyalty.
The Three Dynasties followed each other,
like water quenching fire.
What is called adapting to the times and the art of correcting flaws,
these are the virtues of the Three Kings.
Hegemons controlled scholars with power,
bound scholars with trust,
and employed scholars with rewards.
When trust declines, scholars become alienated;
when rewards are abolished, scholars are no longer employed.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* 左傳 says:
"Chǔ 楚 besieged Sòng 宋.
Sòng 宋 sent an urgent message to Jìn 晉.
Xiān Zhěn 先軫 said:
'Repaying favors and relieving distress,
establishing authority and securing hegemony,
are based on this.'
Hú Yǎn 狐偃 said:
'Chǔ 楚 has just obtained Cáo 曹 and newly allied with Wèi 衛.
If we attack Cáo 曹 and Wèi 衛,
Chǔ 楚 will surely come to their rescue,
then Qí 齊 and Sòng 宋 will be spared.'
Thereupon, he gathered troops at Bèi Lú,
formed three armies,
planned for a commander-in-chief,
and appointed Xì Hú to lead the central army.
The Marquis of Jìn began to enter the state and instruct his people.
After two years,
he wanted to employ them,
but Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know righteousness,
nor are they settled in their dwellings."
Thereupon, he went out to establish King Dìngxiāng,
and returned to focus on benefiting the people,
and the people cherished life.
When he was about to employ them,
Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know trustworthiness,
nor has its use been proclaimed."
Thereupon, he attacked Yuán to demonstrate trustworthiness.
Those who exchanged resources
did not seek abundance;
their words were clearly verified.
The Duke said:
"Is it acceptable now?"
Zǐ Fàn said:
"The people do not yet know propriety,
nor has their respect arisen."
Thereupon, he conducted a grand review to demonstrate propriety,
established officials to regulate their duties,
One listens without being confused and then employs them.
He sent troops out of Gǔ (穀),
relieved the siege of Sòng (宋),
and with one battle achieved hegemony.
This was the teaching of Wén (文)."
These are the virtues of the Five Hegemons.
Therefore, it is said:
"The foundation of governing a state
lies in punishment and virtue.
These two must be mutually dependent and implemented together,
and rely on each other for success.
Heaven uses yin and yang to complete the year,
and people use punishment and virtue to achieve good governance.
Therefore, even if a sage governs,
he cannot rely on only one.
Therefore, those who relied more on virtue
and used less punishment were
the Five Emperors;
those whose use of punishment and virtue was balanced were
the Three Kings;
those who relied more on punishment
and relied less on virtue were
the Five Hegemons;
and those who purely used punishment
and were strong but perished were
Qín (秦).
A saying about governance states:
"The governance of the ancients
His governance has three aspects:
the government of a true king (wángzhě) transforms (the people) through moral influence;
the government of a hegemon (bàzhě) overawes (the people) through authority;
the government of a strong state (qiángguó) coerces (the people) through threats.
Therefore, only after moral transformation fails to change (them) do you overawe them;
only after overawing them fails to change (them) do you coerce them;
only after coercing them fails to change (them) do you punish them.
Therefore, when it comes to punishment,
that is not what a true king values.
Hence, Yú Nán says:
"That Emperor Qín (Qín Huáng)
abandoned benevolence and righteousness and employed force and power;
this allowed him to conquer and annex,
but it would not allow him to maintain (his empire).
This is the failing of relying on punishment."
Someone asked:
"The ways of a true king and a hegemon,
I have already heard your instruction.
I dare to ask, Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì) and Emperor Guāng (Guāng Dì),
both rose up from the fields and paddocks,
clearing away calamity and difficulty,
and subsequently inaugurated a royal enterprise.
Emperor Gāozǔ was open-minded and magnanimous,
Emperor Guāngwǔ was meticulous in details and regulations,
each distinguished in his own way,
like dragons soaring and phoenixes flying;
hence, they were able to restore order and protect the people,
rescuing (them) from this mud and charcoal (suffering).
"However, comparing great virtue,
with heavenly might,
which is superior or inferior?"
Cáo Zhí 曹植 said:
"In the past, at the beginning of the Hàn 漢 dynasty's rise,
Gāo Zǔ 高祖 arose because of the violent Qín 秦 dynasty,
and then eliminated the powerful Chǔ 楚,
gloriously possessing all under heaven,
his merit equal to Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武,
his legacy flowing to later generations,
a primary meritorious deed of emperors and kings,
a magnificent affair for rulers.
However, his name was not purely virtuous,
his conduct not purely aligned with the Dao,
after his death,
at the moment of his collapse,
it truly allowed a wicked woman to indulge her cruel and tyrannical heart,
and a favored concubine to suffer the punishment of being made into a 'human pig'.
The King of Zhào 趙 was imprisoned,
calamity befalling his flesh and blood,
the Lǚ 呂 clan monopolized power,
the state was almost overthrown,
all these affairs,
are they not because Gāo Zǔ 高祖 was short-sighted and shallow in his considerations, leading to this?
However, his brave generals and skilled ministers,
are rare throughout ancient and modern times,
and seldom seen throughout past dynasties,
he was able to appoint them according to their talents and employ them,
Listen to their words and observe their actions;
therefore, he united the world and attained the position of Emperor.
Shìzǔ embodied the excellent virtue of Heaven's spirit,
possessed the pure essence of upright harmony,
followed the wondrous principle of the Golden Mean,
concealed the fine talents of a quasi-sage.
As for his virtue,
he was quick-witted and knowledgeable,
benevolent, wise, and understanding,
serious, cautious, and thorough,
generous in giving and loving towards people.
He encountered an age of unwarranted calamity,
and met with the unfortunate fate of the fiery essence (of the Hàn dynasty).
Suddenly, like thunder, he rose up,
magnificently, like a god.
He exerted military strategies to repel violence,
raised righteous troops to sweep away the remnants of rebellion.
Before his army even left Nánjīng,
Mǎng had already fallen in the western capital.
Therefore, he moved his troops only after securing victory in the ancestral temple,
and marched his army only after establishing his plan.
Thus, he attacked no fortresses he could not capture,
and in battle, there were no fleeing soldiers.
He proclaimed benevolence to harmonize the masses,
and promoted virtue to attract those from afar.
Therefore, Dòu Róng, hearing his reputation, attached himself like a shadow,
and Mǎ Yuán, upon seeing him once, sighed in admiration.
He fostered harmony among his nine branches of kinship,
earning praise like Yáo and Shùn of the Táng and Yú dynasties;
he valued simplicity and sincerity,
possessing the essence of Xī Huáng;
he was humble and accepted those beneath him,
showing the toil of spitting out (food to feed guests);
He kept his attention on all sorts of affairs,
he possessed the diligence of working until the sun slanted.
Therefore, when reckoning achievements, his accomplishments were extraordinary;
when comparing to past rulers, his deeds were different;
when praising virtues, there were no faults;
when discussing words and actions, there was no blemish;
when assessing matters, his power seemed slight;
when discussing assistants, his ministers appeared weak.
In the end, he was able to grasp the auspicious signs of the heavenly map,
and establish indelible lasting achievements.
Metal and stone record his great merits,
and poetry and books record his beautiful accomplishments."
Therefore, it is said:
Guāngwǔ was superior.
Xún Yuè said:
"Gāozǔ rose from among the common people,
brandishing his sword to seize the empire.
He did not obtain it through the abdication of Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn,
nor did he ascend through the ranks of the ministers of Tāng and Wǔ.
Like a dragon rising and a tiger transforming,
he led and followed the winds and clouds.
Conquering disorder and attacking violence,
he cleared the imperial territory.
During the eight years
the whole country was pacified.
Consequently, he shouldered the mandate of Heaven,
ascended to establish the imperial standard.
Since ancient times,
in all the records of books,
there has never been such a thing.
If not for heroic and outstanding talent,
and a broad and enlightened strategy,
ordained by destiny,
and assisted by the gods,
how could one achieve such accomplishments?
Burning the fish and severing the snake,
extraordinary events corresponding to omens,
are these not the feelings of spirits?"
The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says:
"Heaven's work is done through men."
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"Tāng and Wǔ's revolutions
were in accordance with Heaven and responsive to the people."
This is what it means.
The governance of the Xià dynasty valued loyalty.
The flaw of loyalty is rusticity,
therefore the Yīn succeeded it with reverence.
The flaw of reverence is superstition,
therefore the Zhōu succeeded it with refinement.
The flaw of refinement is superficiality,
and the best remedy for superficiality is loyalty.
The Dao of the Three Kings
cycles and begins anew.
The period between the Zhōu and Qín Dynasties
can be said to be a decline of culture.
The Qín Dynasty did not reform,
but instead intensified cruel punishments.
The Hàn Dynasty inherited its faults,
and thus obtained the Mandate of Heaven.
Kǒng Róng said:
"From Zhōu Wǔ back to Hòujì, down to his own time,
there were fifteen generations in succession,
with only auspicious omens of fish and birds.
As for Gāozǔ,
he cultivated virtue in his own person,
and the omens were four or five:
the White Serpent was divided,
the divine mother wept,
he entered the Guān region from the west,
and the five planets aligned.
Moreover, King Wǔ of Zhōu executed Zhòu,
beheading him and exposing his head.
When Gāozǔ entered Qín,
he pardoned Zǐyīng and sent him away.
His leniency
was even greater than that of Gāozǔ."
Yú Nán said:
"An emperor dwells with a teacher,
a king dwells with a friend,
The way a hegemon treats his ministers.
The ministers of Hànzǔ
were the Three Heroes;
the assistants of Guāngwǔ
were the Twenty-eight Generals.
How could Dèng Yǔ and Wú Hàn be compared to Zhāng Liáng and Hán Xìn?
Yet, Hànzǔ's meritorious ministers
were all killed off after the dynasty became strong and prosperous;
Guāngwǔ’s ministers who aided in establishing the dynasty
were all treated with generous salaries and safety.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is truly praiseworthy.
"To eliminate the long and supplement the short"
is second to that."
From these words,
Hàn Gāo was able to defeat Qín and Xiàng,
and establish the Hàn dynasty.
The customs and rites
were passed down to later generations.
Although he did not attain the way of a true king,
the virtue of his hegemony was great.
Someone said:
"Bān Gù said:
"The Zhōu dynasty is spoken of in terms of Chéng and Kāng,
the Hàn dynasty is spoken of in terms of Wén and Jǐng."
Is this statement appropriate?"
Yú Nán said:
"Chéng and Kāng inherited the legacy of Wén and Wǔ,
With Zhōu 周 and Shào 召 as ministers,
they transformed the people with deep sincerity,
relying on accumulated benevolent virtue.
The wind flattening the grass
was not sufficient as a metaphor.
When the Jiāng 漢 and Hàn 漢 emperors first established the foundation,
they had not a moment to spare.
The evils of the destroyed Yíng 嬴 dynasty
still persisted.
Emperor Tàizōng 太宗 embodied this benevolence and forgiveness,
respectfully following profound silence.
He cleansed the cruel violence of the Qín 秦 and Xiàng 項 dynasties,
restoring the pure customs of Xuān 軒 and Hào 昊.
He almost reached the point of putting away punishments.
This was truly difficult!
If he had not been misled by the theories of Xīn Yuán 新垣,
and had not been obsessed with Dèng Tōng's 鄧通 dream,
how reverent and cautious he was!
It was perhaps close to the Way of the King.
Comparing Jǐng Dì to Zhōu Kāng
, then there is still the shame of deficient virtue."
The "Hàn Wén Eulogy" says:
"When Emperor Wén acceded to the throne,
for twenty-three years,
palaces and gardens,
carriages, horses, clothing, and accoutrements
were not increased.
If there was something inconvenient,
he would always remove it to benefit the people.
Wèi Tuō of Nányuè
had declared himself emperor.
He summoned his elder brother,
embracing him with virtue.
Tuō then called himself a subject.
He formed a marriage alliance with the Xiongnu,
but they broke the agreement and invaded.
He ordered the border guards to defend
and did not send troops deep into enemy territory,
hating to trouble the common people.
The King of Wú feigned illness and did not attend court;
the Emperor bestowed upon him a stool and walking stick.
Although the remonstrances of the assembled ministers were earnest,
he often accommodated and accepted them.
Zhāng Wǔ and others accepted bribes of money;
when discovered, they were given additional rewards
to shame them.
He devoted himself to transforming the people with virtue,
therefore, the country within the seas was prosperous,
flourishing in ritual and righteousness,
adjudicating hundreds of lawsuits,
almost reaching a point where punishments were laid aside.
Alas!
What benevolence!"
Someone asked Master Fù, saying:
"Emperor Tàizōng of the Hàn dynasty abolished corporal punishment,
can he be called benevolent?"
He replied:
"It is the benevolence of a common man.
He who rules the world,
is one who greatly brings about benefit,
not what is called a small lack of forbearance.
Speaking from this,
Bān Gù considered Tàizōng to be benevolent,
not because he abolished corporal punishment."
The "Eulogy of Emperor Jǐng" says:
"Confucius said:
'This person,
is the reason why the three dynasties were able to walk the straight path.'
Truly!
The flaws of the Zhōu and Qín dynasties,
were a dense net of strict laws,
yet treachery and deceit could not be overcome.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
it swept away bothersome regulations,
to rest and recuperate the people.
As for Xiào Wén [Emperor Wen of Han],
he furthered this with respectfulness and frugality.
Xiào Jǐng [Emperor Jing of Han] guided these endeavors.
During the fifty or sixty years in between,
it reached the point of shifting customs and changing habits,
and the common people became pure and honest.
The Zhōu [dynasty] is spoken of as Chéng Kāng [referring to the reigns of King Cheng and King Kang],
the Hàn [dynasty] is spoken of as Wén Jǐng [referring to the reigns of Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing]—
how wonderful!
This is the way of the true king."
Someone asked:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn possessed great talent and broad vision.
With which ruler of former generations can he be compared?"
Yú Nán said:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn inherited the achievements of six generations,
and the country was prosperous and rich.
Moreover, he had the innate qualities of a superior person.
Therefore, he was able to gather heroes,
and control outstanding individuals.
Internally, he promoted ritual and music.
Externally, he expanded the borders.
The systems and regulations,
are brilliantly worthy of being recounted.
Compared to the First Emperor [of Qin],
he was clearly superior.
As for arrogance, extravagance, tyranny, and cruelty,
they can be considered similar.
"Achieved great feats but lacked in virtue."
The *Wǔdì Zàn* (Eulogy of Emperor Wǔ) says:
"The Hàn inherited the malpractices of hundreds of kings.
Gāozǔ rectified the chaos and restored order.
Emperors Wén and Jǐng focused on nourishing the people.
As for investigating ancient rituals and institutions,
there were still many deficiencies.
When Xiàowǔ first ascended the throne,
he resolutely banished the Hundred Schools of Thought
and promoted the Six Classics.
Consequently, he widely consulted within the realm
and selected the outstanding talents
to establish achievements with him.
He established the Imperial Academy,
reformed suburban sacrifices,
rectified the calendar,
determined mathematical astronomy,
harmonized musical scales,
composed poems and music,
established the *fēng* and *shàn* sacrifices,
venerated all the gods,
continued the line of the Zhōu descendants.
His decrees and literary works
are brilliantly and worthily recounted.
Later successors were able to follow the great undertaking
and exhibited the style of the Three Dynasties.
If Emperor Wǔ, with his great talent and grand strategy,
had not altered the reverence and frugality of Emperors Wén and Jǐng,
in order to bring things into equilibrium with this person,
then even what is praised in the *Shī* (Book of Odes) and *Shū* (Book of Documents),
what more could be added?"
To extend this line of thought,
both Hàn Wǔ and Qín Huángdì
were rulers who achieved great accomplishments.
not lords who maintained the status quo.
Formerly, when Zhōu Chéng [Zhōu Chéng 周成] succeeded to the throne as a young child,
there was the rebellion of Guǎn and Cài [Guǎn, Cài 管、蔡] and the Four States;
when Hàn Zhāo [Hàn Zhāo 漢昭] ascended the throne at a young age,
there was also the rebellious plot of Yān, Gài, and Shàngguān [Yān, Gài, Shàngguān 燕、蓋、上官].
Chéng Wáng [成王] did not doubt the Duke of Zhōu [Zhōu Gōng 周公],
Hàn Zhāo [漢昭] entrusted authority to Huò Guāng [霍光],
which of the two rulers came first, and which came after?
Emperor Wèi Wén [Wèi Wén Dì 魏文帝] said:
"Zhōu Chéng Wáng [周成王] embodied the auspicious influence of his sage father,
and received the teachings of his virtuous mother from the womb.
Zhōu and Shào [Zhōu, Shào 周、邵] were his tutors,
and Lǚ Wàng [Lǚ Wàng 呂望] was his Grand Mentor.
As soon as his mouth could speak, attendants recited phrases for him;
as soon as his feet could walk, ministers guided his steps in ritual.
His eyes were sated with the beauty of majestic bearing,
his ears filled with the sound of virtue and righteousness.
This is what is meant by being immersed in profound currents
and bathed in a pure breeze.
Yet he still had faults and regrets,
listening to the slander of his two uncles,
causing the Duke of Zhōu [Zhōu Gōng 周公] to move east.
Majestic Heaven was exceedingly angry,
revealing their faults clearly,
and only then did they awaken.
Not trusting the sagely virtue of Zhōu Gōng,
but believing the instructive words of the "Metal-Bound Coffer,"
how could they not be deluded?
Now, the father of Hàn Zhāo (Emperor Zhao of Han) was not Wǔ Wáng (King Wu),
his mother was not Yì Jiāng,
he was nurtured only by Gài Zhǔ,
and his ministers were then Jié and Guāng.
Lacking the substance of benevolence and filial piety,
and assisted by no grand and peaceful governance,
he was what is called "born in the depths of the palace,
and raised by the hands of women."
Yet, virtue and nature matured,
actions and propriety were in harmony,
at the age of twenty-seven,
he was precociously wise and early understanding,
uncovering the deception of the Yān letter,
and appreciating the sincerity of Huò Guāng.
Would he have had to open the "Metal-Bound Coffer,"
and trust the state history,
before he would have awakened?
If Chéng (King Cheng) and Zhāo (King Zhao) had been established at the same age,
if the dynasty had changed generations and been transformed,
if ministers had been exchanged and governance achieved,
if music had been changed and songs sung,
then the Hàn would not be uniquely deficient,
Zhōu did not have much more land."
The Grand General Huò Guāng and Shàngguān Jié held power.
They resented Guāng's favor,
and wanted to kill him.
So they falsely claimed to be the emperor's older brother, Yān Dàn, and presented a memorial,
accusing Guāng of carrying out imperial processions and claiming the right to clear the way in the Shànglín Garden.
The Emperor did not believe them.
Someone said,
"Emperor Xuān of Hàn was insightful in his administration,
could he be considered a peer of Emperor Guāngwǔ?"
Yú Nán said,
"Emperor Xuān of Hàn rose from the common people,
and understood the hardships of the people.
Therefore, he paid close attention to governance,
promoted and employed worthy individuals.
Considering his seeking truth based on reputation,
strict laws and harsh decrees,
it seems to flow from the doctrines of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi.
An old saying goes,
'If one aims for kingship but fails,
the consequence is still enough to achieve hegemony;
if one aims for hegemony but fails,
what will the consequence be?'
Guāngwǔ was benevolent and righteous,
a ruler aiming for kingship;
Emperor Xuān emphasized punishments and titles,
a lord aiming for hegemony.
To compare them as peers now,
I fear he is not one of their kind."
The discussion went:
When Yuán Dì 元帝 was the Crown Prince,
he once remonstrated with Xuān Dì 宣帝,
believing that he was being too strict in upholding the law.
The Emperor changed his expression and said:
"Our Hàn 漢 house mixes the ways of the hegemon and the king,
how can we rely solely on virtuous transformation
and harm governance?"
Even with these words,
I know his vision is not far-reaching,
but the system of leniency and severity has existed since ancient times.
In the past, when Gāo Zǔ 高祖 entered Qín 秦,
he made a covenant of three articles,
and the people of Qín 秦 were greatly pleased.
This speaks of the beauty of lenient punishment.
Guō Jiā 郭嘉 said to Cáo Gōng 曹公:
"At the end of the Hàn 漢 dynasty, governance failed because it was too lenient.
Shào 紹 used leniency to manage affairs,
so people were not intimidated;
you, sir, correct this with severity,
and those above and below know the rules."
This speaks of the appropriateness of strict punishment.
Therefore, the *Commentary* says:
"If governance is lenient, then people become lax;
if they are lax, then correct them with severity;
if it is severe, then people are harmed;
if they are harmed, then implement leniency.
"Lenience used to temper severity,
and severity used to temper lenience;
government is thereby harmonious."
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Punishments are sometimes light and sometimes heavy."
The *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou) says:
"In governing a newly established state, light punishments are used;
in governing a state in disorder, heavy punishments are used;
in governing a peaceful state, moderate punishments are used."
From this perspective,
one should only ask what the era is like!
How small a harm is severe punishment!
Someone might say:
"Hàn Yuándì's talents and arts were gentle and refined,
wasn't he a good ruler who maintained the status quo?"
Yú Nán said:
"The talents of a ruler
lie solely in civil virtue and martial prowess.
For civil affairs, it's about managing the world with wisdom,
issuing decrees and setting policies.
For martial affairs, it's about suppressing violence and ceasing hostilities,
ensuring peace and harmony among the people.
This is the grand plan of one who faces south (i.e., the emperor).
As for playing the zither and flute,
harmonizing songs by the Jiāng River and composing melodies,
these are the duties of musicians;
how could they be the concerns of the Son of Heaven?"
A discussion says:
Emperor Yuán Dì 元帝 possessed many talents and skills,
and was good at playing the *sè* and *qín* zithers.
Although this was the case,
it was not goodness in its highest form.
Why?
Xú Gàn's 徐幹 *Zhong Lun* 中論 says:
"To be meticulous about small matters and neglect the great Way,
to examine nearby objects but be blind to distant principles—
from ancient times to the present,
there has never been a case of such a state not falling into disorder,
nor of such a state not perishing.
What is meant by 'meticulous about small matters, examining nearby objects'
refers to ears being keen to the harmony of string and bamboo music and songs,
eyes being sharp to the patterns of carving and colors,
mouths being eloquent in clever and incisive repartee,
minds being adept at short tales and minor literary compositions,
and hands being skilled in archery, charioteering, writing, and arithmetic.
What is meant by 'distant principles, the great Way'
refers to benevolence sufficient to cover and shelter all living beings,
kindness sufficient to nurture the common people,
clarity sufficient to illuminate the four directions,
wisdom sufficient to govern all things,
authority sufficient to respond to endless changes,
righteousness sufficient to enrich the production of resources,
majesty sufficient to prohibit and suppress treachery and wrongdoing,
military strength sufficient to quell disasters and turmoil,
attentiveness in listening to advice and discernment in selecting officials,
understanding of the origins of rise and fall,
Understanding the distinction between safety and danger.
If it is like this,
then the way of the ruler is complete.”
In the past, Lǔ Zhuāng (魯莊) had many skills and arts,
and the poets criticized him;
Lǔ Zhāo (魯昭) had beautiful looks and deportment,
but met with the calamity of fleeing the state.
From this perspective,
even if you could make the ruler see like Lí Lóu (離婁), hear like Shī Kuàng (師曠), shoot like Yí Yì (夷羿), and write like Shǐ Zhòu (史籀),
it could be said that he is good at the duties of officials,
but what benefit would it be to governing?
Kuāng Héng’s (匡衡) “Letter of Remonstrance to Emperor Yuán (元帝) on Changing the Government” says:
“A king who receives the Mandate [of Heaven]
should strive to establish an enterprise and bequeath a system,
passing it down without end.
A ruler who inherits the throne
must focus on inheriting and proclaiming the virtues of the former kings and extolling their achievements.
Now, Your Majesty’s sagely virtue covers [all],
and Your Majesty’s love extends to the land within the seas,
yet the Yin and Yang are not in harmony,
and wicked men are not prohibited.
This is likely because those who debate have not widely proclaimed the great achievements of the former emperors,
arguing over whether the systems and institutions are unusable.
I secretly regret that the state has abandoned the easily achieved accomplishments,
and is pointlessly engaging in this clamor.
I wish that Your Majesty would carefully examine the matter of inheriting the enterprise;
this is preserving the legacy.”
Someone might say:
"Looking at the false newcomer Wáng Mǎng,
so humble and courteous,
wouldn't you say he was a renowned scholar of his time?
Yet, when he became chancellor and attained high position,
he was arrogant, licentious, tyrannical, and cruel.
Why such a great contradiction between his earlier and later behavior?"
Yú Nán said:
"Wáng Mǎng was inherently cruel
and a deceitful hypocrite.
Before he achieved prominence,
he pursued fame and sought praise;
after he achieved his ambition,
he was boastful of his abilities and arrogant towards others.
Once he had completely exhausted his pretense,
his true nature remained.
Obstinately rejecting advice and considering himself superior,
he ultimately failed to reform and awaken.
Grievances and cruelty prevailed within the realm,
leading to his removal by Guāngwǔ."
Bān Gù said:
"Wáng Mǎng initially rose as a maternal relative
and diligently practiced self-discipline
to gain fame and reputation.
During the reigns of Chéng and Aī,
he diligently served the state,
acted with integrity,
and every action was praised.
Isn't this what is meant by 'He will certainly be known in the state,
At home, one must hear,
are they the "putting on an appearance of benevolence while acting contrary to it" type?
Wǎng (王莽 Wáng Mǎng) was certainly not benevolent,
but possessed the talent of a wicked flatterer,
and also inherited the power of four paternal ancestors through generations.
He encountered the decline of the Hàn dynasty,
the imperial lineage interrupted three times,
and the Empress Dowager enjoyed a long life,
acting as his patron.
Therefore, he was able to give free rein to his treacherous wickedness
to accomplish the calamity of usurpation.
Extending this reasoning,
it also involved the timing of Heaven,
not something achievable by human effort alone.
Once he had stolen the throne and faced south,
occupying a position he shouldn't have,
the situation of collapse
was more perilous than that of Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂),
yet Wǎng (王莽 Wáng Mǎng) remained at ease,
claiming that the Yellow Emperor and Emperor Yú had reappeared.
He then boasted of his powerful deceit,
and inflicted boundless cruelty upon the people.
Because of this, the country was in uproar,
losing their joy in life.
Resentment grew internally and externally,
both the distant and the near were ruined.
Cities and walls could not be defended,
the limbs of the state were divided,
Consequently, he caused the cities and towns of the world to become ruins.
From what is recorded in the *Book of Documents* and its *Commentaries*,
among rebellious ministers and traitorous sons,
and men without principle,
there was none as extreme as Mǎng.
(He was like) the croaking of purple frogs,
an excess portion, a superfluous reign,
to be driven out and eliminated by a sage king."
The King of Wú, Sūn Quán, commented on Lǚ Méng, saying:
"When Zǐ Míng was young,
I thought he was only uncomplaining about difficult or easy tasks,
simply bold and courageous.
As he grew older, his learning increased,
his plans and strategies became extraordinarily astute,
he could be considered second to Gōngjǐn,
in planning to take Guān Yǔ,
he was superior to Zǐjìng.
Zǐjìng answered my letter saying:
'The rise of emperors
all depends on having a driving force (qūchú).
Yǔ is not worth fearing.'
This Zǐjìng inwardly could not discern,
but outwardly made boastful statements.
I also excused him for it,
and did not fault him carelessly."
This is the meaning of *qūchú*.
Shào Kāng of the Xià dynasty and Guāngwǔ of the Hàn dynasty were both restoring rulers,
which one was the greatest?
Yú Nán said:
"Both of these emperors revived their ancestors' legacies,
brilliantly inaugurating their royal enterprises.
Their names are the same,
but their realities are different.
Why is this?
In the time of Guāngwǔ,
he relied on the people who were thinking of rebelling,
executed the cruel and villainous Wǎng,
seizing a disordered and collapsing state.
Achieving success was comparatively easy.
As for Shào Kāng,
the demise of the Xià family had already been two generations
with Yì and Hán Zhuó.
A tiny remnant,
his body was in the womb.
His mother fled,
giving birth in another country.
He did not receive the teachings of his father,
and had no strong or close relatives.
Encountering the difficulties of chaos and disorder,
he sought refuge in improper places,
and yet he was able to struggle amidst the chaos and loss,
and then complete the task of being equal to heaven.
He was a king who restored his dynasty.
This is worthy of being called the foremost."
Wèi's Noble Lord of Gāoguì Township asked Xún Yǐ:
"Once the Xià dynasty had declined,
After Xiàng was extinguished,
Shǎo Kāng gathered the remnants of the Xia people
and restored the achievements of Yǔ.
Gāozǔ rose from the fields
and eliminated the Qin and Xiàng.
Considering their merits and virtues,
who comes first?"
Yǐ and the others said:
"Creation and inheritance are
different in difficulty.
Although Shǎo Kāng's merits and virtues are excellent,
he was still a restorer.
Shìzǔ of the Hàn dynasty is comparable.
As for Gāozǔ,
we believe he is superior."
The Emperor said:
"Shǎo Kāng was born after destruction,
reduced to a vassal of the feudal lords.
He was able to spread his virtue and foreshadow his plans,
finally eliminating Guò and Gē,
restoring the achievements of Yǔ,
sacrificing to Xia and being matched with Heaven,
without losing the old possessions.
If he did not have supreme virtue and great benevolence,
how could he have accomplished this feat?
The ancestor of Hàn took advantage of the collapse of the state,
seized temporary power.
As a son, he repeatedly endangered his father.
As a ruler, he imprisoned a virtuous minister;
as a father, he could not protect his son;
after his death,
the state was nearly overthrown.
If he had been in the same era as Shào Kāng 少康,
he might not have been able to restore the achievements of Dà Yǔ 大禹."
Extrapolating from this statement,
it would be appropriate to rank Xià Kāng 夏康 highly and place the founder of the Hàn 漢 dynasty lower.
The decline and chaos of the Later Hàn 漢 dynasty
were due to the two rulers Huán 桓 and Líng 靈.
Whose evil virtue was the most severe?
Yú Nán 虞南 said:
"Emperor Huán 桓, with his awe-inspiring anger,
executed Liáng Jì 梁冀,
displaying decisive resolve.
However, eunuchs controlled the court,
the partisan banishment of officials arose,
and the chaos of the Zhōngpíng 中平 era
began with Emperor Huán 桓.
An ancient saying states:
'The empire is in turmoil,
it is the capital for a new ruler.'
Emperor Líng 靈 inherited a weary populace,
making it easy to implement good governance;
the common people listened attentively,
all hoping for a restoration.
But the emperor repeated the mistakes of the overturned cart,
his poison exceeding his predecessors,
Causing the downfall of the ancestral shrines and the state.
The reason for serving as emperor,
and reaching a natural lifespan before growing tired of the world,
is already a great fortune."
The discussion went:
Emperor Huán (桓帝) asked the Attendant Counselor Yuán Yán (爰延),
"What kind of ruler am I?"
Yuán Yán (爰延) replied,
"A middling ruler of the Hàn."
"Why?"
"Because if the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Chén Fán (陳蕃), is entrusted with affairs, things are orderly;
if the Regular Attendant and Yellow Gate official interfere in governance, things are chaotic.
Therefore, I know that Your Majesty can be led to do good,
and can be led to do wrong.
This is what is meant by a middling ruler."
Yú Nán (虞南) said:
"When the Mín River (岷江) first springs forth,
its source is so shallow that one can just fill a cup.
But when it flows far,
only a raft can cross it.
During the time of Emperor Yuán (元帝),
he appointed Hóng Gōng (宏恭) and Shí Xiǎn (石顯);
and during the reigns of Huán (桓) and Líng (靈),
he added Dān Chāo (單超) and Zhāng Ràng (張讓);
they ruined the proper relations
and consequently overturned the ancestral state.
The origin of this was gradual.
Therefore, it is said:
"The flickering flame, though dim, will not be extinguished,
How can the blazing fire be controlled?"
This speaks of being cautious at the beginning.
Alas!
After a hundred generations,
let them take warning from this!"
An ancient saying goes:
"The cold are easily clothed,
the hungry are easily fed."
Cháo Cuò said:
"That a state is rich and strong while neighboring states are in chaos
is the capital of an emperor and king."
From these words,
it can be known that a muddle-headed and chaotic ruler
will open the way for a sage-like virtue.
Since the fire virtue declined and ceased to contend,
and the universe and districts crumbled and fell apart,
Cáo Mèngdé, holding the Son of Heaven hostage, commanded the feudal lords;
Liú Xuándé, relying on the strategic barriers of Shǔ Hàn;
Sūn Zhòngmóu, depending on the strength of the Jiāng and Huái regions;
divided the realm into three,
standing like the three legs of a tripod,
all initiating the foundations of a royal enterprise,
gloriously commencing a hegemonic undertaking.
Of the three rulers,
who was superior and who was inferior?
Yú Nán said:
"Cáo Gōng's military strategies and ingenious calculations
It would have been almost impossible to contend with him.
Therefore, he was able to initiate achievements and establish a foundation.
Occupying the central position and serving as chancellor,
he truly possessed the talent of a hero!
However, he was treacherous and inconsistent,
ambitious and suspicious, and extremely jealous.
He went so far as to kill Empress Fú,
poison Xún Yù,
execute Kǒng Róng,
and slaughter Cuī Yǎn.
Lóu Shēng died because of a single word,
and Huán Shào suffered from excessive bowing.
Abandoning virtue and resorting to punishment,
his cruelty was extreme.
To compare him to the Count of the West,
he was truly not that person.
Xǔ Shào's description of him as "a capable minister in times of peace,
and a treacherous hero in times of chaos,"
that statement is fitting."
"Liú Gōng treated Liú Zhāng with the courtesy due to a guest,
and entrusted Zhūgě [Liàng] without suspicion.
Such is the virtue of a ruler,
and it is beautiful indeed.
That Kǒngmíng,
was a rare talent destined by fate,
comparable to Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng.
Sovereign and minister were of one mind,
likened to fish and water.
However, because his state was small and his army weak,
isolated in a corner,
contending against two sides,
he resisted a superior nation.
If he were to trade places with Cáo Gōng 曹公 and occupy his position,
display his far-reaching plans,
unleash the martial prowess of Guān 羽 and Zhāng 張,
and fully utilize Zhūgě 孔明's literary talents,
then the ambition of becoming a hegemon would have been achieved."
"Lord Sūn 孫 relied on his brother's legacy,
employed officials from the previous dynasty,
protected by natural barriers,
and barely managed to preserve himself.
Compared to the two,
he was clearly inferior."
Chén Shòu 陳壽 said,
"Liú Bèi 劉備's strategic acumen and managerial abilities
did not match Wèi Wǔ 魏武,
therefore his foundation was also limited."
Zhāng Fǔ 張輔 said,
"Why is that so?
A ruler who quells chaos
should prioritize recruiting capable ministers and generals as the foundation.
Personal martial prowess alone
is not enough to rely on.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng 諸葛孔明 was versed in rites and understood change,
almost the talent of a king's advisor;
Xuán Dé 玄德, without a strong position, caused him to dedicate his service;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi were both outstanding people.
You should submit to them and employ them.
For brightness and darkness do not work together,
and the capable and the incapable do not serve each other.
Even though Emperor Wǔ was in a secure and powerful position,
he did not employ them.
How much less would he have done so in a time of crisis?
If Xuán Dé had been allowed to occupy the Central Plains,
he would have been comparable to the Zhōu dynasty,
and it would not have been merely a matter of two outstanding individuals."
The Wèi Emperor asked the Wú envoy Zhào Zī:
"What kind of ruler is the King of Wú?"
Zī replied:
"A ruler who is intelligent, perceptive, benevolent, wise, brave, and strategic."
The Emperor asked about his characteristics,
and Zī said:
"Recognizing Lǔ Sù when he was still just an ordinary person shows his intelligence;
this is his intelligence;
elevating Lǚ Méng from the ranks of soldiers shows his perceptiveness;
this is his perceptiveness;
capturing Yú Jìn and not harming him shows his benevolence;
this is his benevolence;
taking Jīngzhōu without bloodshed shows his wisdom;
this is his wisdom;
fighting in three provinces and eyeing the world shows his bravery;
this is his bravery;
submitting himself to Your Majesty
shows his strategic ability."
Sūn Cè 孫策 suffered greatly from his wounds.
He called his younger brother Quán 權 and said:
"To lead the forces of Jiāng Dōng 江東,
to make decisions in the midst of battles,
and to contend with the world for supremacy,
you are not as good as I;
but to promote the virtuous and entrust them with responsibilities,
to allow each person to fully utilize their talents,
and thereby protect Jiāng Dōng 江東,
I am not as good as you."
Chén Shòu 陳壽 said:
"Sūn Quán 孫權 humbled himself and endured insults,
valued talent and esteemed strategy,
possessing the extraordinary qualities of Gōu Jiàn 勾踐.
He was a remarkable person.
Therefore, he was able to independently control the region south of the river,
and establish the foundation for the Three Kingdoms."
Sīmǎ Yì 司馬懿, the Xuān 宣 Emperor of Jìn 晉, possessed grand strategies and brilliant calculations,
Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 was a peerless genius of the world.
Who was superior?
Yú Nán 虞南 said:
"The Xuān 宣 Emperor rose from being a scholar,
assisted in the establishment of the imperial enterprise,
rescued the world from danger and difficulty,
and successfully restored the proper way of kings.
His strategies, both civil and military,
truly deserve praise,
but he relied heavily on secret schemes,
Not following rén yì (仁義),
suspicious, cruel, deceitful, and scheming,
filling his breast.
As for showing deceptive words to Lǐ Shèng (李勝),
entrusting the investigation of prisons to Hé Yàn (何晏),
shameful and contrary to reason,
the gentleman does not do these things.
With this false sentiment,
applying it to all things,
if their strength and power were equal,
and they both met in the Central Plains,
with Zhòng Dá's (仲達) treacherous plans,
facing Kǒng Míng's (孔明) discipline,
I fear they would not be a match."
Wú Zhāng Yǎn's (吳張儼) *Mò Jì* (默記) comments on the merits and demerits of the two ministers Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng (司馬宣王), saying:
"The Hàn (漢) dynasty declined and became a hegemony,
the world was divided and collapsing,
the two lords both encountered opportune moments,
entrusting themselves to enlightened rulers.
Kǒng Míng (孔明) rose from the land of Shǔ Hàn (蜀漢),
treading upon one province,
compared to a great country,
it was about one-ninth.
Leading several tens of thousands of infantry,
making long drives to Qí Mountain (祁山),
with the grand ambition of letting his horses drink from the Yellow River and the Luò River;
Zhòng Dá (仲達) possessed ten times the land under heaven,
relying on a multitude of annexed troops,
Occupying strong cities,
possessing elite troops,
with no intention of capturing the enemy,
focused only on self-preservation.
If that Kǒngmíng were like this and did not perish,
then Liáng and Yōng provinces would not remove their armor,
the Central Plains would not take off their saddles,
and the outcome of victory and defeat would already be decided.
Compared to Sīmǎ,
isn't he superior?"
Someone said:
"Jìn Jǐng and Wén,
which brother was more virtuous?"
Emperor Míng of Wèi died,
and he established his adopted son, Fāng, Prince of Qí,
leaving an edict instructing Cáo Shuǎng and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng to assist in the government.
Xuānwáng executed Shuǎng,
and monopolized power himself.
Xuānwáng died,
his son, Prince Jǐng, named Shī, styled Zǐyuán,
succeeded him in assisting the government,
deposed Fāng, Prince of Qí,
and established the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng.
Prince Jǐng died,
his younger brother, Prince Wén, named Zhāo, styled Zǐshàng,
again succeeded him in assisting the government,
killed the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng,
and established the Prince of Chénliú.
Later, the King of Chénliú 陳留 (Cao Huan) ceded the Wei throne to the Jin.
Emperor Wǔ 武 of Jin, named Yán 炎, styled Ānshì 安世,
ascended the throne and pacified Wu 吳,
unifying the empire.
When his son Emperor Huì 惠 ascended the throne,
the empire fell into great chaos,
and the Five Barbarians entered the Central Plains.
Yú Nán 虞南 said:
"Hé Yàn 何晏 said:
'Only profound men,
are able to understand the ambitions of all under Heaven,
like Xiàhóu Tàichū 夏侯太初;
only insightful men,
are able to accomplish the affairs of all under Heaven,
like Sīmǎ Zǐyuán 司馬子元.'
Therefore, we know that the talent for assisting a ruler
was evident from an early age.
At the time of the extermination of (Cao) Shuǎng 爽,
his wisdom and strategies were already manifest.
(When) Qīn 欽 and Jiǎn 儉 raised troops,
he alone conquered the entire army.
This is sufficient to show his heroic plans.
Although the Dao prospered in a tripartite division,
he remained a subject his entire life,
his awe-inspiring reputation shook the ruler, yet his integrity as a subject was not diminished.
The nobility returned to allegiance completely,
which is admirable.
Emperor Tàizǔ 太祖 continued his achievements,
He was able to quell calamities and disorders,
pacify Huái and Hǎi in the south,
subdue Yōng and Shǔ in the west,
and the labor did not exceed the time limit.
His achievements were significant.
When Gāo Guì ascended the throne,
possessing intelligence and innate wisdom,
he was unable to exhaust his loyalty and assistance,
to emulate the footsteps of Yī and Zhōu.
Consequently, he falsely accused Shì Yàn,
and blamed Chéng Jì,
bringing upon himself a rebellious act,
ultimately enjoying a bad reputation.
The blemish of these words
cannot be erased."
Gān Bǎo's *Comprehensive Treatise on the Jin* states:
"In the past, Emperor Xuān, with his heroic talent and great capacity,
responded to destiny and served.
He encountered the beginning of Emperor Wèi's founding of the dynasty,
planning military affairs and state matters.
His excellent strategies repeatedly hit the mark,
and he submitted to [drawing] the carriage and pillow [for the emperors],
serving diligently for three generations.
His nature was deeply reserved,
and he possessed a deep fortress of mind,
yet he was able to be broad and accommodating.
He implemented methods and techniques to manage affairs,
and he knew people, selected and promoted them.
Therefore, he was able to capture Mèng Dá 孟達 in the west,
and conquer Gōngsūn Yuān 公孫淵 in the east.
Internally, he quelled Cáo Shuǎng 曹爽,
and externally, he attacked Wáng Líng 王陵.
Repeatedly, he resisted the armies of Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 under his command,
and in the east, he supported the flanking position against the Wú 吳 people.
Thus, the people cooperated,
and the grand image of empire began to take shape.
Shìzōng 世宗 inherited the foundation,
and Tàizǔ 太祖 continued the enterprise.
Xuán 玄 and Fēng 豐 caused internal disturbances,
while Qīn 欽 and Dàn 誕 rebelled externally.
Though their secret schemes were covert,
the signs were inevitably revealed in the early stages.
Despite disturbances at Huái 淮 and Pǔ 浦 again,
Xǔ 許 and Luò 洛 were not shaken.
All rebellious plots were rejected,
thus glorifying the accomplishments of their predecessors.
Then, they promoted Zhōng 鍾 and Dèng 鄧,
and led a long expedition into mediocre Shǔ 蜀.
With lightning speed, they swept through the Three Passes,
and Liú Chán 劉禪 became a subject.
The accord between Heaven's Mandate and human affairs,
was thus proven to be true.
Initially, they were subject to ceremonies befitting an extraordinary situation,
and ultimately received the bestowal of complete regalia.
As for Shìzǔ 世祖,
he then enjoyed the supreme position,
Being benevolent means being generous to those below you;
being frugal means practicing economy in expenditures;
being harmonious means not being lax;

Compared to Emperor Tàizǔ of the Sòng, he falls short,
but compared to Emperor Gāo of the Qí, he is superior."
Emperor Wén of the Suí dynasty rose from commoner status,

He pacified Yōng and Shǔ to the west,
Could the Southern Píng 江表 (Jiāng Biǎo),
when compared to Jìn Wǔ 晉武,
be considered similar?
Yú Nán 虞南 said:
"Suí Wén 隋文, relying on the weight of his maternal relations,

He focused on governance,
striving to act with benevolence,
therefore he was able to pacify both the new and old,

His civil and military institutions
were all worthy of admiration.
After conquering the area of Jiāng Huái 江淮,

eagerly awaited peace.
But after the fall of Jīnlíng 金陵,
the king's heart became extravagant and dissipated.
Although his power reached the four seas,

Jīng 荆 jade filled the inner palace,

The decorations of the Réshòu 仁壽 palace,

The strength of the people was exhausted,
and the wealth of the common people was depleted.
In addition, suspicion arose,
and matters of witchcraft flourished,
he slaughtered the consorts of beloved sons,

The affair of the cat-demon arose,

The fundamental principles were already disordered,

The hen crowed at dawn,

He deposed the innocent,

He deposed Crown Prince Yǒng and made him a commoner,

Meritorious officials and excellent assistants

His errors in his later years

His reign was not destined to be long-lasting.
Was it Heaven that destroyed him?"
The discussion said:
"Emperor Gāo of Hàn wanted to replace the Crown Prince with the Prince of Zhào, Rúyì.
Shūsūn Tōng remonstrated, saying:
'In the past, Duke Xiàn of Jìn, because of Lìjī,
deposed the Crown Prince
He established Xī Qí 奚齊,

Qín 秦, because it did not determine Fú Sū's 扶蘇 succession early,

The emperor said:
"I was just joking."
Tōng 通 said:
"The heir apparent is the foundation of the empire,

the empire will be shaken.
How can Your Majesty joke about the empire?"
He then listened to him.
Yuán Shào 袁紹 loved his younger son Shàng 尚,
and therefore made the elder son Tán 譚 the successor to his brother.
Jǔ Shòu 沮授 remonstrated, saying:
"It is said that ten thousand people chase a rabbit,
but only one person catches it.
The greedy all stop,
because the division is fixed.
Moreover, age is based on virtue,
and virtue is based on seniority,
which is the system of ancient times.
May Your Majesty contemplate the admonitions regarding success and failure of previous dynasties,
and consider the meaning of dividing the rabbit when pursuing it.
If this is not changed,
disaster will begin here."
Shào did not heed this advice,
and later they indeed developed a rift.
Therefore, it is said:
When establishing the legitimate son,
one should not allow concubines and favorites to harbor doubts.
Doubt leads to action,
and duality leads to strife.
If there are two sons vying for position,
the family will surely be in turmoil;
if there are two sons vying for position
and the family is not in turmoil,
it is because the parents are still alive.
Relying on parents to avoid turmoil,
once the parents are gone, turmoil is inevitable.
Wise words indeed!
Someone asked:
"The strategies of kings and hegemons
surely involve this principle.
I venture to ask, what is the significance of
establishing posthumous titles,
changing the calendar and starting the year,
and altering the colors of clothing,
to change people's perceptions?"
The answer was:
"The purpose of establishing posthumous titles in ancient times
was to serve as a warning to future generations.
Names were assigned according to conduct,
and there was no concealing the actions of rulers and parents.
Nowadays, ministers and sons do not consider the actual deeds,
but focus on honoring and aggrandizing.
This custom has been declining for a long time."
In the past, Jì Kāngzǐ 季康子 asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子 about the virtues of the Five Emperors.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Heaven has the Five Elements:
wood, fire, metal, water, and earth.
They divide time and nurture growth,
to bring things to fruition."
A year has three hundred and sixty days,
and each of the Five Elements governs for seventy-two days,
transforming, growing, and nurturing.
Their spirits are the Five Emperors,
weaving
the Five Emperors, the spirits of the Five Elements.
Ancient kings
changed their reign titles with each dynasty,
taking the Five Elements as their model.
The Five Elements succeed each other in ruling,
generating each other from beginning to end,
also symbolizing their meaning.
Therefore, in life, they are enlightened kings,
and in death, they are associated with the Five Elements.
Therefore, Tài Hào 太皞 is matched with wood, and
Gōumáng 勾芒 is the Minister of Wood.
Yándì 炎帝 is matched with fire, and
Zhùróng 祝融 is the Minister of Fire.
Shǎo Hào 少皞 is matched with metal, and
Rùshōu 蓐收 is the Minister of Metal.
Zhuānxū 顓頊 is matched with water, and
Xuánmíng 玄冥 is the Minister of Water.
Huángdì 黃帝 is matched with earth, and
Hòutǔ 后土 is the Minister of Earth.
Emperors and kings changed their titles,
according to the virtues of the Five Elements,
each with its own emphasis.
They followed the order of the virtue by which they ruled.
In the case of wood, the next position is fire.
The wood family esteemed red,
because the virtue of wood is righteousness that is universal,
following its mother element (water)
and encompassing its child element (fire).
The Xià hòu shì 夏后氏 dynasty ruled with the virtue of metal and esteemed black.
The Yīn 殷 dynasty ruled with the virtue of water and esteemed white.
The water family should esteem green,
but the reason they esteemed white
was to avoid the Earth family's esteem for green.
The Earth family should esteem white
because earth
is the master of the four elements,
and presides over the four seasons.
The use of the Five Elements,
begins first with Wood.
Therefore, the Tǔjiā 土家 people esteemed the color of wood, which is green.
The Zhōu 周 people reigned with the virtue of Wood and esteemed the color red.
This is the reason why the Three Dynasties differed.
When the Hàn 漢 dynasty began,
Gōngsūn Chén 公孫臣 and Jiǎ Yí 賈誼 considered Hàn to possess the virtue of Earth,
according to the transmission of the Five Elements,
which follows the pattern of being overcome
in a "transmission by transfer."
The Five Emperors succeeded each other,
always following the rule of mutual conquest: Metal, Wood, Water, Fire, and Earth.
Qín 秦 possessed the virtue of Water;
therefore, it was said that Hàn, based on Earth, conquered it.
Liú Xiàng 劉向 and his son believed that the Emperors originated from the direction of Zhen (震),
so Páo Xī shì 庖犧氏 initially received the virtue of Wood,
and thereafter, it was transmitted from mother to son,
ending and beginning again.
From Shénnóng 神農 and Huángdì 黃帝,
down through the dynasties of Táng 唐, Yú 虞, and the Three Dynasties,
Hàn obtained Fire.
Therefore, when Gāozǔ 高祖 first arose,
his divine mother wailed at night,
manifesting the omen of the Red Emperor,
and he obtained the mandate of Heaven.
In the past, Gònggōng 共工, with the virtue of Water, intervened between Wood and Fire,
To share the same fate as Qin,
is not secondary,
therefore none of them are long-lasting.
From my perspective,
the rise of emperors
each originates from the descendants of the Five Emperors,
in order to establish the Five Virtues.
How can this be made clear?
The Hàn
are descendants of Yáo.
Yáo,
ruled by the virtue of fire,
therefore the Hàn embodies fire.
During the time of Yuán Shào, Gěng Bāo said:
"The virtue of red is exhausted,
Yuán is the yellow heir,
thinking Yuán is the descendent of Shùn,
Shùn is a ruler of earth virtue,
therefore I encourage advancement."
From this we know the rise of emperors,
each originates from
the descendants of the Five Emperors,
it has come from this origin.
Now the Qín,
are descendants of Zhuānxū,
of water virtue.
Therefore the Qín embodies water virtue.
From this perspective,
Even after a hundred generations, it can be known.
Your servant ranks tenth.
Your servant ranks tenth.
Now, when sprouts have not yet stirred,
and signs have not yet appeared,
to clearly and uniquely see the seeds of survival and destruction,
the essentials of gain and loss,
to prevent them before they occur,
and to make the ruler stand supremely in a place of obvious glory,
such a person
is a sage minister.
Emptying his heart and exhausting his will,
daily advancing good principles;
encouraging the ruler with propriety and righteousness,
enlightening the ruler with long-term strategies;
following and nurturing his merits,
and correcting and rescuing his evils.
Such a person
is a great minister.
Rising early and sleeping late,
tirelessly promoting the worthy,
frequently citing the actions of the past,
in order to encourage the ruler's intentions.
Such a person
is a loyal minister.
Someone asked Master Yuán:
"Therefore, is Shǎofǔ Yáng Fù
not a loyal minister?"
The reply was:
"He can be called a straightforward official,
but whether he is loyal, I do not know.
Why?
As a minister,
seeing his lord stray from the right path,
pointing out his faults and spreading his wrongdoings,
he can be called a straightforward official,
but not necessarily loyal.
Thus, Sīkōng Chén Qún is different.
He talks all day long,
but never speaks of the ruler's faults.
He submits memorials dozens of times, yet outsiders do not know about it.
Gentlemen say that Chén Qún is a senior figure in this regard.
This is loyalty."
Clearly discerning success and failure,
preventing calamities early and rescuing the situation,
blocking the gaps,
cutting off the sources,
turning misfortune into blessing,
so that the ruler has no worries in the end.
Such a person
is a wise minister.
Acting according to the written law,
fulfilling the duties of one's official position,
not accepting gifts,
To be frugal in food and drink.
Those who are like this,
are *zhēn* ministers.
When the state is benighted and chaotic,
what they do is not to flatter,
they dare to offend the sovereign's stern countenance,
and directly speak of the sovereign's faults.
Those who are like this,
are *zhí* ministers.
These are called the six correct (types of ministers).
Huán Fàn's *Shì Yào Lùn* says:
"Are ministers who are clumsy in speech but skillful in intention,
whose words are contrary but whose actions are compliant,
not to be pardoned for their uprightness?
Are ministers who are simple and foolish and slow of speech,
who appear outwardly detached but are inwardly perceptive,
not to be pardoned for their sincerity?
Are ministers who brave difficulties for the sake of the ruler,
and endure slander for the sake of the state,
not to be pardoned for their loyalty?
Are ministers who uphold righteousness against the consensus of the masses,
and enforce the law while disregarding private desires,
not to be pardoned for their impartiality?
Are ministers who do not compromise themselves to seek agreement,
nor bring disaster to the world to gain fame,
not to be pardoned for their integrity?
Are ministers who rise from humble and lowly positions to make prominent statements,
and from low status present matters of state,
Can one not pardon them for their difficulties?
If a minister is solitary and adheres to principles,
stands aloof and is slandered,
can one not pardon them for their strength (of character)?
These seven instances for pardon
are the means to encourage goodness."
To be content in office and greedy for emolument,
not attending to public affairs,
drifting along with the world,
looking around to see what others are doing—
such a person
is a compliant minister (*jù chén*).
Whatever the ruler says, they all say, "Good,"
whatever the ruler does, they all say, "Acceptable,"
secretly seeking what the ruler likes and offering it,
to gratify the ruler's ears and eyes.
They seek temporary agreement and compromise,
sharing pleasure with the ruler,
not considering future harm.
Such a person
is a flattering minister (*yú chén*).
Inside, they are truly treacherous and perverse,
outwardly appearing meticulously cautious,
with artful words and a pleasing countenance,
and in their hearts, they are jealous of the worthy.
Those they want to advance, they highlight their good qualities,
concealing their faults;
those they want to dismiss, they expose their flaws,
Concealing their goodness,
causing the ruler's rewards and punishments to be inappropriate, and orders not to be carried out.
Such people
are treacherous ministers (jiān chén).
Their wisdom is enough to embellish what is wrong,
their eloquence is enough to implement deceitful arguments,
inwardly alienating close relatives,
outwardly stirring up jealousy and disorder in the court.
Such people
are slanderous ministers (chán chén).
They monopolize power and arrogate authority,
making light things heavy;
they form factions in their private homes,
enriching their families;
they presumptuously fabricate the ruler's commands
to conspicuously aggrandize themselves.
Such people
are traitorous ministers (zéi chén).
They flatter the ruler with obsequious wickedness,
plunging the ruler into injustice,
forming cliques and colluding
to obscure the ruler's discernment,
causing white and black to be indistinguishable, and right and wrong unheard;
causing the ruler's wickedness to spread throughout the country and be heard by the surrounding states.
Such people
are ministers who bring about the downfall of a country (wáng guó zhī chén).
These are called the Six Evils (liù xié).
Huán Fàn's 《Shì Yào Lùn》 says:
"Your servant has one who establishes a small loyalty to achieve great disloyalty,
who practices small trustworthiness to accomplish great untrustworthiness.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as deceitful?
Your servant has one who appears stern but is inwardly weak,
who outwardly adopts benevolence but acts contrary to it.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as insincere?
Your servant has one who harms his peers to monopolize the court,
who blocks communications from below to obstruct those above.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as jealous?
Your servant has one who advances wicked theories to confound what is right,
who uses specious arguments to harm the virtuous.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as slanderous?
Your servant has one who uses rewards to repay personal favors,
who uses punishments to establish his authority.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as treacherous?
Your servant has one who outwardly recommends each other,
but inwardly secretly eliminates each other,
who ostensibly schemes for the public good but actually harbors private interests.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as deceptive?
Your servant has one who serves those at your side to seek advancement,
who relies on important ministers to form alliances.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as hypocritical?
Your servant has one who harmonizes with others to obtain advantage,
who compromises to seek advancement.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as a source of disaster?
Your servant has one who pleases the ruler's intentions to seek favor,
who pleases the ruler's words to gain acceptance.
Should he not be regarded with suspicion as sycophantic?
These nine considerations
are the means of preventing evil."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Chén Línggōng and his ministers engaged in lewd behavior in court.
Xiè Yě remonstrated and was killed.
He is similar to Bǐ Gàn.
Can he be called benevolent?"
The Master said:
"Bǐ Gàn, in relation to Zhòu,
was a close relative, his uncle.
In office, he was the junior tutor.
His loyal and sincere heart
was solely focused on preserving the ancestral temple.
Therefore, he contested it with certain death,
hoping that after his death, Zhòu would regret and awaken.
His fundamental intention was benevolence.
Xiè Yě's position was that of a lower senior officer.
He had no familial ties.
He clung to favor and did not leave.
With his insignificant self,
he wanted to correct the lewd darkness of an entire state.
His death was of no benefit.
He can be called regretful!
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'The people are much inclined to wickedness;
let none set himself to be a patron of it.'
Is it not speaking of Xiè Yě?"
Someone asked:
"Shūsūn Tōng ā Second Emperor's (Èr Shì) intentions,
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"To assess one's ruler and then advance,
is what former sages approved of.
Shūsūn Shēng was rare in his generation,
is that acceptable?"
assessing affairs and creating rituals,
advancing and retreating in accordance with the times, changing with them,
and ultimately becoming the Confucian patriarch of the Hàn dynasty.
The gentlemen of antiquity
were straight but not rigid,
flexible but not unyielding,
great straightness appearing bent,
the Way akin to a winding serpent,
this is likely what is meant."
Discussion:
Grand Duke (Tàigōng) said:
"An official who does not aspire to remonstrate
is not my official."
Zhū Yún continued to press Zhāng Yǔ, saying:
"To hold office and protect one's position
without the ability to come and go (influence matters),
is worthy of execution."
Bān Gù said:
"To rely on the times is to abandon the Way,
to go against custom is to risk danger;
this is why it was difficult for the ancients to accept rank and position."
From these words,
Concerning survival and death,
what is their meaning?
The answer is:
Fàn Yè said:
"If one is solely focused on righteousness, then life will be harmed;
if one is solely focused on life, then righteousness will be diminished.
If righteousness is more important than life,
then sacrificing life is acceptable;
if life is more important than righteousness,
then preserving life is acceptable."
Someone asked:
"In that case, Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fán
contended with the eunuchs in the same court,
and were ultimately killed by them.
Were they wrong?"
Fàn Yè said:
"During the reigns of Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng,
men like Chén Fán
were all able to establish a reputation,
and speak out against the benighted customs,
rushing about in dangerous situations,
to contend with the corrupt officials.
Those who ultimately met their demise,
it was not that they were unable to purify their emotions and aspirations,
and distance themselves from the dust and haze [of the corrupt world].
They pitied that the men of the world,
valued detachment from worldly affairs as a virtue,
and yet human relationships were not cared for;
Considering withdrawing from the world as unrighteous,
therefore he repeatedly declined to leave his position;
taking a benevolent heart as his own responsibility,
even though the path was long, he became ever more vigorous.
When he encountered a favorable opportunity,
he cooperated in strategizing with Dòu Wǔ 竇武,
it can be said to be a once-in-ten-thousand-generations moment.
Although his efforts did not come to fruition,
nevertheless, his trustworthiness and righteousness were sufficient to sway the hearts of the world."
The commentary says:
This is what is meant by righteousness being more important than life,
relinquishing life is permissible.
Someone asked:
"Zāng Hóng 臧洪 dying in the disaster of Zhāng Chāo 張超,
can that be considered equal in righteousness?"
Fàn Yè 范曄 said:
"The siege of Yōngqiū 雍丘,
Zāng Hóng's 臧洪's grief and indignation,
was magnificent!
Considering his followers barefoot and wailing,
donning armor and requesting to attack,
is truly pitiful.
The choices of heroes and powerful figures,
are they different from the heart of upholding righteousness?
As for those who form alliances and join forces,
harboring deceit and scheming to surpass each other,
they are merely concerned with where power and profit lie.
Moreover, since the isolated city was already in danger,
The methods of Cao and Yuan were harmonious,
but Hong in vain pointed to the enemy as the target,
in order to relieve the crisis of being hung upside down.
An army driven by resentment
is what military strategists avoid.
It could be said he cherished the integrity of crying for Qin,
but preserving Jing has not been heard of."
Formerly, the Governor of Guangling, Zhang Chao, entrusted the government to Zang Hong,
and later Yuan Shao also befriended him.
When Cao Cao besieged Zhang Chao in Yongqiu,
Hong heard that Chao was besieged,
so he barefooted and weeping bitterly,

and also requested troops from Shao.
Shao did not listen,
Chao's city fell,
and consequently, Chao was executed along with his clan.
Hong therefore resented Shao,
and broke with him.
Shao raised troops to besiege him,
the city fell, and he was killed.
A discussion says:
Zang Hong, in a time of upheaval,
acted according to the principles of peace and tranquility,
and was not a man to establish merit.
Someone said:
"Jì Bù was a strong man,
but instead subdued his strength and became yielding,
kūn qián fěi nì,
Is it because of this?"
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"With Xiàng Yǔ's spirit,
and Jì Bù being renowned in Chǔ for his courage,
personally commanding armies many times,
seizing
(pronunciation: qǐ lián fǎn)
flags numerous times,
he can be called a brave warrior.
Yet when he was subjected to punishment,

He must have been confident in his abilities,

The worthy indeed value their death.
Now, lowly concubines and servants,

their plans are exhausted,
and there is nothing more for them."
Commentary says:
The Grand Historian said:
"Wèi Bào and Péng Yuè, although formerly base,
had already swept across thousands of miles,
enthroned themselves facing south,
Bloodshed and victory,
daily news.
Cherishing the intention of rebellion,
and upon defeat,
not dying but being captured,
imprisoned, subjected to punishment and execution,
why is that?
People of average talent and above would be ashamed of such actions,
how much more so a king!
He is no different,
therefore, his wisdom and strategy surpass others,
he only worries about not having a position.
If he obtains the power of a small position,
his transformations will be like clouds rising and dragons changing,
desiring to be able to conform to the proper standards,

This describes strategists,
those who strive to establish their achievements.
Furthermore, the "Eulogy of Lord Lìn" says:
"Knowing death is certain makes one brave,

but how one faces death that is difficult.
When Lìn Xiàngrú drew back the jade disc and glared at the pillar,

the consequence was nothing more than execution,
yet scholars are sometimes timid and dare not speak out.
Xiàngrú, with a single sharpening of his spirit,
inspired awe and trust in the enemy state;
He retreated and yielded to Lián Pō 廉頗,
his name carrying the weight of Mount Tài 泰山.
His handling of wisdom and courage
can be said to have been all-encompassing!"
This is a loyal and steadfast minister,
truly knowing where to die.
Guǎnzi 管子 said:
"He is not ashamed of being in prison,
but is ashamed that the world is not well-governed;
he is not ashamed of not dying with Gōngzǐ Jiū 公子糾,

This is someone who is confident in their talent
and takes saving the world as their measure.
These are all examples of how gentlemen conduct themselves,
clear examples of whether to die or not to die.
Someone asked:
"When Zōng Ké 宗殼 was lowly,
he was looked down upon by Yǔ Yè 庾業.
When he became prominent,
he asked Yè 業 to be his Chief Clerk (zhǎngshǐ 長史),
