Péi Zǐyě 裴子野 said:
"To be poor and not feel sorrow,
to be lowly and not feel discontent,
to be content with one's natural disposition,
and to broaden this great plan,
these are the virtues of Zēng Zǐ 曾子 and Yuán Xiàn 原憲.
To lower one's aspirations and disgrace oneself,
to bow one's head and bend one's back,
to endure being under the command of mediocre officials
in order to be able to gallop above the masses of heroes when powerful,
these are the aspirations of Hán Xìn 韓信 and Qīng Bù 黥布.
The actions of humbling oneself are the same,
but the feelings of being in a humble position are different."
"Your Grace should also send Yǔn."
Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi campaigned against Xúzhōu.
He sent Chéng Yù to remain and defend Zhēnchéng.
Zhāng Miǎo rebelled.
Emperor Tàizǔ encountered Lǚ Bù.
Bù captured the mother of the magistrate of Fàn, Jìn Yǔn.
Emperor Tàizǔ sent Yù to persuade Jìn Yǔn,
not to waver because of his mother,
but to firmly defend Fàn.
Yǔn, with tears streaming down his face, said:
"I dare not have a second thought."
Emperor Wéndì of Wèi asked Wáng Lǎng and others:
"In the past, when Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
people could not deceive him;
when Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù,
people could not bear to deceive him;
when Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
people did not dare to deceive him.
Among the talents of these three men,
in relation to the virtue of the ruler, which is superior?"
They replied:
"If the ruler relies on virtue,
then the ministers, moved by righteousness, cannot bear to deceive;
if the ruler relies on observation,
then the ministers, fearing discovery, cannot deceive;
if the ruler relies on punishment,
then the ministers, fearing punishment, dare not deceive.
Relying on virtue and moving with righteousness,
To guide virtue and regulate rituals,
to have shame and thereby be corrected,
these are those who tread the same path;
to rely on investigation and fear wrongdoing,
is like guiding governance and regulating punishments,
avoiding punishment but having no shame,
these are those who return to the same destination.
The difference between superior and inferior
lies in the balance of consideration,
and is not merely a matter of noticing a difference of a few ounces."
Someone asked:
"Jì Wénzǐ and Gōngsūn Hóng,
these two men both practiced frugality and simplicity,
but their reputations are different,
why is that?"
Fàn Yè said:
"Those who benefit from benevolence,
may borrow benevolence to pursue profit;
those who embody righteousness,
do not aim to embody it to accord with righteousness.
Jì Wénzǐ's concubine did not wear silk,
and the people of Lǔ considered it a beautiful story;
Gōngsūn Hóng personally wore hemp bedding,
and Jí Àn criticized him for being deceitful.
The facts are not different, but the reputations are different,
why is that?
Is it because the embodiment is different from the benefit?
Therefore, the previous records say:
The benevolent find peace in benevolence,
the wise profit from benevolence,
those who fear punishment are forced into benevolence.
Comparing those who are benevolent,
their achievements are not noticeably different;
examining the basis of their benevolence,
one cannot help but see differences.
Those who find peace in benevolence
are those whose nature is good;
those who profit from benevolence
are those who vigorously practice it;
those who are forced into benevolence
are those who have no choice.
Comparing these three types of benevolence,
those who find peace in it are superior."
The discussion says:
Truly, a sage's virtue is complete,
and he lacks no ability.
Since the standard of the *Doctrine of the Mean*,
talent has tended to be partial.
Therefore, it is said:
*Chái* was dull,
*Shēn* was slow,
*Shī* was biased,
*Yóu* was coarse.
From this perspective,
those with complete virtue are few!
Since complete virtue is rare,
Then to rely on artifice and exert effort for good!
Yet the world despises artifice and pretense,
and people value entrusting matters to those who are genuine.
If their genuineness lies in being greedy and foolish, and yet you entrust them with matters,
can that be considered wise?
He replied:
Alas!
Why would that be the case?
Human beings emulate the essence of Heaven and Earth,
bearing Yin and embracing Yang.
Although there are differences in their nature, whether clear or turbid, virtuous or foolish,
their innate qualities are different,
their pursuits, movements, desires,
and guiding principles are the same.
Therefore, smooth faces and delicate features
are what people find pleasing;
riding in sturdy carriages and driving fine steeds
are what people love;
enduring hardship and maintaining integrity
are what people find difficult;
sacrificing personal interests for the public good
are what people find painful.
If you do not regulate them with ritual and teachings,
then they will become unrestrained and uncontrolled.
How can you expect them to embrace hardship and live plainly,
to be upright, chaste, and fair,
to be incorruptible when facing wealth, and to be righteous in taking and giving?
Therefore, the *Lǐ* (Book of Rites) says:
"Desires cannot be indulged,
ambition cannot be satisfied."
An ancient saying goes:
"An honest person does not fail to love wealth,
but acquires it through proper means."
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"As if cut, as if filed,
as if carved, as if polished."
All of these speak of artificiality and pretense.
If one indulges their foolish behavior,
follows their base emotions,
and calls it "acting naturally" and praises them for it,
then this is a criminal against the former kings.
Therefore, I believe that artificiality and pretense
are the beginnings of ritual and righteousness;
acting naturally
is the master of greed and baseness.
Can one who earnestly practices benevolence
be easily deceived?
Someone asks:
"Regarding the matter at Chángpíng,
Bái Qǐ buried 400,000 Zhao soldiers alive.
Can he be considered a remarkable general?"
Hé Yàn said:
"Bái Qǐ's surrender of the Zhao soldiers
deceitfully led to the burial of 400,000 of them.
Is this merely a matter of cruelty and violence?
Afterwards, it would be difficult to regain their loyalty!
向使眾人豫知降之必死，
then even Zhāng Xū's empty fist
would have been formidable.
How much more so forty-thousand soldiers, armored and armed?
If the world saw the surrendered generals of Qín
with their heads piled up like mountains,
and the surrendered masses to Qín
with their bones forming hills,
then in future battles,
death would be preferable,
so what army would submit,
what city would surrender?
Thus, although able to dispose of the lives of four hundred thousand men,
it only served to strengthen the resolve of the world to fight.
Intending to gain success in a single dynasty,
it instead further solidified the defenses of the feudal lords.
Therefore, the army advanced and undermined its own momentum,
the army won but ultimately lost its strategy.
Why?
Suppose the Zhào armies were to reunite,
and Mǎ Fú were reborn,
then when future battles arose,
they would certainly not be the same as previous encounters,
especially now that the whole world is preparing for the future!
The reason why they ultimately dared not add troops to Hán Dān
was not only concern about Píng Yuán's patching up of defenses,
or fear that the feudal lords would send reinforcements,
but they simply concealed it and did not speak of it.
Moreover, concerning the matter of Chángpíng 長平,
all the people of Qín 秦 aged fifteen and above
shouldered halberds and faced Zhào 趙.
Given the strength of Qín 秦,
and that among those fifteen and above,
more than half were killed or wounded,
this means the merit of defeating Zhào 趙 was small,
while the loss to Qín 秦 was great.
How then can it be called a remarkable feat?"
The discussion says:
Huáng Shígōng 黃石公 said:
"The gentle can control the strong,
the weak can control the powerful.
Gentleness is virtue,
force is thievery.
The gentle
are those whom people assist;
the forceful
are where resentment dwells."
Therefore,
Zhòu's 紂 hundred victories
ultimately left him without successors;
Xiàng Yǔ's 項羽 troops were strong,
yet he ultimately lost the world.
Thus, Suí Hé 隨何 said:
"If Chǔ 楚 wins,
then the feudal lords will naturally be apprehensive and come to each other's aid.
The strength of Chǔ 楚
It was only enough to bring the armies of the world upon him."
From this perspective,
if the world were already settled,
one could rely on the victory of a single battle,
and deception would be permissible.
But if the country is in chaos,
with the balance of power undecided, and one loses trust and righteousness in the world,
that is the path to defeat and ruin.
During the time of the Seven Kingdoms,
the feudal lords were still strong,
and yet Bái Qǐ 白起 buried the surrendered soldiers of Zhào 赵,
causing the feudal lords to fear him and form alliances against him.
The alliances of the feudal lords
were not to Qín's 秦 benefit,
turning victory in battle into ultimate defeat.
Hé Yàn's 何晏 argument is correct.
Some say:
"Yuè Yì 樂毅 did not massacre the two cities,
and consequently lost his great enterprise,
was that not a mistake?"
Xiàhóu Yuán 夏侯元 said:
"Reading Master Yuè's 樂 letter to King Huì of Yàn 燕惠王,
he probably understood the opportunity and conformed to the Way,
conducting himself with propriety from beginning to end!
Now, one who seeks to exhaust the measure of morality
and strives to have the world at heart,
how could he be confined to the circumstances of the time,
and stop at mere annexation?
Now, as for annexation,
it is not what Yuè Shēng乐生 concerns himself with.
To strengthen Yān 燕 by abandoning the proper way
is also not what Yuè Shēng乐生 seeks.
Not concerning himself with petty gains,
not seeking small accomplishments,
this is because he intends to encompass all under Heaven.
The affair of attacking Qí 齐
was therefore to set his grand design in motion and move the four seas.
Besieging cities while causing no harm to the common people—
this shows his benevolent heart reaching far and wide.
To extend virtuous commands to lead the various states
would be close to the deeds of Tāng 汤 and Wǔ 武.
Yuè Shēng 乐生 was then expanding the grand outline,
in order to release the two cities,
to gain people's clear trust,
and to await their collapse.
He intended to make the people of Jímò 即墨 and Jǔ 莒
hate their superiors,
to open up a broad and expansive path
to await the likes of Tián Dān 田单;
to foster a tolerant and kind spirit
in order to express the aspirations of the scholars of Qí 齐;
to summon them from the Eastern Sea
and incorporate them into the Chinese lands.
If our grace were like spring,
the people would respond like grass,
thinking of supporting the Lord of Yān 燕,
If we but listen to the wind
and these two cities will surely follow,
then the royal enterprise will flourish.
Though we linger in these two cities,
we will hasten the acquisition of the whole realm.
An unforeseen misfortune
is a situation beyond calculation,
defeated just as we were about to succeed;
such is the way of changing times.
But if we press them with arms,
coerce them with force,
wantonly indulge in the cruelty of slaughter,
to show this to the people of the four seas,
even though these two cities are almost ready to surrender,
then the affairs of a hegemon or king
will be very far away indeed.
Could Yuè Yì (樂毅) not have known that capturing the two cities would be quicker?
He was concerned that capturing the cities would ruin the grand design.
Could he not have worried that not acting swiftly might lead to unforeseen changes?
He was concerned that acting swiftly and causing changes are the same thing.
Judging from this,
Yuè Yì's (樂毅) decision not to slaughter the two cities
is immeasurable."
Someone asked:
"Yuè Yì (樂毅) served the weak state of Yān (燕),
defeated the powerful state of Qí (齊),
assembled the troops of five states,
and avenged the shame of his ruler.
To besiege a city without pressing the attack,
and to cause the general to reach the end of his path and submit through righteousness,
this is the army of the benevolent.
They all believe it's a better strategy than that of Wǔ Hóu.
Is this acceptable?"
Zhāng Fǔ said:
"To use the troops of five states to jointly attack one state of Qí is
not worthy of being called strong;
to engage in a great battle west of the Jì River,
with corpses piled up and blood flowing,
is not worthy of being called benevolent.
That Kǒngmíng possessed the virtues of both civil and military leadership,
and waited for the opportune moment with long sighs.
Liú Xuándé, with his discerning eye for talent,
repeatedly visited his thatched hut,
seeking his advice on governing the world,
and from him came forth endless brilliant strategies.
Thereupon, he persuaded Sūn Quán (孫權) in the east,
and resisted the great Wèi (魏) in the north,
with a victorious army,
assisting in the capture of Shǔ (蜀).
And when Xuándé (玄德) was on his deathbed,
he abdicated the great throne to him.
amidst the chaos,
he established a young and inexperienced ruler,
setting up officials and distributing duties,
and ranked and assigned the various talents.
He managed internal affairs through civil administration,
He used military force to break the balance,
and then spread his benevolence to the people within the state.
In his military expeditions,
no one picked up lost items on the road,
and he didn't violate even a hair's breadth of the people's property.
His meritorious achievements reached a point of completion and then he fell (died).
Looking at his surviving writings,
his plans and strategies were vast and far-reaching.
If there was profit, he yielded it to his subordinates;
if there were shortcomings among his subordinates, he personally blamed himself.
When he saw good, he embraced it;
when he received admonishment, he corrected himself.
Therefore, his reputation resounded far and wide.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Hearing of Bó Yí's character,
greedy men become honest."
I believe that seeing Kǒngmíng's loyalty,
treacherous officials would establish their integrity.
He would probably compete for victory with Yī and Lǚ,
how could he merely be ranked with Yuè Yì?"
Someone said:
"Shāng Yāng rose from humble origins,
approached Duke Xiào of Qín,
wielding the strategies of the Three Arts,
swallowed the alliances of the Six States,
and enabled Qín to establish its imperial enterprise.
Could he be considered an assistant to a hegemon?"
Liú Xiàng said:
"Now, Shāng Jūn
inwardly urged the work of cultivation and warfare,
outwardly emphasized rewards for battle achievements,
did not curry favor with the noble and favored,
nor did he discriminate against the distant and estranged.
Although the *Shū* says:
'Be impartial and have no factions,'
and the *Shī* says:
'The road of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
its straightness is known like an arrow,'
the strictness of the *Sīmǎ Fǎ* towards soldiers,
and Hòu Jì of Zhōu's encouragement of agriculture,
cannot surpass this.
This is the reason for annexing the feudal lords.
Therefore, Sūn Qīng said:
'Four generations of having victory,
is not by luck,
but by fate.'
Now, hegemonic rulers like Qí Huán and Jìn Wén,
Huán did not violate the alliance at Kē,
and Wén did not break the agreement at Yuán,
and the feudal lords trusted them.
This was due to the plans of Guǎn Zhòng and Jiù Fàn.
Now, Shāng Jūn betrayed the old favor to Gōngzǐ Áng,
abandoned the clear trustworthiness of dealing with Wèi,
and deceitfully seized the multitude of the three armies,
therefore the feudal lords feared his strength but did not trust him.
Supposing Xiào Gōng encountered Qí Huán and Jìn Wén,
If you could gain control of the feudal lords,
and unite their rulers,
and lead the armies of the world to attack Qin,
then Qin would fall.
The world lacked rulers like Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn,
therefore Qin was able to annex the feudal lords.
Wèi Yāng initially thought himself to understand the virtues of a true king and hegemon,
but examining his actions,
they are inconsistent.
In the past, Duke Shào of Zhōu implemented benevolent governance,
and upon his death,
later generations remembered him fondly.
The poem "Bì Fèi Gāntáng" is evidence of this.
He once rested under a sweet pear tree,
and (the people) could not bear to cut down the tree,
how much more so would they not harm his person?
Guǎn Zhòng seized three hundred households from the town of Biàn belonging to Bóshì,
yet there were no complaints.
Now, Wèi Yāng internally employs harsh knife and saw punishments,
and externally imposes severe axe and execution penalties,
resulting in his death by dismemberment by chariots.
How far removed he is from being an assistant to a hegemon!
He is indeed far removed!
However, it was also wrong for Duke Xiào to kill him.
That was also not right.
He could have been assisted and used,
making Wèi Yāng implement lenient and fair laws,
adding benevolence to them,
If you establish credibility,
you will probably be an assistant to a hegemon!"
It is said:
Shāng Yāng first sought an audience with Duke Xiào of Qín through Jǐng Jiān.
He tried to persuade him with the way of the emperors.
Duke Xiào was not interested,
and kept dozing off.
Later, he spoke with Yāng again,
and was unaware that his knees had moved beyond the mat.
Jǐng Jiān said:
"How did you please our lord?
He was extremely delighted."
Yāng said:
"Initially, I tried to persuade him with the way of the emperors,
but the lord said:
'Too distant!
How can I wait anxiously for several decades or hundreds of years for my descendants to achieve success?'
I then tried to persuade him with the way of the hegemon,
and he desired it but couldn't quite grasp it.
I then persuaded him with the art of strengthening the state,
and the lord was greatly pleased.
However, it is difficult to compare him to the virtue of the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties!"
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ met at Kē and formed an alliance.
Cáo Mò used a dagger to threaten Duke Huán to return the territory invaded from Lǔ.
Duke Huán agreed,
but later regretted it
and wanted to not return the territory to Lǔ and kill Cáo Mò.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"To abandon trustworthiness among the feudal lords,
to lose the support of the world,
is unacceptable."
Thereupon, he returned the land lost in three defeats to Cáo Mò.
The feudal lords heard of this,
and all trusted Qí and desired to attach themselves to it.
The Shān Róng attacked Yān,
and Yān urgently appealed to Qí.
Qí Huán Gōng rescued Yān and returned.
Duke Zhuāng of Yān escorted Huán Gōng into the territory of Qí.
Huán Gōng said:
"If not the Son of Heaven,
feudal lords do not escort each other beyond the border.
I cannot be disrespectful to Yān."
Thereupon, he divided a ditch, ceding to the Duke of Yān the area he had reached with the Duke of Yān,
ordering the restoration of the government of Shào Gōng,
and the payment of tribute to Zhōu.
The feudal lords heard of this and all followed suit.
Qí Huán Gōng thus began his hegemony.
Judging from this,
Shāng Yāng was harsh and uncompromising, abandoning trustworthiness.
It is clear he was not an assistant for a hegemon.
However, Duke Xiào wanted quick results
and did not heed Yāng's words.
Duke Xiào was mistaken.
Shāng Yāng was constrained by the world
and pressured by the ruler,
and could not implement his ideals.
Liú Xiàng's argument that Yāng had no arts of a hegemon or king
is incorrect.
Zhūgě Liàng executed Mǎ Sù because he was defeated at Jiē Tíng.
He killed him.
Later, Jiǎng Wǎn said to Liàng:
"In the past, when Chǔ killed Déchén,
Duke Wén's joy was understandable.
The empire is not yet settled,
and to execute men of wisdom and strategy,
is that not regrettable?"
Liàng, shedding tears, said:
"The reason why Sūn Wǔ was able to achieve victory
was due to the clarity of his legal application.
Therefore, Yáng violated the law,
and Wèi Jiàng executed him.
The world is fragmented,
and warfare has just begun.
If we abandon the law now,
how can we punish the rebels?"
Xí Záochǐ said:
"Is it not fitting that Zhūgě Liàng was unable to unify the Central Plains?
Indeed!
The people of Jìn valued the descendants of Lín Fù even after his failures,
therefore they abandoned the law to achieve success.
Chǔ Chéng already understood the benefits of Déchén,
therefore he killed him to emphasize the gravity of his defeat.
Now, Shǔ is a secluded and backward place,
with fewer talents than the Central Plains,
To kill off its outstanding talents,
and retreat to employ those of inferior ability,
to value strict law over talent,
and not to learn from the path of the three defeats,
intending to achieve success with this,
would it not be difficult?"
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Huánzǐ to battle with Chǔ at Bì.
Huánzǐ returned defeated and requested to die.
The Marquis of Jìn wished to grant it.
Shì Zhēnzǐ said:
"It is not permissible.
In the Battle of Chéngpú,
the Jìn army was quartered and fed for three days,
yet Duke Wén still had a worried expression.
Those around him said:
'To be worried when there is cause for joy,
is it like being joyful when there is cause for worry?'
The Duke said:
'Déchén is still alive;
my worry has not yet ceased.
A trapped beast still fights;
how much more so the state's minister!'
After Chǔ killed Zǐ Yù,
the Duke's joy was then discernible,
and he said:
'This is Jìn's second victory and Chǔ's second defeat.'
Because of this, Chǔ did not contend for two generations.
Today, perhaps this is a great warning to Jìn,
And yet he killed Lín Fǔ.
To magnify the victory over Chǔ,
is this not perhaps uncompetitive?
Lín Fǔ's service to his lord
was that in advancement he considered exhausting his loyalty,
and in retirement he considered making up for his faults;
he was a protector of the state.
How could the lord kill him?
Moreover, his defeat
was like an eclipse of the sun or moon,
what harm does it do to their brightness?"
The Marquis of Jìn had him restored to his position.
What about comparing him with Zhōu Bó, whose merit was great, and Huò Guāng?
How are they?
The answer was:
"Bó was originally a great minister of Emperor Gāo,
to whom the masses turned,
holding the position of Grand Commandant,
possessing a million soldiers.
He had the power of Chén Píng and Wáng Líng,
and also the support of the princes of Zhū Xū.
Lì Jì persuaded and lobbied,
using deception against the Lü family.
Relying on the will of the people,
it was easy to accomplish the task.
As for Huò Guāng,
in a hurried and critical moment,
he received the entrusted responsibility,
He assisted and guided the young ruler,
and the realm was at peace.
He encountered the rebellion of Yān Wáng Wǎn,
exterminated the wicked rebels,
and thereby secured the royal house.
He deposed the Chāngyì king,
enthroned Xiào Xuān (Emperor Xuan),
shouldered the great responsibility of the Hàn dynasty,
promoted the prosperity of its revival,
equaling Yī and Zhōu in reputation,
and became a worthy prime minister of the Hàn.
Examining and verifying the results of his actions,
his merits and demerits are clear."
Yuán Àng asked Emperor Wén of Hàn, saying:
"Your Majesty, what kind of person do you think Jiàng Hóu Zhōu Bó is?"
The Emperor said:
"A minister of the state."
Àng said:
"He can be called a meritorious minister,
but not a minister of the state.
A minister of the state
is one who remains with the ruler when the ruler is present,
and perishes with the ruler when the ruler is gone.
During the time of Empress Lǚ,
the Lǐu clan was on the verge of extinction,
Jiàng Hóu was the Grand Commandant,
in charge of military power,
yet he could not rectify the situation.
After Empress Lü (Lǚ Shì) died,
the high officials conspired to eliminate the Lü clan.
The Grand Commandant was in charge of the military,
and happened to be present when they succeeded.
These so-called meritorious officials
were not ministers of the state."
Later, in the Later Han Dynasty, Chén Fán submitted a memorial recommending Xú Zhì, Yuán Hóng, and Wéi Zhù.
The Emperor asked Fán,
"Who among these three should be ranked first, second, and third?"
Fán replied,
"Hóng was born into a noble family,
and gradually learned the Dao through instruction.
Zhù grew up in the Three Adjuncts region,
in a custom of propriety and righteousness,
where, as they say, without support, one stands upright,
and without carving, one is sculpted.
As for Zhì,
he comes from the humble and impoverished region of Jiangnan,
yet stands out prominently,
and should be ranked first."
Someone asked,
"With whom can Xiè Ānshí, as Prime Minister,
be compared?"
Yú Nán said,
"In the past, when Gù Yōng was ennobled as a marquis,
his family was unaware.
Previous generations praised his substantial and dignified character,
considering him without peer.
Now, considering the decline of the Eastern Jìn dynasty and
the daily alarming state of its borders,
especially with Yǒnggù
(Yǒnggù being the courtesy name of Fú Jiān)
the heroic leader of the six barbarians,
personally leading a million soldiers;
and Fú Róng, a man of outstanding talent and a famous minister,
leading the charge with sharp weapons,
sharpening the claws and teeth of fierce tigers and wolves,
and wielding the sharp edges of long snakes,
even building guesthouses in advance
to await the Jìn ruler.
If we consider their relative strength,
comparing them to a feather and Mount Tài,
it would be an insufficient analogy.
Wénjìng deeply rejected the aid of Huán Pèi,
and was displeased with the letter from Xiè Yuán,
thus the calculation of victory or defeat
was already in his heart.
Now, this man,
would he be moved in the slightest
by the paltry fief of ten thousand households?
If we discuss his magnanimity,
since recent antiquity,
I have not seen his equal."
When Emperor Yáng of the Suí dynasty was in the Eastern Palace,
he once said to Hè Ruòbì:
"Yáng Sù, Hán Qínhǔ, and Shǐ Wànsuì, these three men,
They all praised them as good generals.
What were their respective strengths and weaknesses?"
He replied:
"Yáng Sù 杨素 was a fierce general,
not a strategic general."
He commented:
"Observant of *qì* (气, vital energy), decisive and brave,
he is a fierce general.
Profound and possessing strategy,
he is a strategic general."
"Hán Qín-hǔ 韩擒虎 was a combat general,
not a command general."
He commented:
"Skilled in fisticuffs, quick, brave, and fierce,
he is a combat general.
Commanding the army with order and discipline,
he is a command general."
"Shǐ Wàn-suì 史万岁 was a cavalry general,
not a great general."
He commented:
"Leading a detached force,
invincible in every direction,
he is a cavalry general.
Encompassing heroes,
and employing various talents according to their abilities,
he is a great general."
Tàizǐ said:
"Excellent."
Therefore, from "Liù Zhèng" to "Wèn Jiàng,"
all are examples of the successes and failures of ministers.
An ancient saying goes:
"Yǔ became king of the Xià,
Jié caused the downfall of the Xià;
Tāng became king of the Yīn,
Zhòu caused the downfall of the Yīn."
Hélǘ of Wú won battles
and was unmatched in the world,
but Fūchā was captured by Yuè;
Mù Gōng of Qín became famous and his title was honored,
but the Second Emperor was seized at Wàngyí.
The way they became rulers was the same,
but their achievements were unequal
because of the difference in those they employed.
Therefore, Chéng Wáng, while still in swaddling clothes, received homage from the feudal lords
because the Dōu Gōng managed affairs;
Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng, at the age of fifty, starved to death in Shāqiū
because he employed Lǐ Duì.
Therefore, Wèi had Gōngzǐ Wú Jì,
who reclaimed lost territory;
Zhào employed Lìn Xiàngrú,
and the Qín army did not dare to advance;
Chǔ had Shēn Bāoxū,
and Zhāo Wáng regained his throne;
In Qí, there was Tián Dān,
and King Xiāng attained his state.
Based on this to discuss,
those who possess a state,
if they cannot mold and refine the customs of the world,
select and categorize people,
discuss the gains and losses of right and wrong,
gather the remaining ideas of hegemons and kings,
and yet someone can establish merit and achieve fame,
I have never heard of such a thing before.
Therefore, knowing how to assess ability and assign offices
is the supreme principle and technique.
Chapter Eleven: Standards of Virtue
Chapter Eleven: Standards of Virtue
Confucius said:
"By nature, people are similar;
through practice, they become different."
This means that the root of desires is the same,
but the paths of influence and assimilation are different.
If one is overly deliberate, then one's actions become unnatural;
if one is swayed by external things, then one's will becomes dissipated.
Therefore, the sage guides people with reason,
restrains excess and dissipation,
is careful about what they associate with,
and regulates their biases.
Thus, the *Commentary* says:
"Examine likes and dislikes,
regulate emotions and temperament,
and the kingly way will be complete."
The way to govern one's nature
necessarily involves examining one's own excesses
and strengthening one's deficiencies.
Generally, those who are intelligent and insightful
should guard against being overly discerning;
those who are poorly informed and have seen little
should guard against being closed off;
those who are brave and resolute
should guard against being overly violent;
those who are benevolent and gentle
should guard against being indecisive;
those who are calm and composed
should guard against being tardy;
those who are broad-minded and magnanimous
should guard against being forgetful.
The *Rén Wù Zhì* (人物志, "A Study of Human Abilities and Characteristics") says:
"Those who are sternly upright, resolute, and firm
are talented in correcting others,
but their failing lies in their fierce accusations.
Strong and resolute people
are stubbornly inflexible and unyielding.
If they do not guard against the bluntness of their strength
and consider compliance as weakness,
they intensify their stubbornness.
Therefore,
They can be entrusted with establishing laws,
but are difficult to trust with subtle details.;
Those who are gentle, compliant, peaceful, and tolerant,
excel in generosity,
but fail due to a lack of decisiveness.
Gentle and compliant people
are slow of mind and lenient in their decisions.
They are not wary of their affairs being incomplete
and consider being unyielding as harmful,
being content with their ease.
Therefore,
they can be trusted with following established norms,
but are difficult to trust with making discretionary decisions in doubtful situations.;
Those who are bold, fierce, and robust
excel in courage and bravery,
but fail due to excessive suspicion.
As for fierce people,
their spirit is aroused and their decisions are decisive.
They are not wary of their courage leading to destruction,
and they regard compliance as cowardice,
exhausting their power.
Therefore,
they can be trusted with facing difficulties,
but are difficult to trust with living in simplicity.;
Those who are refined, virtuous, cautious, and conscientious
Goodness lies in respectful caution;
failure lies in excessive doubt.
A scrupulous and careful person
fears trouble and has many apprehensions.
Failing to caution him against his timidity in doing what is right,
but regarding bravery as recklessness,
increases his doubts.
Therefore,
he can be one with whom to enjoy peace and security,
but it is difficult to have him establish principles.
Strength and firmness
are useful in a lever;
failure lies in stubbornness.
A headstrong person
holds to his own ideas with strength and persistence.
Failing to caution him against his stubborn protection of his feelings,
but regarding eloquence as empty,
strengthens his stubbornness.
Therefore,
he can be one with whom to uphold justice,
but it is difficult to have him agree with the masses.
Eloquent argumentation
is good at resolving knots;
failure lies in rambling.
An erudite and eloquent person
is rich in argumentation.
Not being wary of the generality and excess of their words,
they use model examples as a constraint,
and let it be.
Therefore,
one can engage with them in broad narratives,
but it is difficult to establish covenants with them.
Broadly learned and universally connected,
their excellence lies in comprehensive enrichment,
their fault lies in confusion and turbidity.
People of broad and universal character,
their affections are widespread and thorough.
They do not admonish their friends' confusion and difficulties,
but use introduction as a means to expose,
and broaden their turbidity.
Therefore,
one can entrust them with comforting the masses,
but it is difficult to make them rectify customs.
Pure, upright, and uncorrupted,
their virtue lies in frugality and firmness,
their fault lies in being narrow and restrictive.
A man of narrow and upright character,
sharp in criticism and clear in his indignation,
does not warn against the narrowness of his path,
but regards universality as defilement,
increasing his restrictiveness.
Therefore,
Can be relied upon to uphold principles,
but difficult to adapt to changing circumstances.;
Those who are inclined to action are rough and rugged,
their strength lies in climbing high,
their weakness lies in being distant and detached.
People inclined to action,
aspire to surpass others,
they do not guard against their intentions being too unrestrained,
and regard stillness as stagnation,
considering their own sharpness to be paramount.
Therefore,
they can be relied upon to advance quickly,
but difficult to entrust with holding the rear.;
Those who are inclined to stillness are quiet and reserved,
their strength lies in subtle and profound insights,
their weakness lies in being slow and indecisive.
People inclined to stillness,
value returning to the origin,
they do not guard against their stillness being too slow and delayed,
and regard action as being detached,
admiring their own indecisiveness.
Therefore,
they can be relied upon for deep consideration,
but difficult to entrust with swift action.;
Those who are straightforward are direct and plain,
Sincerity lies in inner substance,
failure lies in neglect of the subtle.
For a person who is simple and candid,
suspicion arises in the midst of actual certainty.
If one does not guard against the unrefined straightforwardness of their nature,
but considers it to be exaggeration,
revealing their sincerity,
therefore,
one can establish trust with them,
but it is difficult to have intimate dealings with them.;
The multi-wise hide emotions,
and see expediency in strategies.
The shortcoming is in being indecisive.
Those who are skilled in concealing,
measure situations and seek to accommodate,
but do not guard against the difficulty of rectifying their methods,
and regard complete candor as foolishness,
and value their pretense.
Therefore,
one can cooperate with them in praising what is good,
but it is difficult to correct their transgressions.
These are the talents of stubbornness and arrogance,
not the virtues of the golden mean."
Wén Zǐ 文子 said:
"In general, the way of people is such that,
the mind should be small,
the ambition should be great,
"Wisdom should be round,
conduct should be square,
ability should be abundant,
affairs should be few."
What is meant by "small mind" is
to consider troubles before they arise,
to be wary of disaster and cautious of the minute,
and not to dare indulge one's desires;
what is meant by "great ambition" is
to encompass all nations,
to regulate different customs equally,
where right and wrong converge,
and the center acts as the hub;
what is meant by "round wisdom" is
that it has no beginning or end,
flows afar in all directions,
and is like a deep spring that never runs dry;
what is meant by "square conduct" is
to stand upright and not yield,
to be purely white and not sullied,
not to change one's principles in poverty,
and not to indulge one's will in success;
what is meant by "abundant ability" is
to be fully equipped with both literary and martial skills,
and to be moderate in both action and stillness;
what is meant by "few affairs" is
to govern the vast by holding to the essential,
and to await the agitated by dwelling in stillness.
The Way of Heaven is such that when it reaches its extreme, it reverses; when it is full, it diminishes.
Therefore, for intelligence and broad wisdom,
guard it with foolishness;
for extensive learning and eloquent debate,
guard it with frugality;
for martial strength and resolute courage,
guard it with awe;
for wealth and great power,
guard it with humility;
for virtue bestowed upon the world,
guard it with yielding.
These five are
how the former kings maintained possession of the world.
The *Zhuan* says:
"Do not initiate disorder,
do not rely on wealth,
do not depend on favor,
do not go against conformity,
do not be arrogant towards ritual,
do not be boastful of ability,
do not repeatedly get angry,
do not plot what is not virtuous,
do not violate what is not righteous.
These nine sayings
are how the ancients established themselves."
The *Yùqián Jīng* says:
"To make things clear is shallow;
to not know one's own faults is a defect;
Those who are lost and do not return will be cast aside;
those who invite resentment with their words will encounter disaster;
those whose commands contradict their intentions will be abandoned;
later commands that contradict earlier ones will be destroyed;
those who are angry but lack authority will commit offenses;
those who please the masses but insult others will suffer misfortune;
those who execute and humiliate those they have appointed are in danger;
those who are disrespectful to those they should revere will encounter misfortune;
those whose appearance matches but whose hearts are distant will be isolated;
those who are close to sycophants and distant from the loyal will perish;
those who trust slander and abandon the virtuous will be benighted;
those who appoint people to office based on personal relations will be superficial;
when women's solicitations are openly practiced, there will be chaos;
when subordinates are outwardly grateful, there will be decline;
those who overcome others by oppressing their inferiors are invasive;
those whose reputation exceeds their reality will be depleted;
those who favor themselves and treat others poorly will be abandoned;
those who give sparingly but expect much in return will not be rewarded;
those who reward but forget the humble will not be employed for long;
when people do not obtain their proper positions, there is danger;
those who select officials for others will fail;
those who make decisions based on unkindness are in danger;
those whose secret plans are leaked will be defeated;
those who collect heavily but give sparingly will wither."
This is the general principle of self-governance.
Sūn Qīng 曰:
"One whose mouth can speak and whose body can act is a treasure to the state;
one whose mouth cannot speak but whose body can act is a vessel to the state;
A national treasure is one who,
though his mouth cannot speak,
his body can enact it.
He is a vessel of the state.
One whose mouth can speak it,
but whose body cannot enact it,
is a utility of the state.
One whose mouth speaks good,
but whose body enacts evil,
is a monster of the state."
Therefore, Fù Zǐ said:
"The foundation for establishing virtue,
nothing is more important than rectifying the heart."
When the heart is rectified, then the body is rectified;
when the body is rectified, then those around you are rectified;
when those around you are rectified, then the court is rectified;
when the court is rectified, then the state is rectified;
when the state is rectified, then all under Heaven is rectified.
Therefore, when all under Heaven is not rectified,
rectify it from the family;
when the family is not rectified,
rectify it from the court;
when the court is not rectified,
rectify it from those around you;
when those around you are not rectified,
rectify it from the body;
when the body is not rectified,
rectify it from the heart.
What one cultivates grows nearer;
what one benefits extends farther.
Yǔ and Tāng blamed themselves;
their rise was sudden and flourishing.
This is what is meant by "rectifying the heart."
*Shī Zi* says:
"The heart
is the sovereign of the body.
The Son of Heaven receives commands from the heart for the whole world;
if the heart is improper, then disaster befalls the world.
The feudal lords receive commands from the heart for their states;
if the heart is improper, then the state perishes.
Commoners receive commands from the heart for themselves;
if the heart is improper, then the body is put to death."
Chapter Twelve: Order and Disorder
Chapter Twelve: Order and Disorder
To clearly examine the "Six Masters"
is to observe the virtue of the ruler.
To carefully consider the "Nine Winds"
is to establish the norms of the state.
To investigate the "Four Disorders,"
and examine the "Four Dangers,"
then order and disorder can be known.
What are the "Six Masters"?
Xún Yuè said:
"To be upright in body and benevolent in nature,
With a clear mind and shared aspirations,
acting for the people,
not for oneself,
this is called a "Wáng Zhǔ" (王主, Kingly Ruler).
The commentary says:
A "Wáng Zhǔ" (王主, Kingly Ruler),
refers to one with innate benevolence and virtue.
Able to restrain oneself and be forgiving of others,
fond of asking questions and diligent in practice,
acting in accordance with righteousness,
not according to emotions,
this is called a "Zhì Zhǔ" (治主, Ruling Ruler).
The commentary says:
A "Zhì Zhǔ" (治主, Ruling Ruler),
refers to one who suppresses emotions and curbs desires.
Diligent in affairs and guarding one's enterprise,
daring not to be lazy or negligent,
acting with the public interest first,
not with private interest first,
this is called a "Cún Zhǔ" (存主, Preserving Ruler).
The commentary says:
A "Cún Zhǔ" (存主, Preserving Ruler),
refers to one who adheres to the law and observes regulations.
Disobedient and engaging in strife,
pursuing both public and private interests,
gaining one thing and losing another,
not purely following principles and measures,
This is what is called a "declining ruler" (shuāi zhǔ);
emotion outweighs righteousness,
private interests outweigh public interests,
systems and regulations exceed limits,
governance and teachings lose their constancy;
this is what is called a "perilous ruler" (wēi zhǔ);
intimately employing slanderous and evil people,
exiling loyal and virtuous ones;
indulging emotions and pursuing desires,
disregarding ritual and propriety;
going in and out on excursions,
not adhering to ceremonial prohibitions;
bestowing rewards for private reasons,
exceeding public expenses;
inflicting punishments in anger,
exceeding the principles of law;
consequently excusing wrongdoing and glossing over faults,
and not knowing how to change,
loyal words are blocked and obstructed,
straightforward remonstrations are punished with execution;
this is what is called a "doomed ruler" (wáng zhǔ)."
Therefore, a kingly ruler (wáng zhǔ) can bring about prosperity and peace,
a governing ruler (zhì zhǔ) can rectify his administration,
a preserving ruler (cún zhǔ) can protect his state,
a declining ruler (shuāi zhǔ), if encountering no difficulties, can perhaps maintain his position,
but will be endangered if difficulties arise;
a perilous ruler (wēi zhǔ), if encountering no difficulties, may luckily be spared,
but will perish if difficulties arise;
A state whose ruler is lost is certain to perish.
What are the "Nine Winds"?
Ruler and ministers are close and observe propriety,
The officials are harmonious yet distinct,
Yielding without contention,
Diligent without resentment,
Attending only to their duties.
This is the "Wind of a State of Propriety".
Yǐn Wénzi said:
"The superior does not overcome his inferiors,
The inferiors cannot offend their superiors,
Superiors and inferiors do not overcome or offend each other,
Therefore, prohibitions and orders are carried out,
Everyone is without selfishness,
Even passing through danger and ease, the state cannot be invaded,
This is how to govern a state."
Propriety and customs are not uniform,
Official positions are not valued,
Petty officials slander and are jealous,
Commoners make pronouncements.
This is the "Wind of a Declining State".
Yǐn Wénzi said:
"The ruler is old,
Has many concubines and serving women,
Few sons and grandsons,
Estranges powerful clans,
This is a declining state."
Ruler and ministers contend for reputation,
The court contends for merit,
the high officials contend for fame,
and the common people contend for profit.
This is the "custom of a discordant state."
When the ruler has many desires,
those below engage in many tricks,
laws are not fixed,
and government has many loopholes.
This is the "custom of a chaotic state."
Yǐn Wénzi said:
"When the ruler favors his ministers,
and the ministers take from the ruler,
public law is abandoned,
and private affairs are carried out,
it is a chaotic state."
To consider extravagance as breadth,
to consider arrogance as nobility,
to consider excess as understanding;
to call adhering to rituals as being narrow-minded,
and to call upholding the law as being rigid.
This is the "custom of a desolate state."
Shū Xiàng said:
"When high officials value great emoluments but do not remonstrate fully,
when close officials fear punishment and dare not speak,
and the sentiments of those below do not reach the top,
this is the greatest of calamities."
Those above and below are estranged from each other,
those within and without suspect each other;
Petty officials compete for favor,
great ministers compete for power.
This is the "wind of a state in danger."
The ruler does not inquire of those below,
those below do not remonstrate with the ruler;
the words of women are employed,
private affairs are conducted.
This is the "wind of a state on the verge of ruin."
Yǐn Wénzǐ
said: "If the state is poor and small,
the families rich and large;
the ruler's power is weak,
and the ministers' influence is great,
it is a state heading for ruin.
If there is no exclusive favoritism within,
and no intimate cronies without;
if collateral relatives multiply and thrive,
and elders and juniors are not in disorder,
it is a flourishing state.
If farming and sericulture are done in due season,
granaries and storehouses are full;
if weapons and armor are strong and sharp,
and the borders are well-maintained,
it is a powerful state."
Wénzǐ said:
"A state in disorder appears full,
while a well-governed state appears empty;
a state heading for ruin appears insufficient,
A state is preserved when there is abundance.
Emptiness
does not mean there are no people,
but that each keeps to their duty.
Fullness
does not mean there are many people,
but that all seek advantage at the end.
Abundance
does not mean much wealth,
but that desires are restrained and affairs are few.
Insufficiency
does not mean a lack of goods,
but that people are restless and expenditures are high."
What are the "Four Disorders?"
Guǎnzi said:
"If there is a concubine within the household who makes the wife suspicious,
this is household disorder.
If there is a son of a concubine who makes the legitimate son suspicious,
this is clan disorder.
If there are ministers at court who make the prime minister suspicious,
this is state disorder.
If incompetent officials are appointed,
this is public disorder."
Therefore it is said:
"One who establishes a Son of Heaven
should not allow the feudal lords to doubt him.
One who establishes a feudal lord
should not allow the grand officers to doubt him.
Establishing a legal wife
prevents favored concubines from becoming suspicious.
Establishing an嫡子 dízǐ (the son of the legal wife and heir)
prevents庶孽 shùniè (sons of concubines) from becoming suspicious.
Suspicion leads to unrest,
duality leads to conflict,
and mixture leads to mutual harm.
Therefore, when a minister holds two positions,
the state will surely be in chaos.
If a minister holds two positions and the state is not in chaos,
it is because the ruler is still present.
Relying on the ruler to prevent chaos,
losing the ruler will inevitably lead to chaos.
If two sons hold the same position,
the family will surely be in chaos.
If two sons hold the same position and the family is not in chaos,
it is because the parents are still alive.
Relying on the parents to prevent chaos,
losing the parents will inevitably lead to chaos.
When ministers doubt their ruler,
there is no state that is not in danger.
When favored concubines doubt the lineage (their place),
there is no family that is not in danger."
What are the "four dangers"?
It also says:
"If the senior ministers do not gain the support of the masses,
that is a danger to the state.
If the great ministers are not harmonious and cooperative,
This is a danger to the state.
When the military leader is not to be feared,
this is a danger to the state.
When the people do not cherish their possessions,
this is a danger to the state.
These are the forms of order and chaos.
In general, for those who are in positions of authority,
if laws and methods are clear and rewards and punishments are certain,
then even without words, the situation will govern itself;
if laws and methods are unclear and rewards and punishments are uncertain,
then even if one issues commands,
the situation will inevitably be chaotic."
Guǎnzi said:
"Governing a state has three instruments,
while ruining a state has six assaults.
If an enlightened ruler can overcome the six assaults and establish the three instruments,
then the state will be governed well;
if an unworthy ruler cannot overcome the six assaults and establish the three instruments,
then the state will be in chaos.
What are the three instruments?
They are:
commands, the axe, and rewards.
What are the six assaults?
They are:
relatives, nobility, wealth, lust, skillful flattery, and playthings.
What is the use of the three instruments?
It is:
without commands, there is no way to employ subordinates;
Without axes and halberds, there is no way to awe the masses;
without emoluments and rewards, there is no way to encourage people.
What was the reason for the failure of the six attacks?
It is said:
Even if one does not listen, one can still survive;
even if one violates prohibitions, one can still be exempted;
even if one has no merit, one can still become rich.
If a state has people who can survive even if they do not listen,
then commands are not enough to make subordinates serve;
if there are those who can be exempted even if they violate prohibitions,
then axes and halberds are not enough to awe the masses;
if there are those who can become rich without merit,
then emoluments and rewards are not enough to encourage people.
If commands are not enough to make subordinates serve,
if axes and halberds are not enough to awe the masses,
if emoluments and rewards are not enough to encourage people,
then the ruler has no way to protect himself."
Therefore,
when the situation is well-ordered,
even if affairs are delegated, there will be no chaos;
when the situation is chaotic,
even if one is diligent, there will be no order.
Yáo and Shùn folded their arms and achieved more with non-action,
because the situation was well-ordered.
Hú Hài and Wáng Mǎng drove themselves to exhaustion but still fell short,
because the situation was chaotic.
Shāng Zǐ said:
"Laws and regulations
The lives of the people
are the foundation of governance.
When one rabbit runs, a hundred people chase it,
not because the rabbit can be divided into a hundred parts,
but because the designation of ownership is not yet defined.
Those who sell rabbits fill the market,
yet thieves dare not take them,
because the designation of ownership is defined.
Therefore, when designations are defined,
it is the way of governance through power (*shì*);
when designations are not defined,
it is the way of disorder.
Therefore, governance through power
must not be disordered;
if power is disordered,
it cannot be governed.
If power is disordered and one desires to govern it,
it becomes more disordered;
if power is ordered and one governs it,
then it is ordered.
Therefore, the sage governs order, not disorder.
When the sage makes laws for the people,
he must make them clear and easy to understand,
so that both the foolish and the wise can universally comprehend them.
Therefore, when the sage establishes the world, there are no executions in the world,
not because those who deserve execution are not executed,
but because all people know how to avoid calamity and attain good fortune, and they all govern themselves.
An enlightened ruler governs by building on order,
Therefore, the world will be greatly governed."
Therefore, it is said:
The good leader
seeks [solutions] in the situation (shì),
and does not blame others.
Therefore,
an enlightened ruler examines laws and measures and issues instructions and commands,
and then the world will be well-governed.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"When a state is about to perish,
it will certainly have many regulations."
Dù Yù says:
"[This means] frequent changes in the law."
My Commentary says:
A minister who can rectify the world and assist the government
must first be clear about the ways of prosperity and decline,
understand the numbers of success and failure,
be discerning about the situations of order and chaos,
be versed in what is appropriate to employ and discard,

be able to make decisions when encountering doubts,
and recruiting the worthy while dismissing the unworthy,
these are the prerogatives of the ruler;
a subject should only uphold the law and adhere to his duties,
what does it have to do with recruiting scholars?"
That is how he acted as a general.
Discussion:
This is a case of one being right and one being wrong,
and both contradict each other according to the classics and histories.
Bān Gù 班固 said:
"In the past, when the Way of the King declined,
the feudal lords resorted to force,
and rulers of the time and hereditary lords
had different likes and dislikes.
Therefore, the doctrines of various schools of thought
arose together like swarming bees,
each emphasizing one aspect,
extolling what they considered good,
and using this to travel around and persuade,
seeking to gain the favor of the feudal lords.
Although their words differed,
it was like fire and water destroying each other,
yet also able to generate each other.
Benevolence and righteousness,
respect and harmony,
although actions may be contradictory,
they all complement each other."
The *Yì* 《易》 (Book of Changes) says:
"All under Heaven follow the same path but by different routes,
"Unanimity resulting from a hundred considerations."
This is what it means.

but what they practiced were the affairs of a Hegemon.
Therefore, it is considered a second to virtue.
Now, the governance of the Kingly Way
first removes harm to the people
and satisfies their clothing and food.
It is argued:
"In a residence of five *mǔ*,
plant it with mulberry trees,
let the women raise silkworms,
and those who are fifty years old

With a field of one hundred *mǔ*,
and a family of several mouths,
if they diligently cultivate and manage it,
they can avoid hunger.
Raising chickens, pigs, dogs, and swine,
without missing the proper timing,
the elderly can eat meat.
If those above have no greedy desires,
and those below have no extravagant people,
and taxes are light while corvée labor is not burdensome,
then those who serve as officials
merely receive their salaries,
and do not compete with the people for profit.
Therefore, property is evenly distributed and the gap between rich and poor cannot be too wide."
Then teach them ritual and propriety.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler examines himself and rectifies the standard,
and is cautious in his position.
Palaces, houses, and clothing,
do not exceed the prescribed rituals,
the nine women are correctly ordered within the palace,
and the three high ministers divide their duties outside the palace.
Establish the well-field system to equalize (distribution),
establish the feudal lords to govern them,
To ensure that abundance does not lead to extravagance,
and scarcity does not lead to destitution,
and then to expand the influence of the Bì Yōng (辟雍) school,
and demonstrate proper deportment with respectful gestures,
this is why harmonious qi pervades everywhere,
and calamities and rebellions do not arise.
This is the teaching of the sage kings.
To inspire awe through punishments and executions,
to make people know what to love and hate, what to avoid and approach.
Yú Dì (虞帝) first ordered Yǔ (禹) to regulate the waters and lands,
Hòu Jì (后稷) to sow and cultivate the various grains,
Qì (契) to propagate the five teachings,
Gāo Yáo (皋陶) to refine the laws,
therefore the world was at peace.
Therefore,
great transformations converged from all directions,
and the world was peaceful and happy.
This is the method of the king.
The king
takes Heaven as his father and Earth as his mother,
harmonizes yin and yang,
follows the four seasons and regulates the five elements,
nourishes the common people and nurtures all living things.
Therefore, the meaning of the word "king"
is "to go".
It means that his benevolence and kindness are abundant,
and he is good at nourishing and enriching the world.
The world turns towards him,
Therefore, it is said to be a "Wáng" (王) [King].
The greatest achievement of a "Bà" (霸) [Hegemon]
is to elevate the ruler and humble the ministers,
with authority unified and controlled by one person,
government not operating through two separate channels,
rewards and punishments being trustworthy,
laws and decrees being clear and well-defined,
all officials being well-managed,
and authority and commands being certainly carried out.
The hegemon ruler also eliminates difficulties and promotes benefits for the people,
in order to enrich the state and strengthen the military.
They may have emerged after a period of decline and chaos,
or by raising armies and launching conquests.
All of them have yet to follow established laws and standards, and promote logical principles.
They measure the situation and devise plans accordingly,
adapting to the times and implementing what is suitable,
in order to follow expedient and beneficial strategies,
and focus on achieving merit and establishing accomplishments.
This is the art of the hegemon.
The way of the King is pure and relies on virtue,
while the way of the Hegemon is mixed and relies on law.
This is the difference in superiority and inferiority.
The *Dàodéjīng* (道德經) says:
"I do nothing, and the people transform themselves."
The *Wénzǐ* (文子) says:
"The so-called 'doing nothing'
does not mean that one cannot be drawn to come,
or pushed to go,
This refers to following principle in undertaking affairs,
relying on resources to establish merit,

Therefore, it is said:
"One who is wise and loves to inquire is a sage;
one who is brave and loves to inquire is a victor.
By utilizing the wisdom of the masses,
there is nothing one cannot accomplish;
by employing the strength of the masses,

Therefore, when a sage undertakes affairs,
he never fails to rely on the resources available.
Thus it is said:
Tāng and Wǔ,
were sagely rulers,
yet they could not ride in a língzhōu boat with the Yuè people,
sailing on rivers and lakes.
Yī Yǐn,
was a virtuous minister,
yet he could not ride the yuán horse with the Hú people,
Kǒng and Mò,
yet they could not enter the thickets and undergrowth with those who dwell in the mountains,
Judging from this,
human wisdom concerning things
is shallow.
Yet to desire to illuminate the realm within the seas and preserve the myriad regions,
without relying on the calculations of distance,

Therefore, wisdom is insufficient to govern,
courage is insufficient to strengthen,
and tame the táotú horse.
were broadly knowledgeable,
and emerge from perilous places.
this is clear.
However, a ruler,

The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"Vast Heaven has no form,

the Great Sage has no affairs,

This is called teaching without teaching,

The warmth of the winter sun,
the coolness of the summer shade,

The influence of utmost essence,
comes without being summoned.
To wait for sight to see clearly,
to wait for words to command and order,
it is difficult to govern in this way.
《Wénzǐ》says:
"A three-month-old infant

this is inherent feeling."
Therefore, it is said:
"The use of speech is small;
the use of silence is great."
It is also said:
"To be trusted without speaking,
to be benevolent without bestowing,
to be awe-inspiring without anger—
these are the actions of one who moves and transforms with the mind of Heaven."
To bestow and be benevolent,
to speak and be trustworthy,
to be angry and be awe-inspiring—
these are the actions of one who does so with utmost sincerity.
To bestow without benevolence,
to speak without trustworthiness,
to be angry without being awe-inspiring—
these are the actions of one who does so outwardly.
Gāoyáo was mute but served as the Grand Justice,
and there were no cruel punishments in the land.
Shī Kuàng was blind but served as the Grand Steward,
and there were no chaotic affairs in the state of Jìn.
Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Heaven and Earth possess great beauty but do not speak;
the four seasons possess clear laws but do not deliberate;
All things have established principles but do not speak of them.
The sage acts through non-action (wúwéi),
the great sage does not oppose (natural order),
this is what is meant by observing Heaven and Earth."
Orders given without words,
seeing without looking,
this is how the sage acts as a teacher.
This is the technique of Huáng-Lǎo.
"Wénzǐ" says:
"What the sage follows is called the Dao,
what he does is called affairs.
The Dao is like metal and stone,
once tuned, it cannot be changed;
affairs are like the qín and sè (stringed instruments),
at the end of each piece, the tuning is adjusted.
Therefore, laws, regulations, rites, and music are
the tools of principle,
but not the means of creating principle."
In the past, Cáo Cān served as the prime minister of Qí;
his governance mainly employed the techniques of Huáng-Lǎo,
and the state of Qí was peaceful and secure.
When he replaced Xiāo Hé as the prime minister of Hàn,

"To govern Qí,
consider the prisons and markets as places to be left alone;
be careful not to disturb them."
The successor asked:
"Could there be anything more important than this in governing?"
Cān said:
"No.
Prisons and markets
are places where everyone can be accommodated.
Now you disturb them;
where would treacherous people be accommodated?
That is why I prioritized this."
Judging from this,
the people of Qín rebelled because of extreme punishments,
and Xiào Wǔ's strict laws led to numerous lawsuits.
This was the problem.
The *Classic* says:
"I take no action, and the people transform themselves;
I love tranquility, and the people correct themselves."
Cān wanted to transform the root through the Dào,
not to disturb the branches.
The Grand Historian says:
"Cān served as the chancellor of Hàn,
being pure, tranquil, and having few desires,
and his words aligned with the meaning of the Dào.
However, because the people had just escaped the harsh disturbances of Qín,
Cān rested and took no action along with them,
so the whole world praised his excellence."
It is said:
The style of Huáng-Lǎo
is indeed the way of an emperor.
Kǒngzǐ, in leisure,

"In the past, the enlightened kings cultivated the Seven Teachings internally

When the Seven Teachings are cultivated, one can defend;

In the enlightened king's defense,
Distribute tasks to different departments and manage them accordingly.
Have officials conduct monthly reviews and timely assessments,
promote the virtuous,

Then the virtuous and good will be pleased,

Show compassion to widowers and widows,

relieve the poor,

If these seven things are cultivated,
then within the four seas,
there will be no one subjected to punishment.
If those above treat those below with the intimacy of one's own heart and mind,
as the belly and heart;
then those below will treat those above with the intimacy of a young child to a loving mother.
like a yòu zǐ to a címǔ.
Their trustworthiness
will be like the four seasons;
and the people's belief in them

Therefore, seeing the distant as near
is not because the path is short,

Therefore, without moving soldiers and weapons, they have authority,

This is what is meant by "the defense of a wise king,
"To parry attacks from a thousand *lǐ* away."
The discussion said:
Formerly, Guǎn Zǐ 管子 said to Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓公:
"If you, my lord, wish to become a hegemon,
and undertake great affairs,
then you must start from the root.
The people of the state of Qí 齊 are
the root of you, my lord.
The people are deeply worried about hunger, yet taxes are heavy;
the people are deeply afraid of death, yet punishments are severe;
the people are deeply distressed by labor, yet the government undertakes projects at inopportune times.
If you lighten their taxes,
relax their punishments,
and undertake projects at opportune times,
then the people will be at peace."
This is what is meant by cultivating the root to become a hegemon.
Zēng Zǐ 曾子 said:
"What are the 'Three Perfections' (sān zhì 三至)?"
Kǒng Zǐ 孔子 said:
"Perfect propriety does not yield,
and the world is governed;
perfect reward is not wasteful,
and the scholars of the world are pleased;
perfect music is soundless,
and the people of the world are harmonious."
Why is that?
In the past, enlightened rulers certainly knew all the names of the good scholars in the world.
Having known their names,
You must also understand the reality of the situation.
Having understood the reality of the situation,
then bestow honors upon them based on the noble ranks existing in the realm.
This is what is meant by "Supreme propriety requires no yielding, yet the realm is governed."
Based on the wealth of the realm,
enrich the scholars of the realm.
This is what is meant by "Supreme reward costs nothing, yet the scholars of the realm are pleased."
If this is done,
then the clear reputation of the realm will flourish.
This is what is meant by "Supreme joy is without sound, yet the people of the realm are harmonious."
Therefore it is said:
What is called the supreme benevolence in the realm

what is called the supreme wisdom in the realm
is to be able to employ the harmony of the realm;
what is called the supreme discernment in the realm

Therefore, for the benevolent, there is nothing greater than loving others;
for the wise, there is nothing greater than knowing the worthy;
for the ruler, there is nothing greater than being able to appoint officials.
A virtuous ruler,
cultivating these three,
then within the four seas,
all will simply submit to his commands.
This is what is meant by "repelling attacks from a thousand *lǐ* away."
The expedition of an enlightened king
must be against where the Dao has been abandoned,
punishing its ruler,
To change its government,
to comfort its people,

Therefore it is said:
The campaign of a wise king

its arrival is a joy.
This is what is meant by "returning the army to rest upon their mats,"

Therefore Yáng Xióng 揚雄 said:
"The principle of the Six Classics
values preventing disorder;
the victory of the military strategist

This is the art of Kǒng 孔.
It is discussed:
The teachings of Kǒng 孔
emphasize virtue and righteous conduct,
truly the way of the King.
Mòzǐ 墨子 said:
"In ancient times, people did not know how to build palaces and houses,

Border walls are sufficient to ward off wind and cold.
The height of palace walls

Building palaces in this way

Therefore, their wealth is insufficient to provide for famines and disasters,

Hence, the state is poor and difficult to govern.
Building palaces should not be extravagant.
The discussion says:
This concerns regulating palace construction.
In ancient times, people did not know how to make clothing.
They wore animal skins and belts of straw.
In winter, these were not light but were warm;
in summer, they were not light but were cool.
The sage kings considered this not to accord with human feelings.
Therefore, the sages arose

Regarding the principles for clothing,

in summer, use fine linen,

Adhering to this is sufficient;
it is not for the sake of glorifying the eyes and ears,

Therefore, the people are frugal and easily governed,

The kings of today,

their clothing

Therefore, the people are dissolute and difficult to govern,

For an extravagant ruler
to govern dissolute people,
to desire that the country not be in chaos

The principles for clothing must not be without frugality.”
Comment:
This concerns clothing and attire.
This is the doctrine of Mò Dí 墨翟.
Comment:
The doctrine of the Mòjiā 墨家
discards extravagance and economizes on expenditure,
aiming to strengthen the fundamentals.
Shāng Zǐ 商子 said:
"Laws and decrees
are the lifeblood of the people,

Shèn Zǐ 慎子 said:
"The ruler of men who

resentment will arise.
Therefore, those who divide horses use a tally,

Therefore it is said:
if the great ruler relies on the law and does not act personally,

and superiors and inferiors will be in harmony."
If one rabbit runs,
a hundred people chase it.
It's not because the rabbit can be divided into a hundred parts,
but because its ownership is not yet determined.
If rabbits are sold filling the market,
thieves dare not take them,
because their ownership is determined.
Therefore, when ownership is not determined,

once ownership is determined,

Therefore, the sage's creation of laws and decrees,
establishment of officials,

*Shī Zi* says:
"In employing the masses,

Why is this?
It is because there is nowhere to escape their guilt.
Words also have their place,

If the ruler and ministers share the same position,
then the ministers will have somewhere to escape their guilt.
Therefore, if the plumb line is displayed, then the crooked wood is guilty;
if ownership and responsibility are clarified, then those ministers who are unclear are guilty."
When names and positions are fixed, great deceit becomes genuine trustworthiness,
and even great thieves become sincere and honest,
and each governs themselves."
《Yǐn Wén Zǐ》 says:
"When names are fixed, things are not contended for;
when divisions are clear, selfish actions do not occur.
That things are not contended for
is not because there is no desire,
but because names are fixed,
hence there is nowhere to place one's desire.
That selfish actions do not occur
is not because there is no desire,
but because divisions are clear,
hence there is nowhere to place one's desires.
In that case, everyone has desires,
but being able to be the same as having no desires
lies in having a proper way of governance."
Shēn Zǐ says:
"The ruler is like the body,
the ministers are like the hands;
the ruler establishes the foundation,

To be a ruler,
hold the contract to demand its title.
Title is
the net of heaven and earth,
the talisman of the sage.
Spread the net of heaven and earth,
"If you use the *fú* (tally, symbol) of the sage,

The discussion says:
Hánzi (韓子) said:
"The ruler of men
does not need to have the eyes of Shī Kuàng (師曠) to be considered discerning.
Not relying on the numbers (methods, statistics) and waiting for the eyes to see to be discerning,
what is seen will be little.
This is not a technique for avoiding fatigue.
Not taking advantage of the *shì* (circumstances, momentum),
and waiting for the ears to hear to be considered perceptive,
what is heard will be little.
This is not a way to avoid being deceived.
The enlightened ruler
makes the world have no choice but to see for him,
and makes the world have no choice but to hear for him.
Sitting deep within the palace,
clearly illuminating within the four seas,
and the world is unable to conceal, unable to deceive,
why is that?
The penalty for concealing guilt is heavy,
and the reward for reporting treachery is generous."
Sūn Qīng (孫卿) said:
"Clarify duties,
organize enterprises,
talents, skills, and official abilities,
none are not governed.
If it is like this,
Then those with profound virtue are advanced,
and those with integrity and frugality arise.
He listens to all sides and is impartial and discerning,
and thus all affairs are resolved without delay.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven sees without looking,
hears without listening,
knows without pondering,
and accomplishes without moving.
He sits alone, like a clod of earth, yet the world follows him.
This is how one holds the tally to demand performance."
*Shī Zi* 尸子 said:
"The establishment of an enlightened ruler
is characterized by a dignified appearance,
a vacant mind,
a steady gaze,
and undistorted hearing.
He carefully examines apportionments and responds to words
to establish himself in court.
Thus, those who are hidden and distant,
even if they have complaints,
will not be many.
An enlightened ruler does not rely on extended ears and eyes,
does not engage in espionage,
and does not forcefully seek information.
He observes when forms (of things) arrive,
he listens when sounds arrive,
and he responds when affairs arrive.
If those nearby are not excessive,
Then those who are distant will be governed;
if the clear-sighted do not err,
then even the insignificant will be treated with respect.
This is how nothing in the world can escape (governance)."
Those who move, waver;
those who are still, are secure.
Names arise from themselves;
affairs settle themselves.
Discussion says:
*Shīzi* said:
"The one who managed the floods was
Yǔ;
the one who sowed the five grains was
Hòu Jì;
the one who listened to lawsuits and decided justly was
Gāo Yáo;
Shùn was non-assertive,
yet he was like the father and mother of the world."
This illustrates how names arise from themselves.
Tài Gōng said to Wén Wáng:
"Heaven has constant punishments,
humans have constant lives;
if you share your life with Heaven and humanity,
then the world will be at peace."
This illustrates how affairs settle themselves.
Therefore, those who possess the Dao
rectify based on names,
and settle based on events.
《Yǐn Wénzi》says:
"Because of the usefulness of the virtuous,
ensure they cannot but be used;
because of the uselessness of the foolish,
ensure they cannot be used.
Used or not used,
each obtains its proper use,
why worry about the disorder of things?"
《Shīzi》says:
"The way of attending court
is to give people assigned roles.
If there is a great good deed,
one must ask who recommended him;
if there is a great fault,
one must ask who appointed him,
and then carry out rewards and punishments.
Furthermore, use this to observe the worthy and unworthy,
clear divisions will prevent corruption,
correct titles will prevent emptiness.
If virtuous, then esteem him;
if unworthy, then despise him.
Worthy and unworthy,
loyal and disloyal,
observe them with the Dao,
it is as clear as white and black."
In the past, when Yáo governed the world,
he did so with names.
When his names were correct, the world was governed;
When Jié ruled the world,
he also relied on titles;
because his titles were distorted, the world was thrown into chaos.
Therefore, the sage valued the correctness of titles."
It is argued:
Indeed, a foolish ruler takes the unvirtuous as virtuous,
the disloyal as loyal,
and the unlawful as law,
because of the incorrectness of titles.
Lǐ Sī wrote:
"Hán Fēi states, 'A loving mother has spoiled children,
while a strict family has no rebellious slaves,'
why is this?
It is because punishment is surely applied.
Therefore, Shāng Yāng's laws
punished those who discarded ashes in the road.
Discarding ashes
is a minor offense;
but being punished
is a heavy penalty.
If minor offenses are closely supervised,
how much more so for serious crimes?
Therefore, people dare not commit offenses.
Now, instead of focusing on preventing offenses,
and emulating the means by which a loving mother spoils her children,
then one is not observing the sage's arguments."
Shāng Yāng's laws
all ordered the people to form groups of ten and five
And supervised and governed each other;
those who violated prohibitions and were connected to those who did not report treason;
clearly distinguished the rank and order of the noble and the humble;
each according to their difference in status;
fields, houses, wives, concubines, and clothing
according to family status.
Those with merit were conspicuously honored;
those without merit, even if wealthy, had no glory.
They were dedicated to agriculture and warfare.
This was the law of Lord Shang.
These were the techniques of Shāng Yāng, Shēn, and Hán.
Huán Fàn said:
"The followers of Shāng Yāng, Shēn, and Hán
valued cunning and deceit,
striving to implement harshness.
They abandoned the teachings of ritual and righteousness,
relying on the principles of law and punishment,
not learning from the ancients,
and initially corrupted customs and damaged culture.
These were the sinners of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Zhào.
However, their respect for the ruler and disdain for the subjects,
enriching the state and strengthening its military,
upholding the law and maintaining their techniques,
had some merit.
Reaching the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
there were people like Níng Wèi Qī and Zhì Dū,
who imitated the governance of Shāng and Hán,
specializing in killing and violence as their ability,
To follow the sovereign's will,
to act in accordance with his desires,
to be content with the times and pursue profit,
to dare to carry out acts that lead to disaster and defeat—
these are also the crimes of Shāng and Hán.
However, they suppressed powerful clans,
comforted the orphaned and weak,
kept themselves clean and forbade corruption,
abandoned private interests and established public ones,
and still had some governance.
As for those so-called "capable" individuals of later generations,
they violated the laws of the state,
rushed to the power of private houses,
abandoned the affairs of the common people,
rushed to the affairs of men,
made quick decisions in complicated matters,
and temporarily made expedient arguments.
They ensured that officials had no accumulation of blame,
did not investigate the grievances of the lower people,
and were thus criminals like Shēn, Hán, Níng, and Zhì."
From this perspective,
therefore, we know that those who govern the world
have the ways of kings and hegemons (bà),
the ways of Huáng and Lǎo,
the ways of Kǒng and Mò,
and the ways of Shēn and Shāng.
This is why they differ.
Although their principles and methods are different,
Their methods of remedying ills differ,
yet in bringing peace and benefit to the masses,
each has its own reasons for doing so.
Nowadays, some debaters cite the methods of the Cháng Dài 長代 (Long Generations) era,
questioning the words about remedying ills.
The debate says:
"Remedying ills is like the Xià 夏 people valuing loyalty,
the Yīn 殷 people valuing reverence,
and the Zhōu 周 people valuing refinement."
Others cite the ways of true emperors,
criticizing the policies of the hegemon,
without considering the changes of the times,
and focusing on embellished arguments.
Therefore, discussions of right and wrong
arise in confusion.
To speak falsely and eloquently,
to conform to wrong and make it seem agreeable,
is where resentment is born.
One must examine this carefully.
Twisted Compliance, Chapter Twenty-Seven
Twisted Compliance, Chapter Twenty-Seven
Zhào Zǐ said:
When clouds and thunder signal a time of difficulty,
and the watching crows have not yet settled,
at this time,
the ruler should entrust governing the people to his ministers,
and each should serve their lord by employing their talents.
Therefore, Gāo Zǔ rewarded Jì Bù for his crimes,
and Duke Wén of Jìn praised the attendant's fault.
Although they were previously in dire straits, no one resented it.
This can be said to be understanding the greater picture.
In the past, when Duke Wén of Jìn was initially in exile,
Duke Xiàn sent the attendant Pī to attack him at Pú Chéng,
