crossing the river to station troops east of Hándān 邯鄲;
one army camps at Chénggāo 成皋,
driving the armies of Hán 韓 and Liáng 梁 outside the river;
one army camps at Miǎnchí 澠池,
planning to attack Zhào 趙 with the combined forces of four states.
If Zhào 趙 is defeated,
its territory will surely be divided into four,
therefore,
I dare not conceal my thoughts and hide my feelings,
and first report them to those around you.
Your servant secretly plans for Your Majesty,
It would be better to meet King Zhāo of Qín (秦昭王) at Mǐnchí (澠池),
to meet face-to-face and make a verbal agreement.
Please order the troops to halt their attack,
I hope Your Majesty makes a decision."
Marquis Sù of Zhào (趙肅侯) agreed to it.
Lord Wǔ'ān (武安君) defeated the Zhào (趙) army at Chángpíng (長平),
and captured more than 400,000 of their soldiers,
all of whom were buried alive.
He then advanced to besiege Hándān (邯鄲).
However, the army's food supply was not adequate.
Therefore, he sent Mr. Wèi (衛先生) to speak to King Zhāo of Qín (秦昭王), saying:
"The Zhào (趙) kingdom relies on the dangers of Mount Chángshān (常山) on its right,
and the obstacles of the Hé (河) River on its left.
They have the advantage of Dài (代) horses and chariots.
The people are brave
and fond of military practice and warfare.
They often gather the feudal lords and agree to form a vertical alliance,
making it clear that if Qín (秦) is not weakened, the six states will surely perish.
The reason Qín (秦) has not yet achieved its ambitions in the world
is the trouble caused by Zhào (趙).
Now, thanks to Your Majesty's divine power,
the Zhào (趙) army has been defeated at Chángpíng (長平),
and its loyal ministers and elite soldiers have all died.
Hándān (邯鄲) is empty,
and the hundreds of commanderies are terrified.
The officers and people all resent their ruler.
If you truly take this opportunity to send supplies and provide sufficient military provisions,
Zhào (趙) will surely be destroyed!
"If we destroy Zhào 趙 to overawe the various lords,
the empire can be settled,
and the king's enterprise will be complete!"
The King of Qín 秦 wanted to agree to it,
but Yìng Hóu 應侯 was jealous of his merit,
and did not want him to succeed.
He said to the King of Qín 秦:
"Although Qín 秦 has defeated the Zhào 趙 army,
the soldiers who died or were wounded are also numerous,
the people are exhausted from long-distance transport,
and the country is empty.
If Chǔ 楚 and Wèi 魏 take advantage of the situation to make trouble,
we will have nothing to defend ourselves with,
we should temporarily cease military operations."
The king followed his advice.
Three years later,
he wanted to again send Bái Qǐ 白起 to attack Zhào 趙,
but Qǐ 起 was unwilling.
The king then sent Yìng Hóu 應侯 to rebuke him, saying:
"The territory of Chǔ 楚 is five thousand square *lǐ* 里,
with a million soldiers bearing spears.
You previously led tens of thousands of troops into Chǔ 楚,
captured Yān 鄢 and Yǐng 郢,
burned its suburban temples,
the people of Chǔ 楚 were terrified,
and moved east, not daring to face west.
Hán 韓 and Wèi 魏 together raised a very large army,
you led less than half as many,
and defeated them at Yī Quē 伊闕,
blood flowed, corpses drifted.
Hán 韓 and Wèi 魏 had already submitted,
and to this day are called the Eastern Fiefs.
This is your achievement,
and everyone under Heaven has heard of it.
Now, of the Zhao 赵 soldiers who died at Chángpíng 长平,
seventeen or eighteen out of ten are already dead.
Therefore, I, your servant, wish to have you command,
and I am determined to annihilate them.
You often defeated the many with the few,
and achieved victory like a deity.
How much more so when attacking the weak with the strong,
and attacking the few with the many!"
Lord Wǔ'ān 武安君 said,
"At that time, the King of Chǔ 楚 relied on his country's size,
and did not care about its governance,
and the ministers were jealous of each other's merits,
flattery was used in affairs,
good ministers were alienated and rejected,
the common people were disaffected,
the city walls were not repaired,
and there were neither good generals
nor defenses.
Therefore, I was able to lead the army deep into the country,
seize many towns,
destroy the bridges and burn the boats,
in order to focus people's minds;
They plundered in the countryside
to provide food for the army.
At that time,
the soldiers of Qín
regarded the army as their home
and the generals as their parents.
They were close without any agreement
and trusted each other without any planning.
With one heart and united strength,
they would die without turning back.
The Chǔ people, fighting on their own territory,
all were concerned about their families,
each with divided hearts,
none with the will to fight.
That is why we were able to achieve success.
In the Battle of Yī Quē,
Hán was wary of Wèi
and did not want to be the first to use its forces;
Wèi relied on the strength of Hán
and wanted to push them to the front.
The two armies competed for advantage,
their strength was not the same.
That is why your servant was able to set up a decoy force
to wait for the Hán formation,
concentrating our army and sharpening our strength,
striking Wèi unexpectedly.
Once the Wèi army was defeated,
the Hán army collapsed on its own.
For this reason,
it is possible to achieve success.
All is calculated based on the principles of profit, circumstances, and natural tendencies.
What is there of the divine in it?
Now, the Qín 秦 army defeated the Zhào 趙 army at Chángpíng 長平,
but did not follow up in a timely manner.
They did not take advantage of their shaken fear to destroy them,
but feared and released them,
allowing them to farm and increase their reserves.
They nurtured the orphans and raised the young to increase their population,
repaired their armor and weapons to increase their strength,
and deepened their moats and fortified their city walls to increase their defenses.
The ruler humbled himself to his ministers,
and the ministers devoted themselves to recruit death-defying warriors.
Even those of the Píngyuán 平原 class
all ordered their wives and concubines to sew and mend among the ranks.
The subjects and people were of one mind,
and those above and below exerted their strength together,
just like Gōujiàn 句踐 when he was besieged at Kuàijī 會稽.
If we attack Zhào 趙 now,
they will surely defend firmly.
If we provoke their army to battle,
they will certainly not be willing to come out.
If we besiege their capital city,
we will certainly not be able to conquer it.
If we attack their surrounding cities,
we will certainly not be able to capture them.
If we plunder their countryside,
Definitely nothing will be gained.
If the army lingers long without success,
the feudal lords will become disaffected,
and external aid will certainly arrive.
I see the harm in it,
but have not yet perceived its benefit,
and moreover, I am ill and unable to go."
Yìng Hóu retreated in shame.
Thereupon, Qín sent Wáng Hé as general to attack Zhào.
As expected, Chǔ and Wèi came to its rescue.
Zhāng Yí persuaded King Zhāo of Yān, saying:
"Among those whom Your Majesty trusts,
none is like Zhào.
In the past, Xiàngzǐ of Zhào once made his elder sister the wife of the King of Dài,
intending to annex Dài.
He arranged to meet the King of Dài at the border of Gōuzhù.
He then ordered artisans to make a golden dipper,
with a long handle,
such that it could be used to strike someone.
While drinking with the King of Dài,
he secretly instructed the cook, saying:
'As soon as the wine reaches its height and everyone is enjoying themselves,
present hot broth,
and use the dipper to strike him.'
So, when the wine reached its height and everyone was enjoying themselves,
he called for hot broth.
The cook came forward to pour,
and then used the dipper to strike the King of Dài,
He was killed,
his liver and ribs smeared the ground.
His elder sister heard of it,
and consequently sharpened her hairpin to commit suicide.
Therefore, to this day there is Mount Mójī (磨笄之山, Sharpened Hairpin Mountain),
known throughout the land.
Up to the time of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn dynasty,
Chén Xī (陳豨), as the Chancellor of Zhào, supervised the border troops of Zhào and Dài,
and raised troops in rebellion.
The Emperor himself went to Hándān,
and happily said,
"Xī did not go south to occupy the Zhāng River,
nor did he defend Hándān to the north.
I know he is incapable."
When Xī was defeated,
the Emperor said,
"Dài is located north of Mount Chángshān,
while Zhào is south of the mountains.
There is distance between them."
Therefore, he established two of his sons as kings of Dài.
The wolfish and unkind nature of the King of Zhào
is something Your Majesty clearly sees.
Moreover, do you think Zhào is someone you can be close to?
Zhào raised troops to attack Yān,
besieged the capital of Yān twice,
and threatened Your Majesty.
Your Majesty ceded ten cities as an apology.
Now the King of Zhào 趙王 has already entered the court at Miǎnchí 澠池,
imitating the affairs of Héjiān 河閒 to please Qín 秦.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín 秦 now,
Qín 秦 will send troops down to Yúnzhōng 雲中 and Jiǔyuán 九原,
driving Zhào 趙 to attack Yān 燕.
Then the Yìshui 易水 and the Great Wall
will not belong to Your Majesty.
Now, if Your Majesty serves Qín 秦,
the King of Qín 秦 will surely be pleased,
and Zhào 趙 will not dare to act rashly.
This means you will have the support of the powerful Qín 秦 in the west
and be free from the worries of Qí 齊 and Zhào 趙 in the south.
Therefore,
I wish Your Majesty would carefully consider this."
The King of Yān 燕 listened to Zhāng Yí 張儀,
and Zhāng Yí 張儀 returned to report to Qín 秦.
The King of Yān 燕 sent Crown Prince Dān 丹 as a hostage to Qín 秦.
Qín 秦 wanted to make Zhāng Táng 張唐 the prime minister of Yān 燕,
to jointly attack Zhào 趙,
in order to expand the territory of Héjiān 河閒.
Zhāng Táng 張唐 said to Lǚ Bùwéi 呂不韋,
"I once attacked Zhào 趙 for King Zhāowáng 昭王,
and Zhào 趙 holds a grudge against me.
Now going to Yān 燕,
I must pass through Zhào 趙,
I cannot go."
Bùwéi 不韋 was displeased
and had no way to force him.
His retainer, Gān Luó, was twelve years old.
He said to Bù Wéi:
"Allow me to carry out this task for you, my lord."
Thereupon, he met with Zhāng Táng and said:
"Whose accomplishments are greater, yours or Lord Wǔ'ān?"
Zhāng Táng said:
"Lord Wǔ'ān crushed the powerful Chǔ in the south,
and destroyed Yān and Zhào in the north.
His victories in battle and conquests,
the destruction of cities and demolition of towns,
are too numerous to count.
My accomplishments are not as great as his."
Gān Luó said:
"Whose influence in the service of Qín is greater, Lord Yīng or Lord Wénxìn in sole control?"
Zhāng Táng said:
"Lord Yīng's influence is not as great as Lord Wénxìn's in sole control."
Gān Luó said:
"Formerly, Lord Yīng wanted to attack Zhào,
but Lord Wǔ'ān opposed it.
He was sent ten *lǐ* away from Xiányáng,
and was given death at Dùyóu.
Now Lord Wénxìn has personally requested that you become the chancellor of Yān,
but you are unwilling to go.
I do not know where your place of death will be."
Zhāng Táng, fearful, said:
"Please, I will go because of you, young man."
The day of departure was set.
Gān Luó then said to Wénxìn Hóu:
"Lend me five carriages,
and I will first report to Zhāng Táng on your behalf in Zhao."
Wénxìn Hóu sent him.
Gān Luó went to Zhao,
and persuaded the King, saying:
"Has Your Majesty heard of the Crown Prince Dān of Yan entering Qin?"
He said:
"I have heard of it."
"Has Your Majesty heard of Zhāng Táng becoming the Chancellor of Yan?"
He said:
"I have heard of it."
Gān Luó said:
"The Crown Prince Dān of Yan entered Qin because
Yan would not deceive Qin.
Zhāng Táng became the Chancellor of Yan because
Qin would not deceive Yan.
That Yan and Qin do not deceive each other
makes them no different.
Therefore, they wish to attack Zhao and expand their territory in the Héjiān region.
It would be better for Your Majesty to present five cities to me,
in order to expand Héjiān,
and I will request the return of the Crown Prince of Yan,
and together with a strong Zhao, we can attack a weak Yan."
The King of Zhao said:
"Good."
He immediately ceded five cities to Qin.
When the Crown Prince of Yan heard of this, he returned.
Zhào then attacked Yān,
gaining twenty cities,
and ordered Qín to have ten of them.
Thereupon, Lǐ Sī of Chǔ and Wèi Liáo of Liáng,
advised the King of Qín, saying:
"Since the time of Duke Xiào of Qín,
the House of Zhōu has been weak and insignificant,
and the feudal lords have been annexing each other.
East of the pass are the six states,
and Qín has been taking advantage of victories to invade the feudal lords
for about six generations.
Now the feudal lords submit to Qín
as if they were commanderies and counties.
Their rulers and ministers are all fearful.
If they were to form an alliance and attack unexpectedly,
this would be how Zhì Bó, Fū Chāi, and King Mǐn perished.
May the King not begrudge wealth
and bribe their powerful ministers
in order to disrupt their plans.
Qín will spend no more than 300,000 jīn,
then the feudal lords can be completely conquered."
The King of Qín followed their plan,
secretly sending strategists carrying gold and jade to travel among the feudal lords.
Those famous scholars of the feudal lords
who could be bribed with wealth
were generously provided for;
those who refused
were assassinated with sharp swords.
To separate their ruler and ministers' plans,
he then sent a capable general to follow behind them,
and consequently annexed the various feudal lords.
The scholars of the world formed alliances and gathered in Zhào,
intending to attack Qín.
Yìng Hóu said,
"Your Majesty, do not worry.
Allow me to have it abandoned.
Qín has no grievances with the scholars of the world.
The reason they gather and attack Qín
is only for the sake of wealth and status.
Have you seen your Majesty's dogs?
Several thousand dogs gather in groups,
those lying down rise,
those walking walk,
those stopping
do not fight each other.
Throw them a bone,
and they will readily rise up and snap at each other.
Why?
Because there is an intention to contend.
Now, order five thousand gold pieces to be carried with Táng Suī,
and also load up strange musical instruments to stay in Wǔ'ān.
Hold lavish gatherings and drink together.
Before even three thousand gold pieces are distributed,
the scholars of the world will fight each other."
After Qín had swallowed the world,
He worried about the decline of the Zhōu 周 dynasty,
believing that its weakness led to the loss of territory.
Therefore, he mocked the Three Dynasties (Xià 夏, Shāng 商, and Zhōu 周),
and abolished the ancient laws.
Kǒng Róng 孔融 said:
"In ancient times,
the king's territory extended a thousand *lǐ* 里 in the royal domain,
and within this realm, no feudal lords were enfeoffed."
Jì Gōng 祭公 said:
"The system of the former kings was such that,
within the state there was the *diàn* 甸 service,
outside the state the *hóu* 侯 service,
then *hóu, wèi,* 衛, and *bīn* 賓 services,
then *yí* 夷 and *mán* 蠻, *yāo* 要 services,
and finally *róng* 戎 and *dí* 狄 *huāng* 荒 services.
Those of the *diàn* service made sacrifices (*jì* 祭),
those of the *hóu* service performed ancestral rites (*sì* 祀),
those of the *bīn* service offered tribute (*xiǎng* 享),
those of the *yāo* service presented goods (*gòng* 貢),
and those of the *huāng* service acknowledged the king (*wáng* 王).
Daily sacrifices (*jì* 祭), monthly ancestral rites (*sì* 祀),
seasonal tribute (*xiǎng* 享),
annual presentation of goods (*gòng* 貢),
and ultimate acknowledgment of the king (*wáng* 王)
were the teachings of the former kings.
If they failed to sacrifice (*jì* 祭), then cultivate virtue;
if they failed to perform ancestral rites (*sì* 祀), then cultivate speech;
if they failed to offer tribute (*xiǎng* 享), then cultivate culture;
If they do not offer tribute, then cultivate their reputation.
If they do not acknowledge the king, then cultivate virtue.
If the order is established but they still do not arrive,
then apply punishments.
Therefore, there are punishments for those who do not offer sacrifices,
attacks on those who do not perform the sì sacrifices,
levies against those who do not present offerings,
reprimands for those who do not offer tribute,
and pronouncements against those who do not acknowledge the king.
Therefore, there are laws of punishment,
armies of attack and conquest,
preparations for expeditions,
commands of intimidation and reprimand,
and declarations of edicts.
If they still do not arrive,
then redouble the cultivation of virtue,
without burdening people in distant lands.
This was the ancient system."
They abolished the five ranks of nobility,
changed them to commanderies and counties,
proclaimed themselves "Huángdì 皇帝",
and reduced their sons and brothers to commoners.
Internally, they had no support from close relatives,
externally, they had no territory to defend them.
Wú 吳 and Chén 陳 raised their white pestles
(wooden staves),
and Liú 劉 and Xiàng 項 followed and destroyed them.
Therefore, it is said:
The Zhōu dynasty exceeded its allotted time,
and the Qín dynasty did not reach its full measure;
this was the natural course of national power.
Xún Yuè 荀悅 said:
"In ancient times, states were established either small or large,
in order to learn from the failures of the past,
adapt, and improve.
During the Xià 夏 and Yīn 殷 dynasties,
their territories generally did not exceed one hundred *lǐ*,
therefore the feudal lords were weak and the Son of Heaven was strong.
Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂 were able to indulge in their cruelty and harm.
Zhòu turned Xíng Hóu 邢侯 into dried meat and pickled Guǐ Hóu 鬼侯.
Even with King Wén's 文王 flourishing virtue,
he could not avoid imprisonment in Yǒulǐ 牖里.
The Zhōu dynasty inherited these problems,
so it established large states,
five hundred *lǐ* square,
in order to honor and favor the feudal lords and diminish itself.
But by the end,
the feudal lords grew strong,
invading and attacking each other,
while the Zhōu royal house became weak and insignificant,
and calamities arose.
The Qín dynasty inherited these problems.
Unable to correct the system to find a middle ground,
it abolished the feudal lords entirely,
and changed to a system of commanderies and counties
To use single (壹) authority (威權) to
monopolize (專) the world (天下),
its (其) intention (意) is primarily (主) to benefit (為) oneself (自),
and not (非) to benefit (為) others (人) .
Therefore (故) Qín (秦) was able (得) to control (擅) the power (勢) within the seas (海內),
without (無) any (所) restraints (拘) or inhibitions (忌),
recklessly (肆) indulging in (行) extravagance (奢) and licentiousness (淫),
and acting with violence (暴虐) towards (於) the world (天下).
However (然), it was destroyed (滅) in fourteen (十四) years (年).
Therefore (故), when (人主) the ruler (失) loses (道) the Way,
then (則) the world (天下) universally (遍) suffers (被) its (其) harm (害);
when (百姓) the people (一) are chaotic (亂),
then (則) like fish rotting (魚爛) or earth collapsing (土崩),
no one (莫) can (之) rectify (匡) or save (救) it.
With the rise (興) of Hàn (漢),
inheriting (承) the faults (弊) of Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦),
therefore (故) they used a mixed approach (雜而用之).
However (然), the difficulties (難) of the six (六) kings (王) and seven (七) kingdoms (國)
were indeed (誠) due to (失之於) their strength (強大),
and not (非) the fault (咎) of the lords (諸侯) governing (治) their states (國).
At the beginning (之初) of the rise (興) of Hàn (漢),
the world (海內) was newly (新) stabilized (定),
relatives (同姓) were few (寡少),
learning from (懲) the failure (敗) of Qín (秦)'s isolation (孤立) that led to its demise (亡),
therefore (於是) they divided (割裂) the territory (疆土),
establishing (立) ranks (爵) of two (二) levels (等):
the larger (大者) were kings (王),
the smaller (小者) were marquises (侯).
The number of meritorious officials who were enfeoffed as marquises
exceeded one hundred.
Honoring the sons and younger brothers of the royal family,
he greatly established nine kingdoms.
The large kingdoms
spanned prefectures and encompassed multiple commanderies,
connecting several tens of cities.
This can be said to be overcorrecting a wrong.
However, Emperor Gāozǔ, in establishing the dynasty,
was constantly pressed for time.
Emperor Xiàohuì’s reign was short,
and Empress Gāohòu, as a female ruler, took control of the throne,
yet the empire was peaceful,
without the worry of rebellious and cunning individuals.
Ultimately, they quelled the disturbance of the Zhū Lǚ clan,
laying the foundation for Emperor Tàizōng.
This also depended on the feudal lords.
Indeed, the root causes led to the branches becoming large,
and the overflowing waters led to inundation.
The small lords indulged in lasciviousness and transgressed the law,
while the large lords became alienated, isolated, and perverse,
harming themselves and ruining their states.
Therefore, Emperor Wén adopted the advice of Jiǎ Shēng
to divide Qí and Zhào.
Jiǎ Yì said:
"If you desire the order and peace of the world,
nothing is better than establishing many feudal lords and diminishing their power.
With little power, it is easy to be righteous;
with a small country, there are no wicked intentions.
To control the world
would be like the body controlling the arm,
and the arm controlling the finger.
Your Majesty, divide the land and establish a system.
Let Qí, Zhào, and Chǔ each be divided into a certain number of states,
and let their descendants each receive the land portioned by their ancestors,
ceasing when the land is exhausted.
The Son of Heaven will gain nothing from this."
He also submitted a memorial, saying:
"Even if Your Majesty does not establish a system,
given the current situation,
after only one or two generations,
the feudal lords will still act arbitrarily and without restraint,
establishing themselves strongly and becoming exceedingly powerful,
and the laws of the Hàn dynasty will not be implemented.
What Your Majesty relies on for defense and what the Crown Prince relies on,
are only the two states of Huáiyáng and Dài.
Dài borders the Xiongnu in the north,
being neighbors with a powerful enemy.
If it can protect itself, that is sufficient.
But Huáiyáng, compared to the large feudal lords,
is merely like a black spot on the face,
just enough to bait large states,
and not enough to offer any resistance.
The current system,
rests with Your Majesty,
And to order your son to succeed is only enough to be bait.
How can that benefit myriad generations?
My humble plan is,
I wish to take the land of Huáinán 淮南 and add it to Huáiyáng 淮陽,
and establish an heir for the King of Liáng 梁;
cut off two or three rows of cities on the northern border of Huáiyáng 淮陽 and give them to Dōngjùn 東郡,
to add to Liáng 梁.
If that is not feasible,
one can move the King of Dài 代 and make Suīyáng 睢陽 his capital.
Liáng 梁 starts north of Xīncài 新蔡,
reaching to the Yellow River;
Huáiyáng 淮陽 encompasses south of Chén 陳,
holding it like a bolt to the Yangtze River.
Then, the great feudal lords who harbor dissent
will be frightened out of their wits and dare not plot rebellion.
Liáng 梁 is sufficient to defend against Qí 齊 and Zhào 趙;
Huáiyáng 淮陽 is sufficient to restrain Wú 吳 and Chǔ 楚.
Your Majesty can rest easy
and will ultimately have no worries about the lands east of the mountains;
this is a benefit for ten thousand generations.
I have heard:
wise kings ask their ministers for advice
and do not initiate matters themselves,
so that their ministers may fully express their foolish loyalty.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
Emperor Wén 文帝 then followed Yì's 誼's plan.
He then moved Prince Wǔ 武 of Huáiyáng 淮陽 to be the King of Liáng 梁,
bordering Mount Tài 泰 in the north,
extending west to Gāoyáng 高陽,
having over forty cities in the virtuous and large county;
he moved Prince Xǐ 喜 of Huáiyáng 淮陽 to be the King of Huáinán 淮南,
to care for its people.
Later, when the Seven Kingdoms rebelled,
they could not pass through the land of Liáng 梁,
because of the plan of Jiǎ Shēng.
Emperor Jǐng followed the plan of Cháo Cuò
to reduce the power of Wú and Chǔ.
Cháo Cuò said to the Emperor:
"In the past, when Emperor Gāo first established the empire,
his brothers were few and his sons were weak,
so he greatly enfeoffed those of the same surname.
Thus, his illegitimate son, King Dàohuì of Qí, ruled seventy-two cities;
his younger brother, King Yuán of Chǔ, ruled forty cities;
his nephew, ruled more than fifty cities in Wú.
He enfeoffed three illegitimate scions,
dividing half of the empire.
Now, the King of Wú previously had a dispute over the heir apparent.
Although he claims illness and does not attend court,
according to ancient law, he should be executed.
Emperor Wén could not bear to do so
and thus bestowed him with a staff and seat,
an extremely generous act.
He did not reform or renew himself,
but instead grew more arrogant and unrestrained.
He casts coins in the mountains,
boils the sea for salt,
He induced scholars throughout the land
to plot rebellion and treachery.
Now, if we reduce his territory, he will rebel;
if we do not reduce it, he will also rebel.
Reducing it leads to a quicker rebellion and smaller harm;
not reducing it leads to a later rebellion but greater harm."
Thereupon, the Hàn ministers debated in court the reduction of Wú,
and Wú then rebelled.
Emperor Wǔ implemented Zhǔfù Yǎn's strategy:
the Decree of Grace.
Zhǔfù Yǎn said to the emperor:
"In ancient times, the territories of the feudal lords did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
and their relative strength was easily controlled.
Now, the feudal lords possess several dozen cities in some cases,
with territories spanning a thousand lǐ.
If left unchecked, they become arrogant and extravagant,
easily prone to licentiousness and disorder;
if pressed urgently, they will rely on their strength and form alliances,
to oppose the capital.
Now, if we reduce their territories by law,
rebellious intentions will arise,
as with Cháo Cuò the other day.
Now, the sons and younger brothers of the feudal lords number ten or more, yet only the eldest legitimate son is instated.
The rest, though of the same flesh and blood,
receive not an inch of land as fiefdom.
Thus, the principles of benevolence and filial piety are not promoted.
I wish Your Majesty would order the feudal lords to be allowed to extend grace,
dividing their territories to enfeoff their sons and younger brothers.
Those people were all happy to get what they wanted.
If the emperor is able to bestow favors
and truly divide up their states,
they will surely diminish and weaken on their own."
The emperor followed his plan.
Emperor Jǐng (景) encountered the "Rebellion of the Seven States,"
suppressed the feudal lords,
and reduced and dismissed their officials.
Emperor Wǔ (武) had the plots against Huáinán (淮南) and Héngshān (衡山),
and created the law of "left officials"
(serving as officials under the feudal kings was considered a "left official"),
and established the law of "supplementing benefits"
(granting feudal lords beyond their allotted limits was called "supplementing benefits").
The feudal lords were only allowed to collect clothing, food, and taxes;
they were not involved in governmental affairs.
By the time of Emperors Āi (哀) and Píng (平),
they were all descendants who inherited the throne,
with distant relatives,
born within the walls of the palace,
not respected by the scholars and commoners.
The cadet lines were cut back,
existing in name only, without substance.
The world was left desolate,
and they followed the path of the destroyed Qín (秦) dynasty again.
Therefore, Wáng Mǎng (王莽) knew that the Hàn (漢) dynasty was exhausted both internally and externally,
with both its foundation and its branches weakened,
leaving him with nothing to fear.
(He) conceived his treacherous intentions.
Relying on the power of the Empress Dowager,
he falsely adopted the names of Yī and Zhōu,
and monopolized the exercise of authority.
In the imperial court,
without descending the steps, he managed the world.
Once his deceitful scheme was accomplished,
he then occupied the honored southern-facing position (of the emperor),
dispatched five officers of awe-inspiring power,
who sped throughout the land,
distributing mandates and talismans.
The Han princes and kings kowtowed with broken horns (in surrender),
offering up their seals and ribbons,
fearing to be left behind,
How lamentable is this not?
When Wǎng (Mǎng) was defeated,
the world was in turmoil.
Kuǎi Xiāo commanded troops in Tiānshuǐ.
Bān Biāo fled to him for refuge and followed him.
Xiāo asked Biāo, saying:
"In the past, when the Zhōu lost control,
the Warring States contended together,
the world was divided,
and it took several generations to settle.
I think,
the affairs of alliances and strategies,
will rise again today!
Will the fate that is succeeding and rising alternately,
rests upon a single person.
I wish that you, sir, would elaborate on this."
He replied,
"The rise and fall of the Zhōu 周 dynasty is different from that of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
In the past, the Zhōu had five ranks of nobility.
The feudal lords participated in government.
The root was already weak.
The branches and leaves were strong.
Therefore, at its decline, there were affairs of the strategists;
this was the natural course of events.
The Hàn inherited the Qín 秦 system,
altering it to establish commanderies and counties.
The ruler had the authority to act alone.
The ministers did not have power for a hundred years.
By the time of Emperor Chéng 成,
he relied on his maternal relatives.
Emperors Aī 哀 and Píng 平 reigned for a short time,
and the imperial line was cut off three times.
Therefore, the Wáng 王 clan monopolized the court.
They then usurped the throne.
The danger arose from above.
It did not affect those below.
Therefore, after the true usurpation,
the whole world could not help but stretch their necks and sigh.
In a little over ten years,
the court and the provinces were in turmoil.
Those far away and those nearby all rose up.
Those falsely claiming titles gathered like clouds.
They all claimed to be of the Liú Shì 劉氏 clan,
without conspiring to use the same wording.
Nowadays, among the outstanding figures who control provinces and govern cities,
none possess the hereditary resources of the Seven Kingdoms.
However, the common people sing praises and yearn for the virtue of the Hàn 漢 Dynasty,
from this, the situation can be understood."
Emperor Guāngwǔ 光武 restored the Hàn 漢 Dynasty,
succeeding to the imperial line,
yet he still followed the path of overturned carts (previous failures),
nurturing the chronic illness of a defeated house.
Barely lasting a few generations,
treacherous villains filled the court,
whenever a powerful minister monopolized the government,
the world would follow suit;
if one man acted unscrupulously,
cities and walls would crumble on their own.
How precarious is this!
In the Zhōu 周 Dynasty, when it was difficult to revive the royal house,
there were seven ministers who defied orders,
three sons who encroached upon authority,
and the succeeding king entrusted them with the nine tripods (symbols of power).
Evil clans occupied the heavenly capital (the capital city),
the sounds of gongs and drums shook the inner gates,
and arrows flew within the crimson palace.
Yet the calamity was confined to the capital region,
the harm did not spread far,
and the world remained at peace.
Preparing for chaos with good governance,
Therefore, King Xuān of Zhōu兴 (xīng) rose to prominence during the Gònghé Regency;
Duke Xiāng and Duke Huì revitalized the states of Jìn and Zhèng.
How could this be compared to the brief disturbances within the imperial gates during the two Hàn dynasties,
which led to the empire boiling over?
Where a treacherous minister entered the court in the morning,
and by evening, the nine regions were in chaos.
Looking back to the usurpation of Wáng Mǎng,
and considering the time when Dǒng Zhuó arrogated power to himself,
countless people grieved in their hearts,
and both the foolish and the wise felt the same pain.
Was it that the world lacked ministers comparable to those of old,
or that the scholars lacked the ambition to set things right?
It was likely that past achievements were hindered by the change of times,
and heroic ambitions were thwarted by lowly positions.
Lù Jī said:
"Perhaps because the hereditary positions of the feudal lords
were not always assured,
and foolish rulers and tyrannical lords
sometimes followed each other's paths,
therefore the five ranks system was prone to disorder.
The current governors and prefects
are all advanced based on their mediocrity,
and even if some fail,
their successes are certainly more numerous,
therefore the commanderies and counties are easier to govern.
If the virtue is excellent and bright,
promotion and demotion are practiced daily,
the superiors lead by example, and the subordinates follow in succession,
Everyone diligently performs their duties,
and lascivious and benighted rulers
have no room to make mistakes.
Why worry that the realm will not be well-governed?
Therefore, past dynasties rose because of this.
If things carelessly decline,
all measures will naturally be violated.
If officials are sold
and talent is judged by wealth,
then the seeds of greed and cruelty will all be successors.
How can there be anything but chaos?
Therefore, later kings fell because of this.
And, to put it succinctly:
rulers of fiefs of five ranks think about governing for their own sake,
while heads of prefectures and counties scheme to profit from things.
How can we prove this?
Generally, striving for advancement
is the common ambition of scholars;
cultivating oneself and bringing peace to the people
is something good scholars rarely achieve.
Now, the desire for advancement is sharp,
but the reputation for bringing peace to the people is slow in coming.
Therefore,
those who encroach upon the common people to benefit themselves
have nothing to fear in their positions;
those who harm real affairs to cultivate their reputation
are what officials strive for day and night.
The ruler has no long-term plans,
while the minister harbors temporary ambitions.
The rulers of fiefs of five ranks are not like this:
they know that the state is their own land,
and the people are all their people.
If the people are secure, they themselves benefit;
if the state is harmed, their family will suffer the consequences.
Therefore, the ruler restrains human desires to leave an example for posterity.
Later generations will cherish the structure they built.
As rulers, they have no opportunistic intentions.
The subordinates think of the meaning of steadfast loyalty.
Even if two wise men govern,
their achievements will vary in depth;
if two fools handle chaos,
their mistakes will vary in severity.
So, examining the institutions of the Eight Dynasties,
one can almost understand them with a single principle.
The precedents of the Qín and Hàn dynasties
can practically be summarized in a single statement."
Emperor Wǔ of the Wèi Dynasty, Tàizǔ, possessed a naturally sage and brilliant demeanor,
combined with divine and martial strategies.
He rose like a dragon from Qiáo and Pèi,
and soared like a phoenix over Yǎn and Yù.
Observing the survival and destruction of the Five Dynasties,
he did not adopt their lasting policies.
Seeing the overturning of the preceding cart,
he did not change its tracks.
He enfeoffed his sons and younger brothers with empty territories,
and appointed men who could not command.
Quán jūn pǐfū,
shì qí fánshù.
Nèi wú shēn gēn bù bá zhī gù,
wài wú pánshí zōngméng zhī zhù,
fēi suǒyǐ ān shèjì,
wèi wànshì zhī yè yě.
Qiě jīn zhī zhōumù jùnshǒu,
gǔ zhī fāngbó zhūhóu,
jiē kuà yǒu qiānlǐ zhī tǔ,
jiān jūnwǔ zhī rèn,
huò bǐ guó shù rén,
huò xiōngdì bìng jù,
ér zōngshì zǐdì,
céng wú yī rén xián cè qí jiān,
yǔ xiāng wéichí,
fēi suǒyǐ qiáng gàn ruò zhī,
bèi wànyī zhī lǜ yě.
Shí bùyòng qí jì,
hòu suì língyí.
Cǐ Zhōu, Qín, Hàn, Wèi lì guó zhī shì,
shìyǐ jiū qí shǐzhōng qiángruò zhī shì,
míng jiànjiè yān.
Xún Yuè said:
"After that, all ruled the people through commanderies and counties,
thus eliminating the feudal lords.
The system at that time,
was perhaps not necessarily the way of governance of the hundred kings."
It is argued:
The Zhōu dynasty possessed the empire for over eight hundred years.
In later generations, it declined and weakened,
and the feudal lords ran rampant.
Even when the last descendant, King Xiā [Wáng Xiā], was reduced to a commoner,
they were still able to support each other like branches and leaves,
nominally acting as the common ruler of the empire.
At that time,
the people of Chǔ inquired about the weight of the tripods,
and the Marquis of Jìn requested a separate burial passage.
Although they wanted to spy on the Zhōu court,
they were hindered by the various Jī clans.
How could there not have been treacherous heroes?
It was thanks to the feudal lords that it was maintained.
Therefore, the saying goes:
"A centipede,
even in death, does not fall over.
Because many support it."
Is this what it means?
When the Yíng clan seized the stage,
learning from the mistakes of Zhōu,
they abolished the five ranks of nobility
and established commanderies and counties.
The ruler possessed the whole world,
yet his sons and brothers were commoners.
Meritorious ministers exerted their efforts,
yet the guardians of the state had no fiefs.
Ruling the empire in isolation,
exclusively monopolizing its benefits,
The day he died,
the empire fell apart.
Chén Shèng 陳勝, baring his shoulder, sang out in front,
Liú Jì 劉季, drawing his sword, rose up behind.
Like tigers roaring and dragons glaring,
they extinguished the Qín 秦 clan.
Now, Liú 劉, Chén 陳, and other heroes,
were commoners,
without the power of Wú 吳 or Chǔ 楚, or a place to stand.
Yet, they led a multitude of common soldiers
and were able to contend with the emperor.
The people longed for chaos,
and there was no need to fear the princes diligently serving the king.
Therefore, it is said:
Harsh government and cruel punishments
provide resources for heroes and hasten their own doom.
This is what is meant.
Now, attacking deep roots is difficult to achieve success,
while destroying the rotten and decayed is easy to do.
The Five Orders of Nobility (wǔ děng 五等),
are deep roots;
the commanderies and counties (jùn xiàn 郡縣),
are the rotten and decayed.
Therefore, from the Qín 秦 Dynasty onward,
up to the Zhōu 周 and Suí 隋 Dynasties,
those who lost the imperial regalia were not weak,
and those who gained the empire did not last.
Such was the state of the nation.
Alas!
If governed by commanderies and counties,
then the minds of commoners will arise;
if the Five Ranks were to govern the dynasty,
then there would be disasters of alliances and aggressions.
Therefore, knowing that laws,
all have their drawbacks.
It is not to say that marquises and earls have no symbols that could lead to chaos,
or that commanderies and counties are not tools for achieving order,
but rather that beginning with the aim of abundant fortune,
and ending with the consideration of minimizing misfortune,
hence the esteem for the Five Ranks is greater.
The sage knows that it is thus,
therefore he is diligently and cautiously attentive,
day by day more careful,
cultivating virtue to stabilize it,
and selecting the worthy to employ them.
With virtue cultivated and the worthy selected,
the common people will happily pursue their livelihoods.
Even with the sagacity of Tāng and Wǔ,
sedition cannot arise.
How much more so for the insignificant commoner,
who dares to expose an arm and shout loudly?
This must be carefully examined.
*Sānguó Quán* Nineteenth
*Sānguó Quán* Nineteenth: Shǔ, Wú, Wèi
Commentary states:
I, your servant, have heard that in the past, when the Hàn 漢 dynasty lacked order,
the net leaked, and the wicked and cunning slipped through.
Yuán Běnchū 袁本初 glared like a tiger in the region north of the Yellow River,
Liú Jǐngshēng 劉景升 rose like a magpie in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
Mǎ Chāo 馬超 and Hán Suì 韓遂 were formidable powers in the Guānxī 關西 region,
Lǚ Bù 呂布 and Chén Gōng 陳宮 seized their destiny in the eastern part of China.
Along the Liáo River 遼河 and the Hǎidài 海岱 region,
there were more than ten kings and dukes,
each controlling a hundred thousand soldiers and thousands of iron cavalry.
They formed alliances and made treaties,
becoming outstanding figures of their time.
Yet, Cáo Cāo 曹操, "holding the emperor hostage to command the lords,"
within six or seven years,
had exterminated eighteen or nineteen out of ten.
Only Wú 吳 and Shǔ 蜀, small states that they were,
when viewed on a map,
comprised only the land of four provinces,
not as large as the great cities of the Central Plains.
Their people were timid in public warfare,
but brave in private squabbles,
quick to flee and prone to turning north,
not a match for the soldiers of the various Huá 華 states.
Measuring their length and capacity,
comparing their talents and weighing their strength,
they were not as powerful as the flourishing of the two Yuáns 袁, Liú 劉, and Lǚ 呂.
These two heroes, with newly established and unconsolidated states,
relied on forces that were inherently rebellious and mismatched,
yet they were able to grasp their swords and survey the scene,
contending with the Cáo 曹 family;
riding horses and giving commands,
extending their profits to the South Sea.
Why was this?
It was because the geographical advantages were different.
the circumstances made it so.
Therefore, the *Book of Changes* says:
"Kings and lords establish fortifications to defend their states."
An ancient saying goes:
"One *lǐ* (里) of thickness [in defense],
yet wielding the power of a thousand *lǐ*,
is the advantage of terrain."
Therefore, Cáo Pī (曹丕), facing the river,
seeing the surging waves,
sighed and said:
"This is Heaven's way of limiting the north and south!"
Liú Zī (劉資) called Nánzhèng (南鄭) a "heavenly prison," and the Xié Valley Road (斜谷道) a "five-hundred-*lǐ* stone cave."
Examining previous records,
all feared its depth and impenetrability.
Although it is said:
"When the way of Heaven is favorable,
the advantages of terrain are not as important as the harmony of the people."
If a person of average talent were to guard it,
then prolonging the situation and extending life would be possible.
How could the insignificant Ài (艾) and Jùn (濬) have been able to exert their superior strategies?
Viewing it from this perspective,
the key lies here, not there.
Alas!
"The considerations of the wise
must be mixed with advantages and disadvantages."
Therefore, "If one does not fully understand the harm of employing troops,
then one cannot understand the benefit of employing troops."
This has been the case since ancient times.
Therefore, gathering together its essentials,
this *quán* is made.
To encompass the Five Lakes,
to sweep through the whole of Shǔ,
perhaps one can know the benefit within the harm,
in order to illuminate the strategy of the Wèi family.
Shǔ:
The Heavenly Emperor spreads governance in the chamber of the heart,
leading to order through the stars Cān and Fá.
As for Cān and Fá, the division of Yìzhōu
takes Dōngjǐng, Nángǔ, and Jùxīng as boundaries,
where Dōngjǐng, Nángǔ, and Jùxīng are connected like an axe.
The degree of the star Zī is on the right foot of Cān,
the star held by the Jade Well.
The western Jùxīng is the first star to the west of the three central stars of Cān.
According to the *Zhífāng*, it is within the territory of Yōngzhōu;
according to the *Yǔ Gòng*, it is the domain of Liángzhōu.
The territory is five thousand *lǐ* in area,
with forty commanded prefectures,
Truly a great metropolis.
Cháng Qú's 《Guó Zhì》 says:
"Shǔ,
its trigram corresponds directly to Kūn (坤, Earth),
therefore it has many patterns of colorful brocade;
its zodiacal branch corresponds directly to wèi (未),
therefore it values delicious flavors.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says, of King Wén's influence,
that it extended to the region of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
implying that the land has the civilizing influence of King Wén.
Qín's *Bīn* poems are the same,
Qín and Shǔ share the same territory,
therefore they have the sounds of the Xià dynasty," it says.
Therefore, it was called the "Land of Abundance" in ancient times.
Fertile fields stretch for a thousand *lǐ*,
and there is a reason for this.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
Gōngsūn Shù occupied Shǔ.
Shù's courtesy name was Zǐyáng,
he was from Màolíng in Fúfēng,
and during Wáng Mǎng's reign he served as the Daojiang Zúzheng,
governing Línqióng.
When Gēngshǐ (Emperor Gengshi of Han) was established,
powerful clans each rose up in their respective counties to respond to the Hàn,
Zōng Chéng of Nányáng captured Hànzhōng,
and the merchant Wáng Cén also raised troops in Luò County,
calling himself the General Who Stabilizes the Hàn,
in response to Chéng
. Shù heard of this
and sent an envoy to welcome Chéng.
. Chéng and his followers arrived in Chéngdū
, where they plundered and were violent
. Shù resented this
, and summoned the local heroes and said:
"The whole world suffers under the new dynasty.
They have longed for the Liú family for a long time.
Now I hear that a Hàn general has arrived,
and they rush to welcome him along the roads.
Now the innocent people have their wives and children captured,
and their houses burned down.
These are robbers,
not righteous troops.
I want to defend the commandery and protect ourselves,
to await the true ruler.
Those of you who wish to join forces, stay;
those who do not, may leave."
The notables all kowtowed and expressed their willingness to die for him.
Thereupon, Shù sent someone to falsely claim to be a Hàn envoy from the east,
falsely declaring Shù as the Assistant Hàn General and Governor of Yìzhōu.
He then selected over a thousand elite soldiers and attacked Zōng Chéng and his men,
defeating them.
Separately, he sent his younger brother Huī to attack Zhāng Zhōng, the Governor of Yìzhōu appointed by Gēngshǐ, at Miánzhú,
defeating him as well.
From this, his power greatly shook the Yì region.
Lǐ Xióng, the Chief Clerk of Yì, advised Shù, saying,
"Now, the four seas are in turmoil,
commoners engage in reckless discussions,
generals establish separatist regimes over thousands of *lǐ*,
their territories rivaling those of Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武).
If you were to rouse your might and virtue
to seize this opportunity,
the undertaking of a hegemon or king would be accomplished.
Now, in Shandong (Shāndōng), there is famine,
the people are eating each other,
they are slaughtered by soldiers,
and cities and towns are reduced to ruins.
The lands of Shu (Shǔ) are fertile for thousands of *lǐ*,
the soil is rich and fertile,
the fruits produced
provide satiety without grain.
The work of female artisans
could clothe the whole world.
The renowned timber and bamboo poles
are abundant for implements and weapons,
they cannot be exhausted.
Moreover, there are the profits of fish, salt, copper, and iron,
and the convenience of water transport.
To the north, hold Hànzhōng (漢中),
blocking the narrow passes of Bàoxié (褒斜);
to the east, guard Bā Commandery (Bā Jùn 巴西郡),
defending the mouth of the Hànguān Pass (捍關).
The territory spans several thousand *lǐ*,
with no less than a million soldiers.
When there was profit to be seen, they would send out troops to seize territory;
when there was no profit, they would hold firm and devote themselves to agriculture.
They went east down the Hàn River
to spy on the lands of Qín;
they went south along the flow of the Yangtze River
to awe Jīng and Yáng.
This is what is meant by utilizing the opportune timing of Heaven and capitalizing on the advantages of the land—
the resources for success.
Now, Your Lordship's reputation is known throughout the world,
but your title is not yet established,
causing aspiring individuals to be doubtful.
You should immediately ascend to the great position
so that those from afar have someone to rely upon."
Shù replied:
"The position of Emperor is destined,
what virtue do I possess to deserve it?"
Xióng said:
"The mandate of Heaven is not constant;
the people participate in bestowing it,
and the capable should receive it.
What does Your Lordship doubt?"
Thereupon, he agreed.
In the fourth month of the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he then declared himself Emperor,
establishing the dynasty of "Chéngjiā,"
and adopting white as its color.
He sent General Hóu Dān to open the Báishuǐ Pass
and defend Nánzhèng to the north;
The general, having completed his term, went from Làngzhōng 閬中 down to Jiāngzhōu 江州,
eastward taking possession of Hànguān 捍關.
Thereupon, he completely possessed the land of Yìzhōu 益州.
After Gēngshǐ's 更始 defeat,
Guāngwǔ 光武 was occupied with matters in Shāndōng 山東,
not yet having time to launch a western campaign.
Many heroes of Guānzhōng 關中 led their followers to submit to Shù 述.
Later, Jīng Hán 荊邯 of Pínglíng 平陵, seeing that the East was about to be pacified
and that the army would soon head west,
persuaded Shù 述, saying:
"Warfare
is a great tool of emperors and kings,
something that cannot be abandoned in ancient or modern times.
Kuǎi Xiāo 隗囂 encountered a fortunate opportunity,
seizing possession of Yōngzhōu 雍州.
His army was strong, and his soldiers were loyal,
his power reaching even Shāndōng 山東.
Instead of seizing this moment to weaken the enemy and take advantage of our victories
to contend for the great mandate,
he retreats, desiring to do what the Count of the West did,
ceasing military activity,
humbly serving the Hàn 漢,
lamenting and considering himself like King Wu 武王 rising again.
Now the Hàn 漢 emperor has released himself from worries about Guānlǒng 關隴,
focusing entirely on the eastern campaign,
possessing three-fourths of the empire.
He causes the heroes of the West
to place their hearts in Shāndōng 山東.
He dispatches emissaries
to entice wavering individuals,
and then will possess four-fifths.
If we raise troops in Tiānshuǐ 天水,
we will surely be defeated and collapse.
Once Tiānshuǐ 天水 is pacified,
then nine parts will yield eight.
Your Majesty, with the territory of Liángzhōu,
internally supports the emperor's needs,
and externally provides for the three armies.
The people are burdened and distressed,
unable to bear the imperial orders,
and a rebellion of the Wáng clan is imminent.
This humble subject's foolish plan,
is that you should capitalize on the time when the hopes of Heaven and the people have not yet faded,
and heroes and talents can still be recruited and enticed,
and quickly use this time to dispatch the elite troops of the nation.
Order Tián Róng to hold Jiānglíng,
overseeing the confluence of the Jiāngnán region,
relying on the strength of Mount Wū,
to build fortified defenses and hold firm,
issuing proclamations to Wú and Chǔ;
south of Chángshā,
will surely submit like grass in the wind;
order Yán Cén to emerge from Hànzhōng,
to pacify the Three Fǔ and Tiānshuǐ;
Lǒngxī will surrender with folded hands.
In this way, the realm will be shaken,
I hope for great profit."
He told this to his assembled ministers,
and the erudite Wú Zhù 吳柱 said:
"In the past, when King Wǔ 武王 attacked Zhòu 紂,
the eight hundred feudal lords agreed without prior arrangement,
yet he still withdrew his army to await Heaven's mandate.
I have never heard of anyone without the help of his officials,
wanting to send an army thousands of *lǐ* away,
to expand their territory."
Hán 邯 said:
"Now the Eastern Emperor has no power,
he drives a rabble of men,
charging into the enemy on horseback,
and wherever he goes, he pacifies the area.
If we do not quickly seize the opportunity to contend for success with him,
and instead sit and discuss the sayings of King Wǔ,
it is like Xiāo Kuí 隗囂 wanting to be the Western Overlord."
Fàn Yè 范曄 said:
"He raised the flag and gathered his clan,
falsely creating clear divine signs.
Those who initiate plans and start events
have a way of recognizing the trend.
In the end, he was isolated in one corner,
situated between great powers.
Although the Lǒng 隴 mountain range is narrow,
it does not have the advantage of one against a hundred and two.
Using only two districts to resist the magnificent onslaught,
we know that his path had something to cherish,
Therefore, Qī possessed outstanding individuals from all directions.
When achievements are complete, fame becomes manifest;
when undertakings decline, trouble arises.
To reverse success into loss, and then to be criticized for it,
one has perhaps rarely heard of such a thing!
If Xiāo's fate matched the cycle of fortune,
and his enemies were not aided by Heaven's power,
to sit and criticize the Earl of the West [Xī Bó],
would it not be widely mocked?"
Shù did not listen to Hán's plan.
Guāngwǔ then sent Cén Péng and Wú Hàn to attack Shǔ.
They broke through Jīngmén
and advanced swiftly into Jiāngguān.
Cén Péng was assassinated by an assassin from Shǔ.
Wú Hàn then took command of his army as well,
entering the borders of Qiánwéi.
All the counties defended themselves within their walled cities.
Hàn then advanced his army to attack Guǎngdū,
capturing it.
He sent light cavalry to burn Chéngdū,
and all the smaller cities east of Shì Bridge and Yángwǔ surrendered.
Guāngwǔ cautioned Hàn, saying:
"Chéngdū has a hundred thousand troops;
you must not underestimate them.
Simply hold firm at Guǎngdū,
and wait for them to come and attack.
Do not engage them head-on.
If they dare not come to attack,
He then shifted his camp to pursue them,
waiting for their strength to be exhausted
before attacking them."
Hàn, taking advantage of the situation, led over twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to press on to Chéngdū,
reaching a point just over ten *lǐ* from the city.
He set up camp north of the river, using it as a barrier,
and built a pontoon bridge.
He then sent his deputy general, Liú Shàng, to garrison over ten thousand men south of the river,
a distance of more than twenty *lǐ* apart.
Guāngwǔ, upon hearing of this,
was greatly alarmed
and rebuked Hàn, saying:
"If the enemy sends troops to harass you
and uses the bulk of their forces to attack Shàng,
Shàng will be defeated,
and you will be routed!
Fortunately, nothing has happened yet;
quickly lead your troops back to Guǎngdū."
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Shù indeed sent his general, Xiè Fēng, to attack Hàn,
and sent another general to ambush Liú Shàng,
preventing them from helping each other.
Hàn then closed his camp
and did not come out for three days,
setting up many banners and flags
and ensuring a continuous smoke signal.
That night, with muffled bridles, he led his troops to join forces with Shàng's army,
and Fēng and the others did not notice.
The next day,
he divided his forces to defend against the north of the Jiāng River,
and personally led the attack on the south of the Jiāng River.
Hàn defeated him,
and beheaded Xiè Fēng.
Thereupon he led his troops back to Guǎngdū,
and reported the situation to Guāngwǔ.
The reply came:
"It is very appropriate that you return to Guǎngdū.
It is very suitable.
Shù will definitely not dare to disregard Shàng and attack you.
If you first attack Shàng,
you should lead all your infantry and cavalry from Guǎngdū, fifty *lǐ* away, to reinforce him.
You will likely catch them exhausted.
Defeating them will be certain!"
From then on,
Hàn fought with Shù between and around Guǎngdū,
winning eight battles out of eight,
and eventually surrounded their outer walls.
Shù then scattered all his gold and silk,
and recruited five thousand dare-to-die soldiers,
to be assigned to Yán Cén.
Cén falsely set up banners at the Market Bridge,
beating drums to challenge them,
while secretly sending a surprise force to the rear of Wú Hàn's army,
attacking them by surprise,
and defeating Hàn.
Hàn fell into the water,
This came about due to the horse's tail.
Shù then personally led troops to attack the Hàn.
They fought three times and won three times.
From dawn until midday,
the soldiers were unable to eat
and were all exhausted.
The Hàn then ordered brave soldiers to charge them,
and Shù's troops were greatly defeated.
The army arrived at Chéngdū.
Shù went out to battle,
was initially defeated, and was stabbed,
dying from a pierced chest.
His wife and children were exterminated,
and his palaces were burned.
Guāngwǔ heard of this
and angrily rebuked Hàn, saying:
"The city surrendered three days ago,
and the officials and people were compliant.
To suddenly release soldiers and set fires
is a great loss of the righteousness of executing the general and offering condolences to the people."
He then issued an edict to comfort them.
Those who were loyal, resolute, and righteous
were all honored and recognized.
Lǐ Yù was promoted and employed because of his talent and ability.
Thereupon, the people of the West were moved and pleased,
and all returned to their hearts.
Fàn Yè said:
"In the past, Zhào Tuō was king of Pānyú,
and Gōngsūn Yì also stole the title of emperor of Shǔ Hàn.
Considering that they had no other ability,
and as for their subsequent demise,
was it because the borderland was remote
and not prioritized for royal transformation?
They were unable to capitalize on opportunities to establish merit.
and adapt to changing times,
but instead focused on embellishing his territory,
comforting himself with an image of loftiness and profundity.
This is why Wú Qǐ was ashamed of the Lord of Wèi.
As for his address to the assembled officials,
scrutinizing the mandate of rise and fall,
compared to those who humbled themselves and offered jade tokens,
that is a matter for another day."
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
governance declined and faltered,
the royal house suffered many troubles,
and powerful heroes contended,
dividing the empire.
Liú Yān was appointed as the governor of Yì Province.
Yān
was a descendant of the Prince Gōng of Lǔ.
At that time, brigands and rebels were everywhere,
and Yān believed that the authority of the inspector was too weak.
Therefore, he suggested changing the position to governor,
to pacify the lands,
and carefully selecting high-ranking officials to fill the position,
so Yān was made governor of Yì Province.
At this time,
the bandit Mǎ Xiàng in Liáng Province gathered several thousand exhausted people,
first killing the magistrate of Miánzhú,
then attacking Luò County.
The provincial officer Jiǎ Lóng first led several thousand soldiers in Jiānwéi,
and then gathered officials and people to attack Xiàng.
defeating him.
Thereupon, they selected officials to welcome Yān,
who then became the governor of Yì Province.
When Yān died,
his son Zhāng took over.
The senior officials of the province, such as Zhào Wěi, were drawn to Zhāng's mild and benevolent nature,
and appointed him as Inspector.
Initially,
tens of thousands of families from Nányáng and the Three Commanderies had fled into Yì Province.
Yān gathered all of them as his followers,
calling them
the "Eastern Province Soldiers."
Zhāng, by nature gentle and lenient,
lacked authority and strategic acumen,
and the people from the Eastern Province became oppressive.
Zhào Wěi, taking advantage of the discord among the people,
then allied with the prominent clans within the province.
The people from the Eastern Province, fearing extermination,
united their hearts and forces,
fighting to the death for Zhāng,
and beheading Zhào Wěi.
At that time, Zhāng Lǔ also saw Zhāng as weak and incompetent,
He did not submit to Zhāng,
and consequently became independent in Bāshǔ.
He was besieged by Liú Bèi,
and consequently surrendered.
Bèi moved Zhāng to Gōng'ān,
returning his wealth and treasures.
Later, he died of illness.
Initially,
Liú Bèi was the Governor of Yù Province.
Bèi,
courtesy name Xuán Dé,
was a native of Zhuō County, Zhuō Commandery.
He spoke little,
was good at humbling himself before others,
and his joy and anger did not show on his face.
Táo Qiān, the Governor of Xú Province, recommended the former lord (Liú Bèi) as the Governor of Yù Province.
Later, Qiān fell ill,
and sent someone to welcome the former lord.
The former lord said,
"Yuán Gōnglù is nearby in Shòuchūn;
this man is from a family of four generations of five dukes,
to whom all within the realm turn.
You should give the province to him."
Chén Dēng said,
"Yuán Gōnglù is arrogant and extravagant,
not a lord to govern in times of chaos.
Now, I wish to gather for you ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
with which you can, above, assist the sovereign and aid the people,
Accomplishing the enterprise of the Five Hegemons,
at the very least, one could cede land and defend borders,
recording achievements on bamboo and silk.
If the lord does not heed my words,
Dēng would not dare to listen to the lord either."
Kǒng Róng said to the former lord,
"Is Yuán Gōnglù someone who worries about the country and forgets his family?
Why bother with dried bones in a tomb?
Today's affairs,
the people are capable,
if Heaven grants it and you don't take it,
regret will be irretrievable."
Thereupon he took control of Xú Province.
Chén Dēng sent an envoy to Yuán Shào, saying:
"Heaven has sent down calamity,
disaster has befallen our humble province,
the provincial governor has passed away.
The scholars and people have no leader,
I fear that treacherous heroes will take advantage of the opportunity,
causing the allied lord daily worries.
Therefore, we have jointly appointed the Chancellor of Píngyuán, Lord Liú,
as our leader,
so that the people will forever know they have someone to rely on.
At present, bandits and difficulties are rampant,
and we have no time to take off our armor.
We have carefully sent a lower official to inform you of these matters."
Shào replied,
"Liú Xuándé
is magnanimous, refined, and trustworthy.
Now the people of Xú Province are happy to support him,
truly living up to expectations."
He was defeated by Cáo Gōng,
and fled to garrison in Xīnyě.
At this time, Liú Biǎo died.
Zhūgě Liàng advised him to attack Cóng,
and Jīngzhōu could be had.
The former lord said:
"Jīngzhōu, on the verge of collapse,
entrusted me with its orphans.
I cannot bear to do it."
Many people of Jīngzhōu returned to the former lord.
The former lord traveled only ten-odd *lǐ* per day.
Someone said:
"We should travel quickly to secure Jiānglíng."
The former lord said:
"Those who accomplish great things
take people as their foundation.
Now, the people are returning to me.
How can I bear to abandon them?"
Xí Záochǐ said:
"Although Lord Liú faced perils and hardships,
his trustworthiness and righteousness became even clearer;
though the situation was pressing and dangerous,
his words did not deviate from the proper path;
cherishing the concern of Jǐng Shēng,
he moved the emotions of the entire army;
To cherish those who bravely embrace righteousness,
then one is willing to share in their defeat.
Consider the means by which they gather popular sentiment;
are they merely distributing wine, comforting the borders, enduring hardship, and inquiring after the sick?
That they ultimately achieve great deeds,
is it not fitting?"
Hearing that Zhūgě Liàng personally farmed in Nányáng,
he thrice visited Liàng in his thatched cottage.
Dismissing others, he said:
"The Hàn court is collapsing,
treacherous ministers usurp authority,
the ruler is covered in dust (enduring hardship).
I, disregarding my own virtue and capacity,
wish to promote great righteousness
throughout the land,
but my wisdom and skills are shallow and limited,
and thus I have stumbled and fallen,
to this very day.
Yet my intention remains unfulfilled.
What plan do you think should be devised?"
Liàng replied, saying:
"Since Dǒng Zhuó's time,
heroes have risen together,
those who straddle provinces and connect counties
are too numerous to count.
Cáo Cāo compared to Yuán Shào,
was of humble reputation and small numbers,
yet he was able to defeat Shào.
To turn weakness into strength
depends not only on the opportune moment granted by Heaven,
but also on human planning.
Now, Cáo Cāo 曹操 already commands a million troops,
holding the Son of Heaven hostage to command the lords.
The *Commentary* says:
"To seek the feudal lords,
nothing is better than diligently serving the king."
This is what it means.
Truly, he cannot be directly challenged.
Sūn Quán 孫權, based in Jiāng Dōng 江東,
has already ruled for three generations.
His state is strategically situated, and the people are loyal.
He employs the virtuous and capable.
He can be relied upon for support,
but cannot be taken advantage of.
Jīng Zhōu 荊州 borders the Jiāng 江 and Hàn 漢 rivers to the north,
benefits from the resources of the Southern Sea,
is connected to Wú 吳 and Kuài 㑹 to the east,
and communicates with Bā 巴 and Shǔ 蜀 to the west.
This is a land for military operations,
but its ruler is unable to defend it.
This is perhaps Heaven's way of providing for the general.
Yì Zhōu 益州 is mountainous and difficult to access,
with fertile fields,
truly a land of abundance.
Gāo Zǔ 高祖 relied on it to establish his imperial enterprise.
Liú Zhāng 劉璋 is foolish and weak,
with Zhāng Lǔ 張魯 to the north.
The people are prosperous and the state is rich,
but he does not know how to care for them.
Men of intelligence
long for a wise ruler.
General, you are a descendant of the imperial family,
your trustworthiness and righteousness are known throughout the land,
you oversee heroes,
and thirst for wise men.
If you were to possess both Jīng 荊 and Yì 益 provinces,
secure their rugged terrain,
be at peace with the various Róng 戎 tribes to the west,
pacify the Yí 夷 and Yuè 越 peoples to the south,
establish friendly relations with Sūn Quán 孫權,
and internally cultivate good governance,
when the world falls into turmoil,
then command a senior general to lead the troops of Jīngzhōu 荊州,
heading towards Wǎn 宛 and Luò 洛;
and you yourself, General, lead the troops of Yìzhōu 益州,
emerging from the Qín Chuān 秦川 region,
who among the people would not offer food and drink
to welcome you, General?
If this were truly the case,
then hegemony could be achieved,
and the Hàn 漢 dynasty could be restored."
At that time, Cáo Gōng 曹公 had conquered Jīngzhōu 荊州,
and the late lord fled to Wú 吳.
When the late lord fled to Wú 吳,
commentators thought that Sūn Quán 孫權 would certainly kill him.
Chéng Yù 程昱 predicted,
"Cáo Gōng 曹公 is unrivaled in the world,
having just taken Jīngzhōu 荊州,
his power shakes the region south of the river.
Although Quán is resourceful,
he cannot resist [Cáo Cāo] alone.
Liú Bèi
is a hero.
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi are both enemies of ten thousand men.
Quán will certainly rely on him to defend against me.
It will be difficult to resolve the complex situation,
and Bèi will use this to his advantage.
He cannot be killed."
Quán indeed greatly increased the number of soldiers given to Bèi
to defend against Tàizǔ.
At that time, Liú Zhāng, the Inspector of Yì Zhōu, having heard that Cáo Gōng was attacking Jīng Zhōu,
sent Biéjià Zhāng Sōng to Cáo Gōng.
Cáo Gōng had already pacified Jīng Zhōu
and routed Xiān Zhǔ.
Cáo Gōng did not value or employ Sōng.
Sōng then advised Zhāng to break away [from Cáo Cāo].
Xí Záochǐ said:
"In the past, Qí Huán Gōng, with just one act of boasting of his achievements,
caused nine states to rebel.
Cáo Cāo gradually became arrogant and boastful,
and the empire split into three.
To accumulate diligently over decades,
only to discard it in the blink of an eye,
is this not lamentable?
Therefore, the noble person toils humbly until sunset,
and is concerned with how to treat those below him.
Possessing great merit, they conduct themselves with deference;
Holding high position, they maintain humility.
Only then can they possess their wealth and nobility,
preserve their achievements,
and transmit blessings for a hundred generations.
What reason is there for arrogance and pride?
Therefore, the noble person understands why Cáo Cāo could not succeed in uniting the entire world."
Bèi used Liàng's plan,
to establish friendly relations with Sūn Quán,
together resisting Lord Cáo at Chìbì,
and defeated him.
Lord Cáo returned north,
and Quán then assigned Jīngzhōu to Bèi's control.
Zhōu Yú submitted a memorial, advising:
"Liú Bèi, with the bearing of a枭雄(xiāo xióng, a ruthless and ambitious person),
and Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, as generals of bear and tiger-like ferocity,
surely will not long submit to being employed by others.
I believe the great plan
should be to relocate him to Wú,
lavishly constructing a residence for him,
and providing him with many beautiful women and delightful objects,
to entertain his senses.
Separate these three men,
Each should be stationed in one area.
If you employ people like Yú
and allow them to participate in attacks and battles,
great things can be accomplished.
Now you are rashly ceding land
to provide them with resources.
Gathering these three people together in the border regions
is like allowing a jiāolóng (蛟龍, mythical dragon) to get clouds and rain.
They will no longer be things confined to a pond."
Quán (權, Sun Quan) thought that Cáo Gōng (曹公, Cao Cao) was in the north
and he should be widely recruiting heroes,
so he did not accept this advice.
Páng Tǒng (龐統) said to Bèi (備, Liu Bei):
"Jīngzhōu (荊州) is desolate and ruined,
and its population is depleted.
To the east are the Sūn (孫) of Wú (吳),
and to the north are the Cáo (曹) clan.
With the plan of a three-legged stand,
it will be difficult to achieve your ambitions.
Now, Yìzhōu (益州) is a wealthy and strong state,
with a population of one million households.
The soldiers and horses within the commandery
have everything they need,
and there is no need to seek treasures from outside.
Now you can temporarily borrow it to accomplish great things."
Bèi (備, Liu Bei) said:
"The one who is like water and fire to me
is Cáo Cāo (曹操).
Cāo used haste,
I use leniency;
Cāo used violence,
I use benevolence;
Cāo used treachery,
I use loyalty.
Every time I act contrary to Cāo,
affairs can be accomplished.
Now, to lose faith and righteousness in the world for a small reason,
is what I will not do."
Tǒng said:
"In times of expedient change,
it certainly cannot be determined by one single principle.
Annexing the weak and swallowing the ignorant
was the business of the Five Hegemons;
to seize by force and guard with righteousness,
repaying them with righteousness;
after each affair is settled,
enfeoff them with great states—
how does this violate faith?
If we don't take it today,
it will ultimately benefit others."
Thereupon, Bèi had Guān Yǔ guard Jīngzhōu
and wanted to take Shǔ himself.
At that time, Sūn Quán sent an envoy to inform Bèi,
wanting to take Shǔ together,
saying:
"The rice rebel Zhāng Lǔ resides in Wángbā Hàn,
He served as Cáo Cāo's eyes and ears,
planning to seize Yìzhōu.
Liú Zhāng was unable to defend himself.
If Cáo Cāo obtains Shǔ,
then Jīngzhōu will be in danger.
Now, I want to first attack and seize Zhāng's territory,
then advance to attack Zhāng Lǔ,
coordinating the beginning and the end,
unifying Wú and Chǔ,
even if there were ten Cáos,
there would be nothing to worry about."
Someone suggested to Bèi that he should agree to Xǔ's request,
as Wú would ultimately be unable to cross Jīng to possess Shǔ,
and the land of Shǔ could be obtained.
The chief clerk Yīn Guān said:
"If we become Wú's vanguard,
and fail to conquer Shǔ,
we will instead be taken advantage of by Wú,
then the great cause will be lost!"
Bèi followed his advice,
and refused Quán's request, saying:
"The people of Yìzhōu are wealthy and the state is strong,
the land is rugged and treacherous,
although Liú Zhāng is weak,
he is sufficient to defend himself.
Zhāng Lǔ is deceitful,
and may not be completely loyal to Cāo.
If we suddenly deploy troops to Shǔhàn,
transporting supplies over ten thousand *lǐ*,
hoping to fight and conquer,
achieving victory in every undertaking,
even Wú Qǐ could not guarantee its success,
and Sūn Wǔ could not manage the affair well.
Now Cáo Cāo holds two-thirds of the empire,
and is about to water his horses in the Eastern Sea,
and review his troops in Wú and Kuài.
Yet allies are attacking each other for no reason,
giving Cāo an opportunity to mediate,
allowing the enemy to exploit their weakness,
this is not a good plan."
Quán understood Bèi's meaning,
and then stopped.
It happened that Liú Zhāng heard that Cáo Gōng was heading towards Hànzhōng to attack Zhāng Lǔ,
and was inwardly afraid.
His attendant Zhāng Sōng said to Zhāng:
"Cáo Gōng's army is strong,
unmatched in the world.
If he uses Zhāng Lǔ's resources,
to take the land of Shǔ,
who can resist him?
Liú Yùzhōu,
is your lordship's relative,
and Cáo Gōng's sworn enemy.
If you send him to attack Lǔ,
Lǔ will surely be defeated.
If Lǔ is defeated, then Yìzhōu will be strong,
"Even if Cáo Gōng 曹公 comes,
he will be unable to do anything."
Zhāng Zhāo 張昭 agreed with this,
and sent Fǎ Zhèng 法正 to welcome Xiān Zhǔ 先主 (Liú Bèi 劉備).
At that time, Huáng Quán 黃權 advised,
"The Left General has a reputation for being fierce,
if we treat him with the rank of a subordinate officer, it will not satisfy his ambition.
If we treat him as a guest, then one state cannot contain two rulers.
If the guest has the security of Mount Tài 泰山,
then the host will have the danger of a pile of eggs.
I wish you would close the border and wait for the Yellow River to clear."
At that time, Liú Bā 劉巴 also advised,
"Bèi 備 (Liú Bèi 劉備)
is an outstanding hero.
If he enters, he will surely take action,
he must not be allowed in."
After he entered,
Bā 巴 also said,
"If you have Bèi 備 attack Zhāng Lǔ 張魯,
it would be releasing a tiger into the mountains and forests."
Zhāng Zhāo 張昭 did not listen to any of them.
Xiān Zhǔ 先主 (Liú Bèi 劉備) met with Zhāng Zhāo 張昭 at Fú 涪.
After Zhāng Zhāo 張昭 returned to Chéngdū 成都,
Xiān Zhǔ 先主 (Liú Bèi 劉備) was to lead a northern expedition to Hànzhōng 漢中 for Zhāng Zhāo 張昭.
Tǒng 統 (Pang Tong 龐統) then persuaded Bèi 備 (Liú Bèi 劉備),
"Secretly select elite soldiers,
travel day and night without rest,
and directly attack Chéngdū 成都.
Zhāng (劉) Zhāng, being neither martial
nor having any prior preparations,
when a large army suddenly arrives,
can be settled in one move.
This is the best plan.
Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi,
famous generals of Zhāng (劉) Zhāng,
each rely on strong forces
and guard the passes.
It is said that they have repeatedly sent letters to Zhāng (劉) Zhāng, advising him:
"Order the general to return to Jīngzhōu.
Before the general arrives, send word
say there is an emergency in Jīngzhōu,
and that he wants to return to save it.
And make him prepare
and outwardly give the impression of returning."
These two men both admire the general's great reputation,
and are also pleased that the general is leaving.
They will certainly come to see the general with light cavalry.
Therefore, seize them
and take over their troops,
and then advance towards Chéngdū.
This is the middle plan.
Returning to Báidì
and repeatedly drawing in reinforcements from Jīngzhōu
to slowly plan to take it is
the worst plan.
If you hesitate and do not leave,
"It will bring about great trouble,
it cannot last long."
Xiān Zhǔ 先主 agreed with their plan.
Initially,
Zhāng Sōng 張松 and Fǎ Zhèng 法正 met with Bèi 備.
Bèi 備 received them with private intentions,
showing them utmost courtesy.
He then inquired about the weapons, treasuries, size of the army, and key strategic locations within Shǔ 蜀.
Sōng 松 and the others told him everything in detail.
They also drew a map,
marking the locations of mountains and rivers,
thus allowing him to fully understand the strengths and weaknesses of Yìzhōu 益州.
Xiān Zhǔ 先主 arrived north at Jiāméng 葭萌,
but did not immediately attack Lǔ 魯.
Instead, he generously bestowed favors to win over the people.
The following year,
Cáo Gōng 曹公 attacked Sūn Quán 孫權,
and Quán 權 called upon Xiān Zhǔ 先主 to come to his rescue.
Bèi 備 then requested ten thousand troops and supplies from Zhāng 璋,
intending to go east and rescue Quán 權.
Zhāng 璋 only granted four thousand troops,
and only half the requested supplies.
Thereupon, Bèi 備 stirred up his troops, saying:
"I am campaigning against a powerful enemy for the sake of Yìzhōu 益州,
my officers and soldiers are exhausted from hard work,
not even having time to rest peacefully.
Now, you hoard up great wealth in the treasury,
but are stingy with rewarding merit.
"Can we expect the scholars and officials to fight to the death?"
he asked.
Thereupon, he summoned Yáng Huái 楊懷, the supervisor of Zhāng Zhāo's 張昭 Baíshuǐ 白水 army,
and rebuked him for his lack of respect,
and executed him.
He then ordered Huáng Zhōng 黃忠 and others to lead the army towards Zhāng Zhāo.
Xiānzhǔ 先主 proceeded directly to the pass,

Chapter Forty: Defining Names
Chapter Forty: Defining Names
Principles understood in the heart
cannot be expressed without words;
things defined as existing
cannot be distinguished without names.
If words do not express intentions,
then there is no way to communicate;
if names do not distinguish things,
then discerning judgment is not apparent.
Investigating their origins,
tracing their causes,
things do not have naturally occurring names, nor do principles have necessarily fixed terms.
If you wish to discern their reality,
then differentiate their names;
if you wish to declare your intentions,
then establish their terms.
Therefore, they are called:
Dào (道), Dé (德), Rén (仁), Yì (義), Lǐ (禮), Zhì (智), Xìn (信).
Now, Dào (道) is
what people tread upon.
To dwell knowing what to do,
to act knowing where to go,
to manage affairs knowing what to use,
to move knowing when to stop,
This is called Dào.
It is also said:
Dào
refers to what people tread upon,
enabling all things to not lose what they depend on.
Dé refers
to what people obtain.
Enabling each person to obtain what they desire
is called Dé.
Rén is
love.
To bring about benefit and eliminate harm,
encompassing love without selfishness
is called Rén.
It is also said:
Rén is
what people cherish,
possessing a heart of compassion and empathy,
thereby fostering their growth and development.
Yì is
appropriateness.
To distinguish right from wrong,
establishing what is acceptable and unacceptable
is called Yì.
It is also said:
Yì is
what is appropriate for people,
rewarding good and punishing evil,
To establish merit and achieve deeds.
*Lǐ* (禮, ritual)
means to tread (*lǚ*, 履).
To advance and retreat with measure,
to have distinctions between honored and humble,
this is called *lǐ*.
It is also said:
*Lǐ* (禮, ritual)
is what people tread,
rising early and sleeping late,
in order to complete the order of a lord.
It is also said:
Establishing good and preventing evil,
this is called *lǐ*.
*Zhì* (智, wisdom)
is what people know.
To determine the true nature of gain and loss, right and wrong,
this is called *zhì*.
*Xìn* (信, trustworthiness)
is what people uphold.
Issuing commands and implementing orders
to unify the people's hearts,
this is called *xìn*.
To see the root and know the branch,
to grasp one and respond to ten thousand,
this is called *shù* (術, method).
It is also said:
To control the power of life and death,
To clear pathways blocked and congested,
to weigh the numbers of light and heavy,
to discuss the principles of gain and loss,
to ensure that the true situation, near and far, is certainly seen by the ruler—
this is called "shù" (術, technique).
The *Shuō Yuàn* (說苑, Garden of Stories) says:
"To follow orders to benefit the ruler
is called 'shùn' (順, obedience)."
It also says:
"When the ruler is upright and the subjects follow,
this is called 'shùn'."
"To follow orders that harm the ruler
is called 'yú' (諛, flattery)."
It also says:
"To not speak when one should speak

to not remonstrate when one should remonstrate

It also says:
"When the ruler is biased and the subjects follow,
this is called 'nì' (逆, opposition)."
"To oppose orders to benefit the ruler
is called 'zhōng' (忠, loyalty)."
It also says:
"To distribute wealth to people
is called 'huì' (惠, benevolence);
To teach others goodness,
is called loyalty.
Sūn Qīng

to harmonize the ruler with virtue and supplement him,
is secondary loyalty;
to remonstrate with right against wrong and anger him,
is the lowest loyalty."
To defy orders and harm the ruler,
is called rebellion.
It is also said:
"To reward without merit,

If the ruler has faults

This is called *fǔ* (輔, "assistance").
To resist the ruler's orders,
to oppose the ruler's actions,
